p.seg: 1.1 The First Debate on Fundamentals
In the sixth year of the Shǐyuán era,
an imperial edict ordered the Chéngxiàng and Yùshǐ to converse with the recommended Xiánliáng and Wénxué.
They inquired about the hardships among the people.
The Wénxué responded:
"We have heard that the way to govern people
lies in preventing the sources of excess and indulgence,
broadening the beginnings of virtue and morality,
restraining secondary profits while promoting benevolence and righteousness,
not leading them with gain.
Only then can education flourish,
and customs be transformed.
Now, the commanderies and states have monopolies on salt, iron, and liquor,
and the equal distribution system,
competing with the people for profit.
This dissipates the simplicity of honesty and sincerity,
fostering a culture of greed and baseness.
Hence, few among the common people engage in fundamental pursuits,
while many chase secondary gains.
When ornamentation flourishes, substance declines;
when secondary pursuits thrive, the fundamentals suffer.
If secondary pursuits are cultivated, the people become extravagant;
if fundamentals are cultivated, the people remain sincere.
When the people are sincere, wealth and resources are sufficient;
when the people are extravagant, hunger and cold arise.
We wish to abolish the salt, iron, and liquor monopolies,
along with the equal distribution system,
to advance the fundamentals and retreat from the secondary,
thus benefiting agriculture broadly—this is expedient."
The Dàfū said:
"The Xiōngnú have rebelled and refuse submission,
repeatedly raiding and plundering our borders.
Preparing defenses exhausts our central lands' soldiers,
yet without preparation, their invasions and thefts do not cease.
The late emperor pitied the long suffering of the border people,
distressed by their capture by the enemy,
so he built barriers and fortifications,
repaired beacon towers,
and stationed garrisons for defense.
Border expenditures were insufficient,
hence he initiated the salt and iron monopolies,
established the liquor monopoly,
and set up the equal distribution system,
to increase goods and grow wealth,
thereby aiding border expenses.
Now, those who propose to abolish these
would deplete the state treasury internally,
and leave us lacking resources for defense externally,
causing the soldiers guarding the frontiers and manning the walls to suffer hunger and cold.
How then shall we provide for them?
Abolishing these
is not expedient."
The Wénxué said:
"Confucius said:
'Those who rule states or families
worry not about scarcity but about inequality,
not about poverty but about instability.'
Thus, the Son of Heaven does not speak of abundance or lack,
the feudal lords do not speak of advantage or harm,
the Dàfū do not speak of gain or loss.
They nurture benevolence and righteousness to influence others,
broaden virtuous conduct to win them over,
so that those nearby draw close and those afar submit gladly.
Hence, those skilled in overcoming do not fight,
those skilled in fighting do not need armies,
those skilled with armies do not need formations.
Cultivating this in the court,
they repel the enemy and turn back troops.
When a true king practices benevolent governance,
he is invincible under heaven;
what need is there for such expenditures?"
The Dàfū said:
"The Xiōngnú are cunning and fierce,
arbitrarily and wantonly entering our borders,
invading and harming the central lands,
killing the commandery and county officials and the Shùofāng commandant,
greatly treacherous and unruly.
The time to punish and subdue them has long been due.
His Majesty bestows great kindness,
pitying that the people are not yet well-provided for,
and cannot bear to expose his officers and men to the wilds.
Even if we could don armor and take up arms,
with the resolve to face north and retaliate against the Xiōngnú,
to also propose abolishing salt, iron, and the equal distribution system,
disrupting border funds,
undermining military strategy,
showing no concern for the border—
this is not expedient in principle."
The Wénxué said:
"In ancient times,
they valued virtue and disdained the use of arms.
Confucius said:
'When distant people are not submissive,
cultivate civil virtue to attract them.
Once they have come,
make them content.'
Now, abandoning virtue and morality, you rely on weapons and armor,
raising armies to attack them,
stationing troops to guard against them,
exposing soldiers and armies,
to sustain a prolonged conflict,
endlessly transporting grain and supplies,
causing soldiers on the border to suffer hunger and cold abroad,
and the common people to toil in hardship at home.
Establishing salt and iron monopolies,
you first set up profit-seeking offices to supply this,
but this is not a long-term strategy.
Therefore, abolishing them is expedient."
The Dàfū said:
"Those who established states in ancient times
opened paths for both fundamentals and secondary pursuits,
facilitating the use of what is present and absent,
using markets to unify their needs,
attracting scholars and commoners,
gathering myriad goods,
so that farmers, merchants, and artisans each obtained what they desired,
trading before withdrawing.
The Yìjīng says:
'Make changes accessible,
so the people do not grow weary.'
Thus, if artisans do not produce,
farm tools become scarce;
if merchants do not trade,
precious goods are cut off.
If farm tools are scarce,
grain does not grow;
if precious goods are cut off,
wealth and resources are depleted.
Therefore, salt, iron, and the equal distribution system
serve to circulate stored wealth and balance urgency and need.
Abolishing them
is not expedient."
The Wénxué said:
"Guide the people with virtue, and they will return to honesty;
show the people profit,
and their customs become shallow.
When customs are shallow, they turn their backs on righteousness and chase profit;
chasing profit, the people mingle on the roads and in the markets.
Lǎozi said:
'A poor country may seem to have surplus.
Not because it has abundant wealth,
but because desires are many and the people are restless.'
Therefore, the true king honors the fundamentals and restrains the secondary,
using ritual and righteousness to guard against the people's desires,
and solidifying beans, grain, and goods as wealth.
In the market,
merchants should not circulate useless items,
artisans should not make useless tools.
Thus, merchants exist to relieve stagnation,
artisans to prepare tools and equipment—
these are not the fundamental tasks of governing a state."
The Dàfū said:
"Guǎnzǐ stated:
'A state may have fertile land in abundance, yet the people lack sufficient food
because tools and equipment are not完备.
It may have goods from mountains and seas, yet the people lack sufficient wealth
because merchants and artisans are not完备.'
The cinnabar, lacquer, plumes, and feathers of Lǒng and Shǔ,
the leather, horn, and ivory of Jīng and Yáng,
the nanmu, catalpa, bamboo, and arrows of Jiāngnán,
the fish, salt, felt, and furs of Yān and Qí,
the lacquer, silk, hemp, and ramie of Yǎn and Yù—
these are the means for nurturing life and providing for the dead,
awaiting merchants to circulate them,
and artisans to complete them.
Thus, the sages created boats and oars for use,
to traverse rivers and valleys,
harnessing oxen and driving horses,
to reach hills and lands;
penetrating distant and deep places,
thereby exchanging all goods and benefiting the people.
Hence, the late emperor established iron offices to supply farm implements,
and opened the equal distribution system to satisfy the people's wealth.
Salt, iron, and the equal distribution system
are what the myriad people rely on and draw from;
abolishing them
is not expedient."
The Wénxué said:
"A state may have fertile land in abundance, yet the people lack sufficient food
because commerce and craftsmanship flourish while the fundamental occupation languishes;
it may have goods from mountains and seas, yet the people lack sufficient wealth
because efforts are not directed toward the people's needs, and excessive finery abounds.
Thus, a river's source cannot fill a leaky cup,
mountains and seas cannot satisfy a ravine's greed.
Therefore, Pángēng lived in simplicity,
Shùn stored away gold,
and Emperor Gāozǔ forbade merchants from holding office—
all to curb the customs of greed and baseness,
and purify the atmosphere with utmost sincerity.
Even when suppressing markets and blocking profit's gate,
the people still do wrong;
how much more if those above pursue profit?
The Zhuàn says:
'If the feudal lords love profit, the Dàfū become base;
if the Dàfū are base, the scholars become greedy;
if the scholars are greedy, the commoners turn to theft.'
This is opening a gate to profit and building a ladder to crime for the people."
The high official said:
"In the past,
the various feudal lords and commanderies each transported their local products as tribute,
resulting in complicated and burdensome journeys,
with many goods being of poor quality,
sometimes not even covering the cost of transportation.
Therefore, commanderies established transportation offices to facilitate supply and transport,
making tribute from distant regions more convenient,
hence the term 'Equal Transportation.'
Establishing storage facilities in the capital,
to gather goods.
Buy when prices are low,
sell when prices are high.
Thus, the government does not lose out on actual value,
and merchants have no opportunity for speculative profits,
hence the term 'Balanced Standard.'
With the Balanced Standard, the people do not lose their livelihoods;
with Equal Transportation, the people share labor and leisure equally.
Therefore, the Balanced Standard and Equal Transportation
serve to stabilize all goods and benefit the common people,
not to open profit-seeking avenues and create ladders for people's crimes."
The literati said:
"In ancient times, when imposing taxes on the people,
they relied on what the people were skilled at,
not demanding what they were unskilled in.
Farmers contributed their harvests,
women presented their handiwork.
Now, ignoring what they have,
demanding what they lack.
The common people sell their goods cheaply,
to meet the demands from above.
Recently,
some commanderies ordered people to produce cloth and wadding,
officials arbitrarily created obstacles,
engaging in trade with them.
What the officials obtain,
is not just the silk from Qí and Ē,
or the cloth from Shǔ and Hàn,
but also what is produced by the common people.
Practicing deceit and selling at fixed prices,
farmers suffer doubly,
women workers are taxed again,
we see no equality in transportation.
When the government hastily issues orders,
monopolizing the market behind closed doors,
then all goods are bought up.
When all goods are bought up,
prices soar.
When prices soar,
merchants profit equally.
When officials engage in trade themselves,
it allows for corruption.
Powerful officials and wealthy merchants hoard goods waiting for emergencies,
unscrupulous merchants and corrupt officials buy cheap to sell high,
we see no balance in the standard.
The ancient Equal Transportation
was to equalize labor and leisure and facilitate tribute transport,
not for profit and trading in all goods."
1.2 "On Encouraging Agriculture, the Second"
The high official said:
"The king controls natural resources,
regulates passes and markets,
maintains standards and seasons,
governing the people through economic control.
In abundant harvest years,
store reserves to prepare for shortages;
in years of famine,
distribute currency and goods;
redirecting surplus to adjust for scarcity.
In the past, during Yǔ's floods and Tāng's droughts,
the people were destitute,
some lending to each other for food and clothing.
Yǔ used the metal from Lìshān,
Tāng the copper from Zhuāngshān,
casting coins to redeem his people,
and the world praised their benevolence.
Previously, when funds were insufficient,
some soldiers went without pay,
and Shāndōng suffered disasters,
with Qí and Zhào experiencing great famines,
relying on the reserves of Equal Transportation,
the stored grains in granaries,
soldiers were supported,
and famine victims were relieved.
Therefore, the goods from Equal Transportation,
the wealth in the treasuries,
are not for trading with the myriad people solely to supply the military,
but also to relieve the distressed and prepare for flood and drought disasters."
The literati said:
"In ancient times,
taxation was one-tenth,
marshes and weirs were accessible seasonally without restrictions,
all common people worked the southern fields without neglecting their duties.
Thus, three years of farming yielded a surplus for one year,
nine years of farming provided reserves for three years.
This is how Yǔ and Tāng prepared for floods and droughts and secured the people's livelihood.
If grasslands are not cleared,
fields not cultivated,
even controlling the wealth of mountains and seas,
and profiting from all secondary trades,
still cannot suffice.
Therefore, in ancient times, they emphasized labor and focused on fundamentals, planting abundantly,
personally farming timely to have ample food and clothing,
so even consecutive bad years did not trouble the people.
Thus, food and clothing are the people's foundation,
farming is their essential task.
When these two are well managed,
the state becomes prosperous and the people secure.
The Book of Songs says:
'All households are full,
women and children are at peace.'"
The high official said:
"The sage's way of governing the family is not limited to one treasure,
enriching the state not to one path.
In the past, Guǎn Zhòng achieved hegemony through strategic power,
while the Jì clan perished by overemphasizing fundamentals.
If managing a household and sustaining life must rely solely on farming,
then Shùn would not have molded pottery and Yī Yǐn would not have been a cook.
Therefore, those skilled in governing the state,
when the world devalues, they value highly,
when the world considers light, they consider heavy.
Trading non-essentials for essentials,
using the insubstantial to obtain the substantial.
Now, the wealth from mountains and marshes,
the stores of Equal Transportation,
are means to control economic balance and subdue the feudal lords.
The gold from Rǔ and Hàn,
the tribute of fine goods,
are used to lure foreign states and fish for the treasures of the Qiāng and others.
A single plain silk from the Central Plains
can obtain valuable goods worth much gold from the Xiōngnú,
depleting the enemy's resources.
Thus, mules, donkeys, and camels
enter the frontier in lines,
fine horses of various breeds,
all become our livestock,
sables, foxes, and raccoon dogs,
colorful felts and patterned carpets,
fill the inner treasury,
while jade discs, corals, and lapis lazuli
all become national treasures.
Thus, foreign goods flow inward,
and benefits do not leak out.
When exotic goods flow inward, state resources abound;
when benefits do not leak out, the people's needs are met.
The Book of Songs says:
'All households are full,
women and children are at peace.'"
The literati said:
"In ancient times,
merchants circulated goods without deceit,
craftsmen made sturdy products without falseness.
Thus, whether the gentleman farms or fishes,
the principle is the same.
Now merchants excel in fraud,
craftsmen in deceptive adornment,
harboring deceit without shame,
so the dishonest cheat and the honest become shallow.
In the past, Jié filled his palaces with female musicians,
adorned with embroidered garments,
so Yī Yǐn left to travel to Bó,
and the female musicians ultimately led to the state's ruin.
Now, the utility of mules and donkeys
cannot match the work of oxen and horses;
sables and felts
do not surpass the value of brocade and silk.
Beautiful jade and corals come from Kūnlún,
pearls, rhinoceros horns, and ivory from Guìlín,
these places are over ten thousand lǐ from Hàn.
Considering the effort of farming,
and the cost of resources,
a single item sells for a hundred times its price,
one handful equals ten thousand zhōng of grain.
When those above cherish rare curiosities,
extravagance spreads below;
valuing distant goods
causes wealth to flow outward.
Thus, the king does not treasure useless things to economize for the people,
nor love exotic goods to enrich the state.
Therefore, the way to govern the people
lies in frugality and emphasizing fundamentals,
dividing land and implementing the well-field system, that is all."
The high official said:
"From the capital in all directions,
crossing mountains and rivers,
passing through commanderies and states,
all prosperous major cities,
have streets connecting everywhere,
where merchants gather,
and all goods are traded.
Thus, the sage follows the timing of heaven,
the wise utilize the resources of the earth,
the superior man draws from others,
the average man labors physically.
Cháng Jǔ and Jié Nì
had no accumulation of a hundred gold,
while followers of Zhí and Jué
lacked the wealth of Yī Dùn;
in Yuān, Zhōu, Qí, and Lǔ,
merchants travel throughout the world."
Thus the wealth of merchants,
some accumulating ten thousand in gold,
is the result of pursuing profit and multiplying surplus.
Why must enriching the state rely on fundamental agriculture?
Why must satisfying the people depend on the well-field system?"
The Literati said:
"When the great flood overwhelmed the heavens,
there was Yǔ's achievement;
when the Yellow River overflowed,
there was the success of the Xuānfáng project.
When King Zhòu of Shāng was tyrannical,
there was the stratagem at Mèngjīn.
When the world is troubled and disturbed,
there emerges wealth from surplus multiplication.
In the supreme governance of high antiquity,
the people were simple and valued fundamentals, content and with few desires.
At that time,
roads were rarely traveled,
and markets grew wild grass.
Thus, those who did not farm vigorously had nothing to fill their emptiness,
those who did not weave diligently had nothing to cover their bodies.
Even with the essentials of gathering and meeting,
or the methods of Táo and Wǎn,
there was no place to apply their cleverness.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been one who gained reward without giving,
or achieved merit without labor,
this has never existed."
1.3 "On Circulation and Abundance - Third"
The Grand Master said:
"Zhuō and Jì of Yān,
Hándān of Zhào,
Wēn and Zhǐ of Wèi,
Xíngyáng of Hán,
Línzī of Qí,
Wǎn and Chén of Chǔ,
Yángzhái of Zhèng,
and Èrzhōu of Sānchuān,
wealthiest within the seas,
all are famous cities under heaven,
not because they were helped by farming their fields and tilling their land,
but because they reside at the hub of five routes,
straddling the paths of streets and avenues.
Thus where goods are abundant, the people prosper;
where dwellings are near markets, families grow rich.
Wealth lies in methods and calculations,
not in bodily toil;
profit lies in advantageous location,
not in strenuous farming."
The Literati said:
"Jīng and Yáng have the bounty of Guìlín to the south,
and the profits of rivers and lakes within;
to the left, the gold of Língyáng,
to the right, the timber of Shǔ and Hàn.
They fell trees to plant grains,
burn weeds to sow millet,
farm with fire and weed with water,
the land vast and rich in materials;
yet the people are lazy and live idly,
fond of fine clothes and sweet food,
even in thatched huts and grass shelters,
singing songs and playing lutes,
daily needs met but monthly supplies exhausted,
singing in morning but lamenting at dusk.
Zhào and Zhōngshān are girdled by the great river,
gathering spiritually connected thoroughfares from all directions,
standing at the world's crossroads,
merchants crisscrossing the roads,
lords meeting on the paths;
yet the people indulge in loving trivialities,
extravagant and not attending to fundamentals,
fields not tended,
men and women adorning themselves ostentatiously,
homes without even pecks and pints,
yet lutes sounding within.
Thus the people of Chǔ and Zhào,
are equally poor with few rich.
Sòng, Wèi, Hán, and Liáng,
devoted to fundamental farming,
registered households and uniform people,
all have households prosperous and people provided.
Thus profit lies in self-restraint,
not in advantageous location or street corners;
wealth lies in frugal effort and timely action,
not in annual officials or feather-gathering."
The Grand Master said:
"The Five Phases:
the east belongs to wood,
yet Dān and Zhāng have mountains of metal and copper;
the south belongs to fire,
yet Jiāozhǐ has great sea rivers;
the west belongs to metal,
yet Shǔ and Lǒng have forests of famous timber;
the north belongs to water,
yet Yōudū has lands of accumulated sand.
This is how Heaven and Earth balance having and not having, and connect all things.
Now the bamboo of Wú and Yuè,
the timber of Suí and Táng,
cannot all be used,
yet in Cáo, Wèi, Liáng, and Sòng,
they use crude coffins and abandon corpses;
the fish of rivers and lakes,
the blowfish of Lái and Huáng,
cannot all be eaten,
yet in Zōu, Lǔ, Zhōu, and Hán,
they eat wild herbs and plain vegetables.
Heaven and Earth's benefits are not insufficient,
and mountains and seas' goods are not unrich;
yet the common people are destitute,
resources and supplies insufficient,
abundance and scarcity unbalanced,
and the world's wealth not distributed."
The Literati said:
"In ancient times,
they did not carve the wooden rafters,
nor trim the thatched roofs,
wore cloth and coarse garments,
ate from earthen bowls,
cast metal for plows,
kneaded clay for vessels,
artisans did not create exotic wonders,
the world did not treasure what could not be worn or eaten,
each content in their dwelling,
happy with their customs,
satisfied with their food,
comfortable with their utensils.
Thus goods from distant places were not exchanged,
and jade from Kūnlún Mountains did not arrive.
Now common customs are corrupted and compete in extravagance,
women pursue extreme finery,
artisans ultimate skill,
carving simplicity and valuing rare curiosities,
drilling mountain rocks seeking gold and silver,
diving deep abysses seeking pearls and gems,
setting traps seeking rhinoceros and ivory,
spreading nets seeking kingfisher feathers,
seeking goods of Mán and Mò tribes to dazzle the Central States,
transporting goods from Qióng and Zuó,
bringing them to the Eastern Sea,
exchanging wealth across ten thousand miles,
wasting days and expending labor,
with no benefit for practical use.
Therefore, common men and women,
toil until exhausted and strength spent,
yet have insufficient clothing and food.
Thus the kingly way prohibits excessive profits,
and curbs wasteful spending.
When excessive profits are prohibited, people return to fundamentals;
when wasteful spending is curbed, the people's needs are met.
Thus in life none lack resources,
in death none have abandoned corpses."
The Grand Master said:
"In ancient times,
palaces and rooms had their measures,
carriages and robes according to merit;
uncarved rafters and thatched roofs,
were not the system of former kings.
The nobleman moderates extravagance and criticizes excessive frugality,
for frugality leads to rigidity.
Formerly Minister Shū'áo of Chǔ,
his wife wore no silk,
his horses ate no grain.
Confucius said:
'This cannot be,
great frugality becomes extreme baseness.'
This is why the 'Cricket' was composed.
Guǎnzǐ said:
'If palaces are not adorned,
then timber cannot be fully used;
if kitchens are not filled,
then birds and beasts do not decrease their lifespan.
Without secondary profits,
then fundamental occupations have no output;
without embroidered patterns,
then women's work cannot be applied.'
Thus artisans, merchants, and craftsmen,
are for the use of the state,
and preparation of tools and equipment.
This has existed since ancient times,
not only here.
Xián Gāo sold oxen in Zhōu,
the five-ram-skinned man hired carts to enter Qín,
Master Gōngshū used compass and square,
Ōu Yě melted and cast.
The Analects say:
'Various artisans dwell in their workshops,
to accomplish their tasks.'
Agriculture and trade exchange,
to benefit fundamentals and secondary.
Dwelling in mountains and marshes,
in rough land with overgrowth,
goods and materials circulate,
having means to balance them."
Thus, those with abundance do not solely have surplus,
and those with scarcity do not solely suffer famine.
If each remains in their place,
consuming their own food,
then oranges and pomelos would not be sold,
the salt from Qǘlǔ would not be exported,
felt and woolen fabrics would not be marketed,
and the wealth of Wú and Táng would not be utilized. "
The Literati said:
"Mèngzǐ stated:
'Do not interfere with the farming seasons,
and grain will be more than enough to eat.
Raise silkworms and hemp in their proper times,
and cloth and silk will be more than enough for clothing.
Enter the forests with axes only in season,
and timber will be more than enough for use.
Hunt and fish in their appropriate times,
and fish and meat will be more than enough to eat.'
But if instead, palaces and rooms are adorned,
terraces and pavilions increased,
carpenters chop large pieces into small,
turn round shapes into square,
creating cloud patterns above,
and mountain forests below,
then timber will not suffice for use.
When men abandon fundamental work for trivial pursuits,
even carving and engraving,
imitating birds and beasts,
exhausting forms and exploring variations,
then grain will not be enough to eat.
When women adorn with fine details and work on minutiae,
creating intricate patterns,
pushing skills and craftsmanship to the limit,
then silk and cloth will not be enough for clothing.
When cooks slaughter pregnant animals and eggs,
fry, roast, and mix flavors,
exhausting all five tastes,
then fish and meat will not be enough to eat.
In the present age,
the worry is not that birds and beasts are not reduced,
or that timber is insufficient,
but that extravagance and waste know no bounds;
the worry is not the lack of felt, woolen fabrics, oranges, or pomelos,
but the absence of humble huts and chaff for the poor. "
1.4 On Currency Control, Fourth
The Grand Master said:
"When currency circulates and goods are exchanged,
yet the people's needs are not met,
it is because goods are monopolized.
Calculating the root and measuring the stores,
if there are people starving,
it is because grain is hoarded.
The wise achieve the work of a hundred men,
while the foolish cannot even recover their capital.
If the ruler does not regulate,
the wealth among the people can differ ten-thousandfold.
This is why some have reserves lasting a hundred years,
while others are not satisfied with chaff and husks.
If the people become too wealthy,
they cannot be directed by official salaries;
if too powerful,
they cannot be intimidated by punishments.
Only by dispersing accumulations and equalizing benefits can disparities be balanced.
Therefore, the ruler accumulates food,
controls its use,
restrains surplus,
adjusts shortages,
prohibits excessive profits,
blocks the paths of greed,
and only then can every household be well-supplied and every person content. "
The Literati said:
"In ancient times,
virtue was esteemed and profit despised,
righteousness valued and wealth lightly regarded.
During the era of the Three Sovereigns,
they alternated between prosperity and decline.
In decline, they were supported;
when faltering, they were stabilized.
Thus, Xià emphasized loyalty, Yīn reverence, and Zhōu culture,
with education in schools,
rituals of respect and deference,
brilliantly observable.
But later,
when rites and righteousness slackened and collapsed,
customs died out,
even gentlemen living on official salaries
turned from righteousness to compete for wealth,
the strong and weak devouring each other,
fiercely overthrowing one another.
This is why some have reserves for a hundred years,
while others have nothing to fill their stomachs or cover their bodies.
In ancient times, officials did not farm,
farmers did not fish,
gatekeepers and night watchmen
all had fixed duties,
not allowed to monopolize benefits or exhaust resources.
Thus,
the foolish and the wise achieved equally,
without overthrowing each other.
The Book of Songs says:
'There, a leftover sheaf;
here, a lingering ear of grain;
these are for the benefit of the widow.'
This means not exhausting all resources. "
The Grand Master said:
"Tāng and Wén succeeded in times of decline,
Hàn rose by addressing flaws.
Shifting from substance to refinement,
was not a careless change of norms.
When customs are flawed, laws are altered,
not necessarily to change the old,
but to correct errors and support the weak.
Thus, teachings change with customs,
and flaws shift with the times.
The Xià used black shells,
the Zhōu used purple stones,
later generations used metal coins, knives, and cloth.
Things reach an extreme and then decline,
such is the cycle of beginnings and ends.
Therefore, if mountains and marshes are untaxed,
ruler and minister share benefits alike;
if coinage is unrestricted,
deceit and honesty operate together.
When ministers grow rich, they become extravagant;
when inferiors monopolize profits, they overthrow each other. "
The Literati said:
"In ancient times,
markets operated without coinage,
each exchanging what they had for what they lacked,
simply carrying cloth to trade for silk.
Later, turtle shells, cowries, and metal coins emerged,
used in transactions.
As currency changed frequently, the people grew more deceitful.
To counter deceit, use substance;
to prevent loss, use ritual.
Tāng and Wén succeeded in decline,
reforming laws and transforming customs,
thus the ways of Yīn and Zhōu flourished.
At the beginning of Hàn, facing flaws,
without making changes,
hoarding profits and altering currency,
hoping to return to fundamentals,
is like using frying to stop burning,
or fire to halt boiling.
If those above value ritual, the people discreetly cultivate themselves;
if those above crave goods, the subordinates die for profit. "
The Grand Master said:
"During Emperor Wén's time,
the people were allowed to mint coins, smelt iron, and boil salt.
King of Wú monopolized the coastal marshes,
Dèng Tōng controlled the Western Hills.
Crafty men from Shāndōng
all gathered in the state of Wú,
while Qín, Yōng, Hàn, and Shǔ followed Dèng's lead.
Wú and Dèng's coins spread everywhere,
hence the ban on private minting.
Once restrictive laws were established,
deceit and falsification ceased;
with deceit ended,
the people no longer hoped for ill-gotten gains
and each attended to their duties;
why would they not return to fundamentals?
Thus, with unification,
the people are not divided;
with currency controlled from above,
those below have no doubts. "
The Literati said:
"In the past,
with diverse currencies and flowing wealth, the people were content.
Later,
gradually abandoning old coins,
switching to white metal, turtle, and dragon coins,
the people often counterfeited the new currency.
Frequent changes in currency increased public suspicion.
Then, all other coins were abolished,
and only the Shuǐhéng's three officials were appointed to mint.
Officials and craftsmen seized profits,
some not meeting standards,
hence variations in thickness and weight.
Farmers, unfamiliar with them,
compared them to goods,
trusting the old, suspecting the new,
unable to distinguish genuine from fake.
Merchants traded good for bad,
exchanging half for double.
Buying, they lost value;
selling, they lost fairness,
and suspicions grew even stronger.
Though laws against counterfeiting metal coins exist,
the quality of coins has not improved from before.
Selecting coins causes goods to stagnate,
and the users suffer especially.
The Spring and Autumn Annals say:
'If calculations do not extend to the Mán and Yí, they will not work.'
Therefore, the true king does not block coastal marshes externally to facilitate the people's use,
nor restrict coinage internally to enable the people's transactions. "
1.5 On Banning Private Production, Fifth
The Grandee said:
"If a family possesses a precious vessel,
they would still store it in a box,
let alone the mountains and seas under the sovereign's rule?
Places of power and profit
are inevitably located in deep mountains and remote marshes,
and only the powerful can exploit their benefits.
In the past,
before salt and iron were monopolized,
commoners like Qú Bǐng,
and rulers like the King of Wú,
were all part of the initial discussions on salt and iron.
The King of Wú monopolized the riches of the mountains and marshes,
levied light taxes on his people,
relieved the poor and needy,
thus building his personal authority.
As personal authority accumulated, rebellious intentions arose.
If the source is not cut off early and only the symptoms are worried about,
it is like breaching the Lǚliáng dam,
where the torrent
would inevitably cause great damage.
Tai Gōng said:
'If one family harms a hundred families,
a hundred families harm the feudal lords,
and feudal lords harm the empire,
the king's laws must prohibit it.'
Now, if the people are allowed free access to power and profit,
and salt and iron monopolies are abolished to empower the violent and strong,
indulging their greed,
then various evils will gather,
private factions will form cliques,
and the powerful will become increasingly uncontrollable,
leading to the formation of monopolistic and treacherous practices."
The Literati said:
"The common people store their wealth at home,
feudal lords store it within their states,
and the Son of Heaven stores it throughout the land.
Thus, the common people use walls as their storage,
while the Son of Heaven uses the four seas as his box.
When the Son of Heaven visits a feudal lord,
he ascends from the eastern steps,
the feudal lord surrenders the keys,
holding the register to listen to commands,
showing none dare claim ownership.
Therefore, the true king does not hoard wealth,
but stores it among the people,
avoiding fleeting profits,
and focusing on righteousness for the people;
when righteousness and propriety are established,
the people will be transformed by their superiors.
If this is so, even if Tāng or Wǔ were alive today,
they would have no cause for concern.
How could any treachery arise
from the affairs of artisans and merchants,
or the responsibilities of Ōu Yě?
The Three Huán families controlled Lǔ,
and the Six Ministers partitioned Jìn,
not because of salt and iron.
Thus, deep power and profit
lie not in the mountains and seas,
but in the court;
one family harming a hundred families
occurs within the screen wall,
not in Qú Bǐng."
The Grandee said:
"With restrictions on mountains and seas,
the people do not compete excessively;
with fixed prices for high and low,
the people have no doubts.
The government sets standards and measures,
allowing people to follow their desires;
even a child going to the market
cannot be cheated.
Now if these are abolished,
the powerful will monopolize their use and profits.
Decisions made in alleys and markets,
prices determined by mere words,
with no constant value for high or low,
sitting idly while the people grow powerful,
thus nurturing the strong and suppressing the weak, storing wealth with bandits.
When the strong are nurtured and the weak suppressed,
the common people diminish;
like weeds flourishing and harming the five grains.
One family harming a hundred families
does not lie in Qú Bǐng—
how can this be?"
The Literati said:
"Mountains and seas
are treasure troves of wealth and resources.
Iron tools
are the lifeblood of farmers.
When the lifeblood is used,
enemies are eliminated,
enemies eliminated,
fields are opened up,
fields opened up and the five grains ripen.
When treasure troves are accessible,
the people are provided for and resources supplied,
resources supplied then the state grows rich.
When the state is rich and taught with propriety,
then conduct on the road shows courtesy,
artisans and merchants do not interfere with each other,
people treat each other with honesty and simplicity,
and none seek profit from others.
Qín, Chǔ, Yān, and Qí
have different soil strengths,
varying conditions of hardness and softness,
uses for large and small,
appropriate straight and curved shapes,
diverse customs and practices,
each with its own suitability.
If the government monopolizes and standardizes them,
iron tools lose their appropriateness,
and farmers lose their convenience.
When tools are inconvenient,
farmers toil in the fields yet fail to clear the wilds.
If the wilds are not cleared,
the people suffer hardship and want.
Thus, places of salt smelting
mostly rely on mountains and rivers,
close to iron and charcoal,
all situated remotely with harsh labor.
Conscripts in the commanderies on rotation duty,
mostly cannot endure it,
and hire substitutes.
Some counties impose iron levies by household,
and undervalue the standard price.
Respectable families, by order of the route,
hire transport for salt and iron, causing trouble and expense,
bringing suffering and hardship to the people.
I humbly observe that one official's harm extends a thousand lǐ,
yet I do not see it in Qú Bǐng."
1.6 Restoring Antiquity (Chapter 6)
The Grandee said:
"Former Commandant of Shanshui, Péng Zǔ, upon returning to court,
stated:
'The ordinances on salt and iron,
the ordinances are very clear.
Conscripts and laborers are clothed and fed by the government,
casting iron tools,
providing for many uses,
without burdening the people.
Yet some officials are incompetent,
prohibitions are not enforced,
hence the people suffer annoyance and hardship.'
The intent of the ordinances is to unify salt and iron,
not solely for profit,
but to establish fundamentals and suppress non-essentials,
disband factions,
prohibit extravagance,
and block the path to monopoly.
In ancient times,
famous mountains and great marshes were not enfeoffed,
to prevent subordinates from monopolizing profits.
The profits from mountains and seas,
the stores of vast marshes,
the treasures of heaven and earth,
should all belong to the Shàofǔ;
yet His Majesty shows no selfishness,
assigning them to the Dàsīnóng,
to assist the common people.
Drifters and opportunists,
eager to monopolize the goods of mountains and seas,
to build their wealth,
exploiting the common people,
thus many obstruct affairs and criticize.
Iron tools and weapons,
are of great use to the empire,
and not something the masses should engage in.
In the past,
powerful and great families,
gained control over the profits of mountains and seas,
mined iron ore and smelted,
boiled seawater for salt.
One family gathering followers,
sometimes over a thousand people,
mostly recruiting displaced and wandering people.
They left their hometowns far behind,
abandoned their ancestral graves,
attached themselves to great families,
gathering in deep mountains and remote marshes,
engaging in deceitful trades,
wielding the power of factions,
their readiness to do wrong was great indeed!
Now,
broadening the paths for recruiting the worthy,
selecting and training governors and commandants,
we need not abolish salt
and iron to pacify the people."
The Literati said:
"A skilled carpenter can erect a structure that will not collapse,
a good foundation can reach great heights without
toppling.
Yī Yǐn used the ways of Yáo and Shùn as the foundation for the Yīn state,
so his descendants inherited the throne,
lasting for a hundred generations without end.
Shāng Yāng used severe punishments and harsh laws as the foundation for the Qín state,
thus it was usurped by the second generation.
Since the penalties were already severe,
he also created laws of collective responsibility,
invented defamation charges,
increased corporal punishments,
leaving the common people trembling with fear,
not knowing where to place their hands and feet.
Taxes were already numerous and frequent,
yet externally he prohibited access to mountains and marshes,
internally he established profits a hundredfold,
leaving the people no avenue to voice their opinions.
Exalting profit while neglecting righteousness,
valuing force while崇尚 merit,
it's not that they didn't expand territory and acquire land,
but it was like a person suffering from water retention,
where adding water only deepens the illness,
knowing that he opened the path for Qín to become an empire,
but not realizing he was leading Qín to the way of destruction.
A crooked chisel hole,
even Gōngshū Zǐ couldn't fit a proper tenon into it.
A basket-of-earth foundation,
even the finest craftsman cannot build it high.
It's like autumn tumbleweed touched by frost,
when struck by wind it scatters and falls,
even if there were ten Zǐ Chǎn,
what could be done?
Thus Biǎn Què could not put flesh on white bones,
Bī Zǐ and Jī Zǐ could not save a perishing state."
The Grand Master said:
"Speaking is not difficult,
acting is what's difficult.
Therefore the worthy base themselves on reality and demonstrate achievements,
not merely presenting empty rhetoric.
In the past, Lord Shāng understood the methods of opening and blocking,
wielded the power of his time,
created benefits and accomplished deeds for Qín,
thus they conquered in battle and captured territories,
annexing nearby states and destroying distant ones,
overrunning Yān and Zhào,
overwhelming Qí and Chǔ,
until the feudal lords straightened their garments,
facing westward to follow his influence.
Afterwards,
Méng Tián campaigned against the Hú
and expanded territory by a thousand lǐ,
crossing north of the Yellow River,
as easily as breaking rotten wood.
Why was this?
Because of Lord Shāng's lasting strategies,
well-prepared and long-cultivated.
Thus every action brought benefit,
every move achieved merit.
The accumulation of resources and planning,
is how a state becomes strong.
Therefore, to relax and return these to the people,
is to fail to see grand strategy and comprehend the great Way."
The Literati said:
"Shāng Yāng's methods of opening and blocking,
were not ineffective;
Méng Tián's repelling the Hú a thousand lǐ,
was not without merit;
their might shaking the world,
was not without strength;
the feudal lords following westward with the wind,
was not without compliance;
yet all these were reasons for Qín's destruction.
Shāng Yāng endangered the Qín state through cunning schemes,
Méng Tián destroyed the Qín empire while gaining a thousand lǐ.
These two men,
knew benefit but not harm,
knew advancement but not retreat,
thus indeed they died and their followers were defeated.
This is what's called the intelligence of the short-sighted,
the planning of fools,
how could this be the great Way?
Therefore it is said:
'Petty men agree at first but oppose later,
though they may ride high initially,
they must end in tears of blood.'
This refers to them."
The Grand Master said:
"Virtuous and good people,
are envied by the deformed;
worthy and wise scholars,
are hated by the worthless.
Thus Shàngguān Dàfū slandered Qū Yuán before Qǐng Xiāng,
and Gōngbó Liáo accused Zǐ Lù before Jìsūn.
Now Lord Shāng rose from common cloth,
came from Wèi to Qín,
within a year became its minister,
reformed laws and clarified teachings,
and the Qín people were greatly well-governed.
Thus when troops moved, territory was cut;
when troops rested, the state grew rich.
Duke Xiào was greatly pleased,
enfeoffed him with the lands of Yú and Shāng, five hundred lǐ square,
achievements like mountains,
name passed down to later ages.
Ordinary people cannot accomplish this,
hence they jointly envy his ability and find fault with his achievements."
The Literati said:
"The noble man advances necessarily by the Way,
retreats without losing righteousness,
is exalted but not arrogant,
toils but does not boast,
holds high position but acts humbly,
has great achievements but follows principle;
thus commoners do not resent his ability,
and the age does not envy his work.
Now Shāng Yāng abandoned the Way and used cunning,
discarded virtue and relied on force,
imposed harsh laws and severe punishments,
made cruelty and violence customary,
betrayed old friends to claim merit,
punished the royal clan to establish authority,
showed no kindness to the common people,
kept no faith with the feudal lords,
individuals harbored grievances against him,
families regarded him as an enemy,
though he achieved merit and received enfeoffment,
it was like eating poisoned meat - pleased with fullness but suffering the consequences.
Sū Qín organized vertical and horizontal alliances,
governed and managed six states,
his achievements were not small;
Jié and Zhòu are mentioned together with Yáo and Shùn,
and remain known to this day,
their names are not short-lived;
yet what is wrong is not worthy of honor.
Thus deeds should not be indiscriminately multiplied,
names should not be indiscriminately transmitted."
The Grand Master said:
"White silk cannot keep itself separate from black ink,
worthies and sages cannot preserve themselves in chaotic times.
Thus Jīzǐ was imprisoned,
Bǐgān was executed.
Wǔ Yuán assisted Hé Lǘ to hegemony,
but Fū Chāi was unprincipled,
exiled him and had him killed.
Yuè Yì proved his merit to Yān Zhāo,
but was suspected by King Huì.
Ministers exhaust their integrity to follow their name,
yet encounter rulers who do not employ them.
Minister Wén Zhǒng assisted the King of Yuè,
devised deep strategies for him,
finally captured powerful Wú,
occupied the Eastern Yi,
yet in the end was given the sword Zhǔ Lòu and died.
Arrogant rulers betray kindness and virtue,
listen to rumors,
and do not consider their ministers' achievements,
how could this be the ministers' own fault?"
The Literati said:
"Bǐgān had his heart cut out,
Zǐ Xū was stuffed in a leather sack,
not because they lightly offended their lords to endanger themselves,
or forcefully remonstrated to seek fame.
Their pained loyalty,
stirred within their hearts,
made them forget that disaster would erupt externally,
their will was to correct their lord and save the people,
thus they died without resentment.
The noble man can act rightly but cannot ward off wrong,
though he may suffer punishment and execution,
it is not his crime.
Thus when Bǐgān died, the Yīn people resented it,
when Zǐ Xū died, the Wú people hated it.
Now Qín's resentment and hatred of Shāng Yāng's laws,
exceeded personal enmity,
thus when Duke Xiào died,
the whole state attacked him,
with nowhere to flee east, west, north, or south,
he looked to heaven and sighed:
'Alas,
the failings of governance
have reached this extreme!'
Finally he was torn apart by chariots and his clan exterminated,
becoming the laughingstock of the world.
This man destroyed himself,
no one else destroyed him."
2.2 《Cháo Cuò Eighth》
The Grand Master said:
"The method of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
is that toward one's lord and parents there should be no plotting,
and plotters must be executed.
Thus no minister's crime is heavier than regicide,
no son's crime is heavier than patricide.
In the past,
the kings of Huáinán and Héngshān cultivated literature and arts,
gathering wandering scholars from all directions.
Confucians and Mohists from Shāndōng all converged between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
holding discussions and collective debates,
producing several dozen books.
Yet they ultimately turned their backs on righteousness and refused submission,
instigating plots of rebellion,
leading to the execution of their entire clans.
Cháo Cuò altered laws and changed traditions,
disregarding established systems,
pressuring the imperial clan,
encroaching upon and reducing the territories of the feudal lords.
The vassal lords did not submit,
and blood relatives grew distant.
Wú and Chǔ accumulated grievances,
resulting in Cháo Cuò's execution at the eastern market,
to appease the soldiers of the three armies and apologize to the feudal lords.
So, who was it that caused his death?"
The literati replied:
"Confucius would not drink from the stream of Dào Quán,
and Zēng Zǐ would not enter the lane of Shèng Mǔ.
If the names alone were repulsive,
how much more so for those who are disloyal and unfilial?
Thus, Confucius bathed and then attended court,
to report to Duke Āi.
Chén Wénzǐ had ten chariots with horses,
yet abandoned them and left.
The 'Zhuàn' says:
'A gentleman may be honored or humiliated,
punished or executed,
but cannot be made to cause disorder.'
As for those who adorn their appearance outwardly but lack substance within,
reciting texts with their mouths but not following the path in their actions,
they are thieves,
and thus associated with thieves, not tolerated in the realm of gentlemen.
The 'Spring and Autumn Annals' does not use the few to offend the many;
the principle of punishment and eradication has its limits,
not combining resentment and hatred.
Therefore, when Shun executed,
he executed Gǔn;
when he promoted,
he promoted Yǔ.
If, due to a flaw in the jade,
one discards the uncarved gem,
or because of one person's crime,
condemns the multitude,
then the world would have no precious treasures or trustworthy scholars.
Cháo Cuò argued that the feudal lords' lands were too vast,
and wealth led to arrogance and extravagance,
while urgency prompted alliances.
Thus, citing Wú's faults, he reduced its territory in Kuàijī,
and citing Chǔ's crimes, he seized its land in Dōnghǎi,
all to balance the light and heavy,
divide their power,
and plan for ten thousand generations.
Xián Gāo deceived Qín but was trusted by Zhèng,
while Cháo Cuò was loyal to Hàn but became an enemy to the feudal lords.
Ministers each die for their lords,
serving their states,
which is why Jiě Yáng was esteemed by Jìn but slighted by Jīng."
2.3 "Critique of Power, Ninth"
The Grand Master said:
"Now, the Jù Qū of Yuè,
the Yún Mèng of Chǔ,
the Jù Yě of Sòng,
the Mèng Zhū of Qí,
are the wealth of the state and the resources for hegemony.
If the ruler controls and guards them, the state is strong;
if not restricted, it perishes.
Qí gave its core resources to others,
allowing powerful families to grow unchecked,
branches becoming too large and breaking the trunk,
monopolizing the riches of the vast sea and controlling the profits of fish and salt.
Their influence was enough to command the masses,
their generosity sufficient to care for subordinates,
so Qí internally split and externally submitted.
Power shifted to the ministers,
government fell to the families,
the ducal house declined while the Tián clan grew strong,
with nearly three thousand chariots transporting goods by sea,
losing the root and making the branches irreparable.
Now, the resources of mountains, rivers, and seas
are not limited to Yún Mèng and Mèng Zhū.
Casting and boiling salt
inevitably occur in deep, secluded valleys,
where people rarely go.
Cunning individuals communicate in these remote areas,
fearing the rise of great treachery.
Riding on profits, they grow arrogant and excessive,
corrupting simplicity and fostering falseness,
so few people value the fundamental.
The Salt and Iron Ministers of the Grand Agriculturist, Xiányáng and Kǒng Jǐn, petitioned:
'We wish to recruit people to bear their own costs,
using government equipment,
to boil salt for use,
to block the path of falseness and excess.'
From this perspective:
the decrees aim to subtly prohibit,
and the officials' considerations are far-sighted."
The literati replied:
"The officials' considerations are far-sighted,
but the powerful families' profits are immediate;
the decrees aim to subtly prohibit,
yet the paths of extravagance and presumption are evident.
Since the establishment of profit and harm,
and the rise of the three industries,
the households of the noble
move like clouds on the roads,
chariots clashing in the streets,
usurping public law,
asserting private interests,
spanning mountains and marshes,
monopolizing official markets,
not just the vast sea's fish and salt;
holding the state's authority,
exercising it across the land,
not just the power of Tián Cháng or the authority of petty ministers;
their might heavier than the six ministers,
wealth surpassing Táo
and Wèi, carriages and attire presuming those of kings and dukes,
palaces exceeding regulations,
merging and acquiring rows of residences,
isolating neighborhoods,
with interconnected elevated passages,
sufficient for leisurely tours,
digging ponds and winding paths,
enough for galloping,
fishing by the deep waters,
releasing hounds to chase rabbits,
boasting strength like fierce jackals,
playing kickball and cockfighting,
Zhōngshān's plain-clad girls playing melodies in the halls,
drums and Bā Yú music resounding below,
women clad in sheer silks,
maids and concubines trailing fine linens,
sons and grandsons with rows of chariots and riders,
hunting in and out,
skilled with bows and arrows.
Thus, farmers set aside plows and do not toil,
the people dissolve like ice and grow slack.
Why?
They do it themselves, yet others take it,
extravagance and presumption imitate each other,
rising without cease,
this is why the people become more false and rarely return to the fundamentals."
The Grand Master said:
"High officials have generous salaries,
beautiful roots have lush branches.
Thus, King Wén's virtue led to his descendants being enfeoffed,
and the Duke of Zhōu's ministership made Bó Qín rich.
Wide waters breed large fish,
honored fathers have noble sons.
The 'Zhuàn' says:
'Rivers and seas moisten a thousand li.'
Great virtue reaches the four seas,
how much more one's wife and children?
So, the husband is honored at court,
the wife honored at home,
wealth is called excessive beauty,
the way of antiquity.
Mencius said:
'A prince is like others,
yet he is as he is
because of his position.'
To be among the common households
and expect the status of ministers' and chancellors' descendants
is like a lame man wanting to match Lóu Jì,
or having no money but desiring priceless treasures—
isn't that an empty hope?"
The literati replied:
"Yǔ and Jì, from common cloth attire,
thought of anyone in the world suffering unjustly
as if they had pushed them into a ditch themselves,
so they rose to assist Yáo,
pacifying and managing water and land,
teaching the people farming.
They shouldered the world's burden so heavily,
how could one say they took salaries just to support their wives and children?
Those who feed on the labor of ten thousand people
bear their worries,
and shoulder their toils.
If one person loses his position,
or one office is not well managed,
it is a burden on the dukes and ministers.
Thus, when a gentleman takes office,
he practices righteousness,
not reveling in power.
He receives a salary to nurture the worthy,
not for private gain.
He does not conceal the worthy when he sees them,
nor monopolize the salary he receives;
this is why Gōng Shū was considered cultured,
and Wèi Chéngzǐ was deemed virtuous.
Thus, King Wén's virtue was accomplished before his descendants were enfeoffed,
and the world did not see it as factionalism.
The Duke of Zhōu achieved merit before receiving his fief,
and the world did not see it as greed."
But now it is not so.
Relatives push one another forward,
factions promote their own,
fathers hold high positions,
sons overflow with excess at home,
husbands are honored at court,
wives exert influence outside.
They possess the wealth of the Duke of Zhōu without his virtue,
the extravagance of Guǎn Zhòng without his achievements.
Thus, it is like a lame commoner hoping to walk swiftly."
2.4 "Critiquing Restoration - Tenth"
The Grand Officer, with a stern expression and displeased heart,
said:
"Those who stay at home do not know the toil of carrying loads;
those who comment from the sidelines have different concerns from those involved.
Now, as the central region of the empire,
with all the feudal lords gathering,
and internal and external affairs unsettled,
my heart is anxious as if crossing a great river,
encountering wind before reaching the shore.
Thus, day and night I ponder the needs of the state,
lying down but forgetting sleep,
hungry but forgetting food,
calculations never leaving my front,
all affairs reviewed in my mind.
The assistants and clerks are of small capacity,
not worthy of consultation;
alone I ponder the great Way,
longing to see the Literati,
as if awaiting Zhōu and Shào while hoping for Gāozi.
The Imperial Censor investigates affairs in the commanderies and kingdoms,
examining integrity and recommending talented worthies—
each year does not lack such.
Now over sixty worthy and talented Literati have gathered,
carrying the arts of the Six Classics,
expressing their thoughts exhaustively in debate.
They should be like opening light to the unenlightened,
yet they trust in the past and deviate from the present,
speak of antiquity but fail to match contemporary affairs.
Is it that they are insufficient to understand scholars?
Or do they embellish words and falsify abilities to confuse reality?
How difficult it is to see true worthy scholars!
Since Qiānchéng and Ní Kuān, through mastering the Shàngshū, reached the highest ranks of the Nine Ministers,
and the recommended scholars I have heard of or seen
have been promoted and honored quite notably,
yet I have not seen any unparalleled ones
who could help the government revive neglected areas and achieve merit."
The Literati said:
"When Carpenter Shū worked with timber,
he corrected his compass and square, and the mortise and tenon fit.
When Master Kuàng harmonized the five tones,
he corrected the six pitch pipes, and the gōng and shāng were in tune.
The artisans of today,
if they cannot adjust the mortise and tenon,
change the compass and square;
if they cannot harmonize the sounds,
alter the old pitch pipes.
Thus, the mortise and tenon are jagged and do not fit,
the sounds are scattered and discordant.
To apply the compass and square and know what is fitting,
to blow the pitch pipes and know the changes—
that is the highest;
to follow tradition without creating,
awaiting the right person—
that is the next best.
Thus, Chancellor Cáo drank strong wine daily,
while Minister Ní kept his mouth shut and did not speak.
Therefore, governing great matters must not be troublesome—
trouble leads to chaos;
governing small matters must not be negligent—
negligence leads to ruin.
The Chūnqiū says:
'When governance is broad and lofty,
broad and lofty governance qualifies one to be a minister or chancellor.
When governance is minute and scrutinizing,
minute and scrutinizing governance qualifies one to be a common man.'
If the guiding principles are not upheld,
and ritual and righteousness are not practiced,
that is the worry of the dukes and ministers.
As for the documents on the desk,
and the scheduled meetings—
those are the responsibilities of the assistants and clerks.
The Shàngshū says:
'With outstanding talents in office,
all officials emulate one another,
all artisans are timely,
and the various officers are truly harmonious.'
This means that offices are filled with suitable people,
and people are entrusted with their tasks.
Thus, offices are well-managed and not chaotic,
affairs are initiated and not abandoned,
scholars guard their duties,
great officers manage their positions,
and the dukes and ministers only oversee the essentials and grasp the general principles.
Therefore, those who appoint the capable achieve results without toil,
while those who rely on themselves see affairs ruined without merit.
Duke Huán regarding Guǎn Zhòng,
listened and observed him.
Thus, the nobleman toils in seeking the worthy,
but is at ease in employing them—
how can one say it is perilous?
In the past, when the Duke of Zhōu served as minister,
he was humble and not arrogant,
laboring for the scholars of the world.
Thus, outstanding talents filled the court,
and the worthy and wise crowded the gates.
Confucius, without rank or position,
as a commoner, gathered over seventy talented scholars,
all fit to be feudal lords, ministers, or chancellors—
how much more so for one in the honored position of the Three Dukes, nurturing the scholars of the world!
Now, with the high positions of the dukes and ministers,
and the beauty of their ranks and emoluments,
if they cannot attract scholars,
then they lack the way to advance the worthy.
When Yáo recommended Shùn,
he treated him as a guest and gave him his daughter.
When Duke Huán recommended Guǎn Zhòng,
he treated him as a guest and honored him as a teacher.
For the Son of Heaven to give his daughter to a commoner—
this can be called being intimate with the worthy.
For a feudal lord to honor a commoner as teacher—
this can be called respecting a guest.
Thus, the worthy followed them like a flowing stream,
returning without doubt.
But the current holders of office,
lacking neither Yān Zhāo's humility toward scholars
nor the joy in the worthy expressed in 'Lù Míng,'
instead practice the intentions of Zāng Wén and Zǐ Jiāo,
obstructing the worthy and envying the capable,
exalting their own wisdom,
slandering others' talents,
self-satisfied without inquiry,
despising scholars without friendship,
using position to look down on the worthy,
using salary to be arrogant toward scholars—
and yet they seek to employ scholars;
isn't that difficult indeed!"
The Grand Officer fell silent, discomfited,
while the Worthy and Talented sighed deeply.
The Imperial Censor stepped forward and said:
"Tàigōng assisted King Wén and King Wǔ to rule the empire;
Guǎn Zhòng assisted Duke Huán to hegemonize the feudal lords.
Thus, when the worthy obtain position,
it is like a dragon obtaining water,
or a soaring serpent swimming in mist.
Chancellor Gōngsūn, using the Chūnqiū to persuade the former emperor,
quickly reached the Three Dukes,
standing in the ranks of Zhōu and Shào,
commanding the power of ten thousand lǐ,
setting the standard for the empire.
He wore no double colors,
ate no mixed flavors,
leading the world by example,
yet it did not benefit governance.
Erudites Chǔ Tài, Xú Yǎn, and others,
receiving the bright decree,
established authority and sped through relays,
touring and inspecting the commanderies and kingdoms,
recommending the Filial and Incorrupt,
encouraging the common people,
yet the corrupt customs did not change.
Summoning and recommending the Worthy and Talented, the Upright, and the Literati,
promoting them in office and rank,
some even to ministers and high officials—
was this not like Yān Zhāo's recommendation of scholars,
or King Wén's broadening of the worthy?
Yet we have not seen the achievements and merits accomplished.
Perhaps they are not the talent of dragons and snakes,
whom the 'Lù Míng' would joyfully honor as worthy."
The Literati said:
"Ice and charcoal cannot share the same container;
the sun and moon cannot shine together.
In Gōngsūn Hóng's time,
the ruler was devising plans and focusing on the four barbarians.
Thus, cunning and deceptive strategies advanced,
and men from Jīng and Chǔ were employed.
Generals and commanders even reached enfeoffment and estates,
and those who achieved victory all received rich rewards.
Hence, warriors and attackers arose from this.
Afterward,
warfare did not cease,
armies were constantly seen,
armored soldiers were worn out,
the state's resources were insufficient.
Thus, ministers who set up barriers and promoted profit arose,
while scholars like those from Pánxī and the bear and panther recluses hid away.
Canals were built at Jīng and Wèi for water transport,
Dōngguō Xiányáng and Kǒng Jǐn established salt and iron monopolies,
planning various profits.
The rich bought ranks and sold offices,
avoided punishment and escaped crimes.
Public expenses grew more while the actors served private interests,
both high and low sought gain,
The people could not endure it,
so they turned to the law in their exhaustion and distress,
thus harsh and urgent officials advanced,
and laws of prosecution and obstruction arose.
Men like Dù Zhōu and Xián Xuān
became honored for using severe statutes to decide cases,
while figures such as Wáng Wēnshū gained prominence for striking down opponents like hawks.
Those who wished to uphold benevolence and righteousness to guide their rulers were few,
while those who flattered and sought favor were many.
With only a Gōngsūn Hóng,
what could be done?"
2.5 "Discourse on Confucians XI"
The Censor said:
"You literati trace your teachings to Zhòngní,
praising his virtue,
believing that from ancient times to the present,
there has never been his equal.
Yet when Confucius cultivated the Way between Lǔ and Wèi,
and spread his teachings along the Zhū and Sì rivers,
his disciples brought about no change,
his era saw no order,
and Lǔ's decline only deepened.
When King Xuān of Qí honored Confucians and revered learning,
figures like Mèng Kē and Chúnyú Kūn
received salaries of senior ministers,
discussing state affairs without holding office,
with nearly a thousand scholars gathered at Qí's Jìxià academy.
At that time,
it wasn't just one Gōngsūn Hóng.
Yet when weak Yān attacked Qí,
charging straight to Línzī,
King Mǐn fled,
dying in Jǔ without being saved;
and when King Jiàn was captured by Qín,
he was taken prisoner along with his state, unable to preserve it.
In this way,
the Confucians' claims to stabilize states and honor rulers
have never proven effective."
The Literati said:
"Without whip and bridle,
even Zàofǔ could not control a team of horses.
Without authority and position,
even Shùn and Yǔ could not govern the myriad people.
Confucius said:
'The phoenix does not come,
the river gives forth no chart -
I am done for!'
Thus even with a light carriage and fine horses,
there is no way to gallop;
with sage virtue and benevolence,
there is no place to apply them.
During the times of Kings Wēi and Xuān of Qí,
when worthies were promoted and scholars advanced,
the state grew wealthy and strong,
its power influencing rival states.
But when it came to King Mǐn,
building on the achievements of two generations,
he raised armies against Chǔ and Huái in the south,
annexed great Sòng in the north,
enveloped twelve states,
crushed the Three Jìn in the west,
repelled powerful Qín,
secured the submission of five states,
and made the rulers of Zōu and Lǔ,
along with various lords of the Sì region, all become his vassals.
But he boasted of achievements without cease,
until the people could bear no more.
When the various Confucians remonstrated but weren't heeded,
they scattered in different directions -
Shèn Dào and Jié Zǐ fled,
Tián Pián went to Xuē,
and Xún Zǐ went to Chǔ.
With no good ministers within,
the various lords conspired to attack.
King Jiàn listened to rumors,
believed in slander,
followed Hòu Shèng's advice,
refused to ally with other lords,
and thus lost his state.
Being captured by Qín
was only fitting, was it not?"
The Censor said:
"Yī Yǐn served Tāng by cooking,
Bó Lǐ sought Duke Mù's favor by tending oxen -
at first they merely accommodated,
yet eventually helped them become hegemon kings.
In this way,
what words went unheeded?
What ways went unimplemented?
Thus when Shāng Yāng advised Duke Xiào on the kingly way
and wasn't heeded,
he immediately proposed the way to strengthen the state,
and ultimately achieved success.
When Zōu Yǎn tried to influence the worldly rulers with Confucian methods
and wasn't heeded,
he immediately presented theories of cyclical change,
and ultimately gained fame.
Thus a horse proves itself by covering a thousand miles,
not necessarily being from Hú or Dài;
a scholar is valued for success,
not necessarily for literary elegance.
Mèng Kē clung to old methods,
unaware of worldly affairs,
thus he was stranded between Liáng and Sòng.
Confucius could be square but not round,
thus he went hungry at Líqiū.
Nowadays Confucians cultivate virtue diligently,
yet often face poverty and want,
their words being considered wrong,
and thus not implemented.
Since the Zhōu dynasty,
over a thousand years,
there have been only Kings Wén, Wǔ, Chéng, and Kāng
who could fully match such descriptions.
To praise what one cannot achieve
is like a cripple who can speak of distant places but cannot walk to them.
Sages follow different paths but reach the same end,
some acting, some refraining,
but their essential purpose is the same.
Though Shāng Yāng reformed laws and changed teachings,
his aim was to strengthen the state and benefit the people.
Zōu Yǎn's works
on the art of transformation
also ultimately return to benevolence and righteousness.
Jì Zhòng humbled himself to exercise discretion,
responding to the times.
Thus accepting small deviations to uphold greater principles
is what gentlemen do.
Now to obstinately cling to a single way,
invoking Wěi Shēng's rigid stance,
would mean considering Duke Wén of Jìn's clever dealings with lords to honor Zhōu as unworthy,
and Guǎn Zhòng's enduring disgrace to preserve states as unpraiseworthy."
The Literati said:
"When Yī Yǐn sought out Tāng,
he recognized a sage ruler.
When Bó Lǐ went to Qín,
he recognized an enlightened lord.
These two men could recognize hegemonic rulers
because the signs were already evident in themselves,
not because they decided matters blindly in the dark.
Confucius said:
'If names are not correct, words do not follow;
if words do not follow, affairs cannot be accomplished.'
How could they achieve hegemony through mere accommodation?
The gentleman holds to virtue and upholds righteousness in action,
thus even in haste he remains so,
even in turmoil he remains so.
Mencius said:
'To maintain one's position in today's court
without changing its customs,
and achieve the power of a thousand chariots -
this cannot be maintained for a single morning.'
Better to live in poverty and hunger in a narrow lane
than change oneself to follow vulgar customs.
When Hé Lǘ killed Liáo,
Prince Zhá left for Yánlíng,
never entering the state of Wú again.
When Duke Lǔ killed Zǐ Chì,
Shū Miǎn withdrew into seclusion,
refusing to eat his salary.
To gain honor by compromising righteousness,
to seek favor by distorting the Way -
they would rather die than do such things.
We have heard of abandoning office and withdrawing when the right way doesn't prevail,
but never of distorting the Way to seek favor."
The Censor said:
"The Analects say:
'Where the ruler personally does evil,
the gentleman will not serve.'
Yet there are such words but insufficient follow-through in action.
When the Jì family acted without principle,
expelling their ruler
and seizing his government,
Rǎn Qiú and Zhòng Yóu still served them.
The Rites state:
'Men and women should not touch when giving and receiving,
nor share cups.'
Yet when Confucius went to Wèi,
he used the favorite minister Mí Zǐxiá to meet Lady Wèi,
making Zǐ Lù displeased.
Zǐxiá
was a flattering minister,
yet the Master used him -
this was improper.
Men and women should not interact,
yet Confucius met Nánzǐ -
this was contrary to ritual.
If ritual and righteousness come from Confucius,
yet even he compromised principle to seek favor,
how can you speak of abandoning office and withdrawing?"
The Literati said:
"When the world lacks peace,
and various states know no tranquility,
this concerns the enlightened king.
When above there is no Son of Heaven,
below no feudal lords,
and the world falls into turmoil and chaos,
this concerns the sages and worthies."
Thus, Yáo worried about the great flood,
Yī Yǐn worried about the people,
Guǎn Zhòng was bound and restrained,
and Confucius traveled throughout the states,
all concerned about the calamities of the common folk and seeking to secure them in their perils.
Therefore, they bore cauldrons and sacrificial stands, endured imprisonment and constraints, and crawled on their hands and knees to rescue them.
Hence, those chasing after the fleeing press forward urgently,
and those saving the drowning get soaked themselves.
Now that the people have fallen into ditches and pits,
even if one wishes not to get wet,
how can it be avoided?"
The Imperial Censor remained silent and did not respond.
2.6 "Chapter Twelve: Concern for the Frontiers"
The Grand Master said:
The Literati state:
"'When the world is not at peace,
and the various states are not tranquil,
it is the worry of the enlightened king.'
Thus, the king's relation to the world
is like that within a single household;
if even one person is not in their proper place,
it is said to be a cause for unhappiness.
Therefore, to let the people drift and drown without rescuing them
is not the way of a benevolent ruler.
To not worry when the state faces difficulties
is not the mark of a loyal minister.
Holding fast to integrity and dying in adversity
is the duty of a subject;
providing clothing and food to the hungry and cold
is the way of a compassionate father.
Now that our sons and younger brothers labor far away on the frontiers,
the ruler is restless day and night because of it,
and all ministers exhaust their efforts and deliberations,
planning to increase the state's resources.
Thus, the assistants and directors of the Lesser Treasury request the establishment of a liquor monopoly,
to support the frontiers,
supply the warriors,
and save the people from hardship.
As fathers and elder brothers,
how can we refrain from this!
Reflecting inwardly and reducing our own food and clothing to show compassion for those abroad
is still not enough;
now you wish to abolish various expenditures,
and reduce the expenses for supporting the frontiers—
this cannot be considered the action of a compassionate father or worthy elder brother."
The Literati said:
"In the late period of the Zhōu dynasty,
the Son of Heaven was weak and insignificant,
the feudal lords governed by force,
so the rulers of states were unsettled,
and strategist ministers dashed about.
Why was this?
Because there were many rival states and the altars of soil and grain were in danger.
Now the nine provinces share the same domain,
the world is unified under one rule,
Your Majesty leisurely strolls through the palace corridors,
observing the extreme arguments and ultimate discourses of your ministers,
inwardly chanting the 'Yǎ' and 'Sòng' [sections of the Classic of Poetry],
outwardly the harmonious bells [of the carriage] chime,
pure virtue shines brilliantly,
matching that of Táng [Yáo] and Yú [Shùn],
and your achievements and glory will flow down to your descendants.
The people of the Mán and Mò tribes,
and lands that yield no food—
how are they worth troubling your thoughts,
to the extent of having worries from the Warring States period?"
If Your Majesty does not abandon them,
but adds virtue to them,
and extends kindness to them,
the northern barbarians will surely turn inward,
knocking at the frontier passes to come of their own accord.
Then you can regard the Hú as external subjects,
and the Xiōngnú will, to the end of their days, not consume what you provide."
The Grand Master said:
"The sage ruler, concerned that the central states are not yet peaceful,
and the northern frontiers not yet secure,
sent the former Commandant of Justice Píng and others to inquire about the sufferings among the people.
They rescue and show compassion for the poor and lowly,
and comprehensively provide for those in want.
The ministers who proclaim the virtue of the enlightened king
and bring peace within the four seas—
not having grasped the guiding principles,
thus consulted the various scholars.
The scholars' discussions either do not reach the heavens or plunge into the abyss;
they wish to use the governance of village lanes
to compare with the great affairs of state—
is that not almost hopeless!
Sprung from the fields,
emerging from poor alleys,
they do not know the cold of ice and water,
as if drunk or newly awakened from sleep;
they are truly not worth speaking with."
The Literati said:
"The way to secure the people and enrich the state
lies in returning to the root;
when the root is established, the way will grow.
Following the principles of Heaven,
utilizing the benefits of the earth,
then achievement comes without toil.
Not cultivating the source but attending to the flow,
having no root to unify it,
even if one exhausts one's spirit
and spends all one's thoughts,
it will not benefit governance.
The attempt to secure it may precisely lead to its endangerment;
the attempt to save it may precisely lead to its ruin.
The beginning of order and chaos
lies solely in the root and the branches;
one can attain the way without necessarily laboring one's mind.
Confucius said:
'It is difficult to discuss governance with those who do not understand principles;
with those whose way is different,
one does not plan together.'
Now the high ministers have biased intentions,
therefore the words of the Literati
cannot be used."
The Grand Master said:
"I have heard that as subjects, one should be utterly loyal in fulfilling one's duties;
as sons, one should show filial piety to carry on the family enterprise.
If the ruler has faults,
the minister should cover them up.
If the father has faults,
the son should conceal and avoid them.
Thus, when the ruler passes away,
the minister does not change the ruler's policies;
when the father is gone,
the son does not alter the father's way.
The Spring and Autumn Annals criticizes the destruction of the Quán Terrace,
because it demolished what the ancestors had done,
and exposed the faults of the ruler and father.
Now the salt, iron, and equal distribution policies
have been in place for a long time;
to wish to abolish them—
would that not harm the achievements of the late emperor,
and impair the virtue of the sage ruler?
The officials rely on the path of loyalty and filial piety;
this way differs and does not align with the plans of the Literati."
The Literati said:
"The wise change with the times;
the knowledgeable adapt their systems to the age.
Confucius said:
'The hemp cap
is prescribed by ritual.
Nowadays, it is made of silk,
which is more economical;
I follow the majority.'
Thus, the sage honors the worthy without departing from antiquity,
and conforms to customs without being biased.
Lord Dìng of Lǔ arranged the order of ancestral temples,
following the sequence of ancestors and father;
Lord Zhāo abolished some ministers and officers
to reduce affairs and economize—
this cannot be called changing the ancestors' actions
or altering the father's way.
The Second Emperor [of Qín] expanded the Epāng Palace to glorify his inheritance,
and Zhào Gāo piled up Qín laws to broaden his authority—
yet they cannot be called loyal ministers or filial sons."
3.1 "Chapter Thirteen: Parks and Ponds"
The Grand Master said:
"Feudal lords regard their state as their family,
so their worries lie within.
The Son of Heaven takes the eight extremes as his boundaries,
so his concerns lie without.
Therefore, those with small domains have meager expenditures,
while those with great achievements have large expenses.
Thus, the court opens parks and ponds,
controls the mountains and seas,
to generate profits that aid taxes and tribute,
repair canals and ditches,
establish various agricultural offices,
expand fields and pastures,
and enrich gardens and enclosures.
The Grand Coachman, Director of Waters and Parks, Lesser Treasury, and Grand Minister of Agriculture
annually assess the income from fields and pastures,
the leasing of ponds and preserves,
and the appointment of agricultural officials on the northern frontier,
to supply various needs—
and still it is not enough.
Now you wish to abolish these,
cut off their source,
block their flow;
both high and low will be exhausted,
resulting in hardship and want.
Though you may prefer to reduce affairs and economize,
how can it be done?"
The Literati said:
"In ancient times,
the regulated land was sufficient to nourish the people,
and the people were sufficient to support their superiors.
A state of a thousand chariots,
with a territory of a hundred lǐ,
for dukes, marquises, earls, counts, and barons—
each had their demands met and desires satisfied.
Qín annexed the lands of ten thousand states,
possessed the wealth of the four seas,
yet its intentions were not satisfied—
