not because its domain was small or expenditures meager,
but because its desires were many and those below could not bear its demands."
As the saying goes:
'When the kitchen has rotten meat,
the state has starving people;
when the stables have fat horses,
the roads have the famished.'
Now the feeding of dogs and horses,
the food for insects and beasts,
how could their cost be limited to just rotten meat and fat horses!
Useless officials,
non-urgent constructions,
extravagant changes in clothing,
those who eat and dress at the government's expense without merit are numerous;
thus, those above are insufficient and those below are impoverished.
Now, without reducing the root, they wish to provide for the branches,
setting up mechanisms for profit,
creating fields and livestock,
competing with the common people for pasture,
contending with merchants for market profits,
this is not the way to illuminate the ruler's virtue and assist the state.
For men to farm and women to weave
is the great enterprise of the world.
Therefore, in ancient times, land was divided and settled,
fields were regulated and attended to.
Thus, no land was left uncultivated,
and no people in the state were idle.
Now the government extensively establishes parks, public fields, ponds, and marshes,
the state has the name of controlling and leasing,
but the profits go to powerful families.
The Sānfǔ region is close to mountains and rivers,
the land is narrow and the population dense,
people from all directions gather here,
grains, firewood, and vegetables
cannot suffice for all.
Public fields are subleased,
mulberries, elms, vegetables, and fruits are not cultivated,
and the land's potential is not fully utilized.
I foolishly believe this is wrong.
The former emperor's opening of parks and
enclosed marshes
could be assigned and returned to the people,
with the government only collecting rent and taxes.
Though the names of lease and tax differ, their essence is the same.
If this were so,
the strength of every man
would be devoted to farming,
the strength of every woman
would be devoted to hemp and flax.
If fields and wilds are opened up,
and hemp and flax are well managed,
then both high and low would have plenty,
how could there be any poverty?"
The Grand Master was silent,
and looked at his Chancellor and Censor.
3.2 "On Light and Heavy: Chapter Fourteen"
The Censor stepped forward and said:
"In the past, Tàigōng was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū,
where he cleared the wilderness and settled.
The land was poor and the population sparse,
so he promoted the ways of profitable secondary occupations,
and perfected the skills of women's work.
Thus, neighboring states traded with Qí,
wealth was accumulated and goods multiplied,
making it a powerful state for generations.
Guǎn Zhòng served as minister to Duke Huán,
continuing the work of previous rulers,
implementing changes in light and heavy policies,
subduing the powerful Chǔ in the south and hegemonizing the feudal lords.
Now the Grand Master Lord cultivates the methods of Tàigōng, Huán, and Guǎn,
unifying control over salt and iron,
opening up the benefits of mountains and rivers, causing all things to flourish.
Thus, the government's resources are abundant and sufficient,
the people are not impoverished,
both primary and secondary occupations are profitable,
high and low are both well-provided for,
this is achieved through planning and calculation,
not solely through farming and agriculture."
The Literati said:
"Ritual and righteousness
are the foundation of the state,
while power and profit
are the ruin of governance.
Confucius said:
'Can one govern a state by ritual and deference?'
What difficulty is there?
Yī Yǐn and Tàigōng raised their lords from territories of a hundred lǐ,
Guǎn Zhòng had sole authority under Duke Huán,
yet with the thousand-chariot state of Qí,
he could not achieve true kingship,
because what he pursued was wrong.
Thus, his achievements and fame crumbled, and the Way was not realized.
At that time,
the feudal lords could not rule by virtue,
but contended for public profit,
so they used power to overthrow each other.
Now the world is united as one family,
why should the pursuit of secondary profits be practiced?
Why should excessive cleverness be applied?
The Grand Master Lord uses mental calculations to plan state expenditures,
manipulates the feudal lords,
supplements with liquor monopolies,
Xiányáng and Kǒng Jǐn added salt and iron monopolies,
Jiāng Chōng, Yáng Kě, and others,
each with their sharpness,
analyze profit-seeking matters down to the finest detail,
leaving no gaps.
This is not merely Guǎn Zhòng establishing nine treasuries
and controlling mountains and seas.
Yet the state declines and resources dwindle,
cities and walls are empty.
Therefore, without exalting benevolence and righteousness, the people cannot be transformed;
without strengthening fundamental agriculture, the state cannot be enriched."
The Censor said:
"Where there are otters in the water, the pond fish are harried;
where there are powerful oppressors in the state, the common people are diminished.
Thus, under dense forests, there is no lush grass;
between great clods of earth, there are no fine seedlings.
The way to govern a state
is to remove the vile and uproot the powerful,
only then can the common people be equal and peaceful,
each content in their dwelling.
Chief Justice Zhāng established laws and statutes,
clarifying regulations to bind the world,
punishing the crafty and treacherous,
eliminating those who engage in monopolies,
so the strong do not bully the weak,
and the many do not oppress the few.
The Grand Master Lord devises strategies,
establishes state expenditures,
controls all profits from salt, iron, and other resources,
to push back against wealthy merchants and great traders,
selling offices and redeeming crimes,
reducing surplus,
supplementing insufficiency,
to equalize the common people.
Thus, with military campaigns east and west,
taxes are not increased yet expenditures are sufficient.
Matters of reduction and increase
are understood by the worthy,
not known by the masses."
The Literati said:
"Biǎn Què felt the pulse and knew whence the illness arose;
when yang energy was excessive,
he reduced it to harmonize yin;
when cold energy was excessive,
he reduced it to harmonize yang;
thus, the energy and pulse were harmonized,
and pathogenic energy had no place to linger.
The clumsy physician, not knowing the texture of the pulse principles
or the division of blood and energy,
pointlessly punctures without benefiting the illness,
only harming the skin and flesh.
Now, wanting to reduce surplus
and supplement insufficiency,
the rich become richer,
the poor become poorer.
With strict laws and reliance on punishment,
seeking to prohibit violence and stop treachery,
yet treachery does not cease;
it seems this is not Biǎn Què's use of acupuncture stones,
so the masses have not found their proper place."
The Censor said:
"When Zhōu established its state,
there were about eighteen hundred feudal lords.
Afterward,
the strong swallowed the weak,
the large annexed the small,
merging into six states.
These six states waged war and entangled in conflicts for centuries,
resisting enemy states internally,
repelling the four barbarians externally.
From this, we observe:
weapons and armor never rested,
battles and campaigns were never lacking,
yet the army was supplied externally,
and granaries and treasuries were full internally.
Now, with the wealth of the world,
the resources within the seas,
tributes from hundreds of commanderies,
it is not merely the stores of Qí and Chǔ,
or the treasuries of Zhào and Wèi.
Calculating reserves and measuring income,
even if urgently needed,
there should be no time of shortage.
Yet the Grand Minister of Agriculture and others, using techniques to personally engage in farming,
emulating the achievements of Hòu Jì,
with armies deployed in all directions, supplies do not follow;
is this not due to heaven's resources being scarce?
Using acupuncture stones,
harmonizing yin and yang,
equalizing having and not having,
supplementing insufficiency,
is this also not correct?
The Senior Grand Master Lord and the Commandant for Grain Management oversee the affairs of the Grand Minister of Agriculture,
applying moxibustion and acupuncture to stagnation,
opening benefits in all vessels,
thus all things flow freely,
and the government is wealthy and substantial."
The registration of population numbers was initiated by corrupt officials,
hence the practice was imitated,
with many abandoning the worst to seek the slightly better.
The "Tradition" says:
" 'Under lenient governance, the people die for it;
under harsh governance, fathers and sons are separated.'
Thus, fields and lands daily fall into neglect,
and city walls stand empty.
The way to shepherd the people
is to remove what pains them,
suit what comforts them,
keep them at ease without disturbance,
employ them without toil,
so that the common people are encouraged in their work and gladly pay public taxes.
If this is so,
then the ruler need not provide relief to the people,
nor the people seek profit from the ruler;
above and below deliberate together, and songs of praise arise.
Thus, taking from them, the people do not resent it;
employing them, the people do not suffer.
The poem 'Líng Tái'
was not made by anyone forcing them;
the people composed it themselves.
If so,
then how could the ruler ever lack for anything?"
The Imperial Censor said:
"In ancient times,
at fifteen, one entered the Great Academy,
and undertook minor duties;
at twenty, capped as an adult,
one joined military affairs;
above fifty,
when blood and vitality are full and strong,
they were called 'ài zhuàng' (vigorous elders).
The 'Book of Songs' says:
'Fāng Shū, the venerable elder,
could still strengthen his plans.'
Thus, the army of Shāng was like crows,
the army of Zhōu was like reed flowers.
Now, His Majesty pities the common people,
lenient in the policy of labor service,
beginning taxation at twenty-three,
exempting at fifty-six,
thereby assisting the vigorous and giving rest to the aged.
Adults manage their fields and villages,
the elderly tend their ponds and gardens,
frugal in effort and timely in work,
without the worry of hunger or cold.
To not manage one's household but instead sue the officials
is also perverse."
The Literati said:
"Those below nineteen are considered 'shāng' (minors),
not yet adults;
at twenty, capped;
at thirty, married,
then they may join military affairs;
above fifty are called 'ài lǎo' (aged elders),
using staffs at home,
not subjected to labor service,
thereby supporting the insufficient and resting the elderly;
the ritual of the village drinking ceremony,
with special dishes for the elderly,
serves to honor the aged and clarify the practice of caring for the old.
Thus, the elderly are not full without meat,
not warm without silk,
cannot walk without a staff.
Now, those from fifty to sixty,
along with their sons and grandsons, perform hauling and transport,
and are also levied for corvée labor,
which is not the intent of caring for the aged.
In ancient times, for those with great mourning,
the ruler would not call at their door for three years,
to allow the practice of filial piety,
and fulfill their hearts of grief.
What the nobleman values and exerts himself in,
is it not the mourning for parents?
Now, some, with corpses stiffened,
cast off mourning garments to follow military affairs,
which is not the way to treat the people as children,
nor to accord with hearts of filial piety and fraternal duty.
The Duke of Zhōu held King Chéng to hear the empire,
his kindness filled the realm,
his beneficence reached to the four borders;
how much more for those with human faces,
embracing benevolence and preserving virtue,
that none should fail to find their place.
The 'Book of Songs' says:
'Day and night, he laid the foundation of his mandate with deep secrecy.'
His Majesty is young in years,
entrusting matters to great ministers,
with dukes and ministers assisting in governance,
yet governance and teaching are not yet balanced,
hence the commoners debate."
The Imperial Censor remained silent and did not reply.
4.1 "Dì Guǎng Dì Shíliù" (On the Breadth of the Land, Chapter 16)
The Grand Master said:
"The king embraces and covers all,
loves universally without partiality,
not bestowing heavily for the near,
nor neglecting kindness for the distant.
Now, all are equally people,
all equally subjects,
yet their safety, danger, toil, and ease are not equal;
should they not be adjusted?
To not consider them but only calculate for oneself,
is this not fondness for debate?
The people along the border,
dwelling in cold and bitter lands,
facing the threat of the strong Hú,
once the beacon fires stir,
bear the risk of losing their lives.
Thus, the border people fight a hundred battles,
while the central states sleep peacefully,
because the border regions serve as their shield.
The 'Book of Songs' says:
'All are the king's affairs,
yet I alone toil.'
It criticizes inequality.
Therefore, the sage king grieves for the unique hardship of the four quarters,
raises armies to repel the Hú and Yuè,
removes distant bandits and calms disasters,
distributes the surplus from the central states' fertile lands,
to adjust the border regions;
when the borders are strong,
the central states are secure;
when the central states are secure, there is tranquil peace.
What more could one seek, and why not remain silent?"
The Literati said:
"In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven stood at the center of the world,
within the royal domain, not exceeding a thousand lǐ square;
the feudal lords and states,
did not reach inedible lands;
the 'Tribute of Yǔ' extended to five thousand lǐ;
the people each supported their ruler,
the feudal lords each protected their states,
thus the common people were evenly adjusted,
and corvée labor was not toilsome.
Now, pushing back the Hú and Yuè for thousands of lǐ,
with roads winding and remote,
the soldiers are weary and exhausted.
Thus, the border people face the disaster of slit throats,
while the central states suffer the peril of death,
this is why the common people are clamorous and not silent.
The way to govern a state
proceeds from the center outward,
beginning with the near.
When the near are attached,
then the distant will come;
when the common people are internally sufficient,
then they can care for the external.
Hence, when ministers debated wanting to farm in Lúntái,
the enlightened ruler did not permit it,
considering it essential to first address urgent tasks and the fundamental occupation in time.
Therefore, an edict was issued saying:
'The tasks of the present time
lie in prohibiting harsh violence,
stopping arbitrary taxes,
and focusing on fundamental agriculture.'
The dukes and ministers should follow this intent,
request reduction and removal of the unfit,
to aid the urgency of the common people.
Now, the decay and neglect of the central states are not worried about,
efforts are focused on the borders.
It seems that lands are vast but not farmed,
much sown but not weeded,
effort is spent without achievement.
The 'Book of Songs' says:
'Do not farm the large fields,
the weeds will grow proudly.'
Is this not what it refers to?"
The Grand Master said:
"The campaigns of Tāng and Wǔ
were not because they liked using arms;
King Xuān of Zhōu expanded the state a thousand lǐ,
not out of greed for invasion;
it was to eliminate bandits and rebels and secure the people.
Thus, the nobleman does not launch armies without merit;
the sage king does not covet useless lands.
The Former Emperor raised the armies of Tāng and Wǔ,
settled the difficulties of the three borders,
controlled the enemy with one front,
the Xiōngnú fled,
thus using rivers and mountains as defenses,
therefore abandoned sandy, salty, inedible lands,
cut off remote and isolated counties,
discarded the land of Zàoyáng to give to the Hú,
reduced winding fortresses,
relied on river barriers,
guarded strategic points,
to ease corvée labor,
and protect the soldiers and people.
From this perspective:
the intent of the sage ruler
is not merely to broaden lands and toil the masses."
The Literati said:
"The military campaigns of Qin
can be called extreme,
with Méng Tián expanding the borders
to what could be considered distant.
Now we cross Méng Tián's frontiers,
establishing commanderies and counties in bandit-occupied lands,
where the farther the territory, the more the people toil.
North of Shuòfāng,
and north of Cháng'ān,
the achievements of new commanderies,
the expenses of outer walls,
are beyond calculation.
Not only that,
Sīmǎ and Táng Méng opened roads through the southwestern tribes,
exhausting Bā and Shǔ with Qiōng and Zuó;
the Admiral crossed the sea to subdue the southern tribes,
tower ships garrisoned Eastern Yuè,
exhausting Jīng and Chǔ with Ōu and Luò;
the General of the Left attacked Cháoxiān,
opening Líntún,
burdening Yān and Qí with Huì and Mò;
Zhāng Qiān reached extremely distant lands,
bringing in useless things,
so that the treasury's stores
flowed to foreign states.
This is not merely the expense of remote corners
or the campaign of Zàoyáng.
From this we see
it is not the ruler's intention,
but ministers fond of ventures who plan errors for the court."
The Grand Master said:
"Those possessing Guǎn Zhòng's wisdom
are not made to do menial tasks.
Those harboring Táo Zhū's foresight
do not dwell in poverty.
The Literati can speak but cannot act,
remaining below yet criticizing those above,
in poverty yet condemning the wealthy,
uttering grand words but not following them,
lofty in speech yet base in conduct,
slandering and criticizing,
to seek fame and gather praise in their time.
Those whose emolument doesn't fill a handful
are unqualified to discuss governance;
those whose households lack even a dàn of grain
are unqualified to deliberate on affairs.
All Confucians are poor and weak,
their robes and caps incomplete—
how could they understand state administration
or court affairs?
What do they know of remote corners and Zàoyáng!"
The Literati said:
"Low status does not impair wisdom,
poverty does not hinder virtue.
Yán Yuān was often in want,
yet this didn't make him unworthy.
Confucius found no acceptance,
yet this didn't make him un-sagely.
If we must judge people by appearance
and advance scholars by wealth,
then Tàigōng would have终生 wielded his butcher's knife,
and Nìng Qì never left his ox-tending.
The noble person of old
upheld the Way to establish their name,
cultivated themselves while awaiting their time,
not changing principles due to poverty,
not altering aspirations due to low status,
dwelling only in benevolence,
acting only with righteousness.
Facing wealth, if obtained improperly,
seeing profit that contradicts righteousness,
becoming wealthy through unrighteousness,
becoming noble without reputation—
the benevolent do not act thus.
Thus Zēng Shēn and Mǐnzǐ
did not trade their benevolence for the wealth of Jìn and Chǔ.
Bó Yí did not trade his conduct for a feudal lord's position,
so although Duke Jǐng of Qí had a thousand teams of horses,
he could not contend with them in reputation.
Confucius said:
'How admirable Huí is!
With a single bamboo dish of rice,
a single gourd dipper of drink,
living in a humble lane,
others could not endure the hardship,
yet Huí did not change his joy.'
Thus only the benevolent can find joy in hardship
and poverty, while the petty person when wealthy becomes violent,
when poor becomes unrestrained.
Yángzǐ said:
'The benevolent are not wealthy,
the wealthy are not benevolent.'
If we put profit before righteousness,
the seizure and plunder would be insatiable.
Dukes and ministers accumulate hundreds of millions,
grand masters accumulate thousands of gold,
scholars accumulate hundreds of gold—
all gathering wealth for their own benefit;
while the common people suffer cold and hardship,
wandering displaced on the roads.
How alone could Confucians keep their robes and caps intact?"
4.2 Chapter 17: Poverty and Wealth
The Grand Master said:
"I bound my hair and cultivated myself at thirteen,
fortunately obtained the imperial guard position,
served beneath the imperial carriage,
reaching the position of minister and grand master,
receiving emoluments and rewards,
for over sixty years now.
Expenses for carriages, horses, and clothing,
costs for wife, children, and servants,
I measured income against expenditure,
dwelling frugally and thriftily,
with salaries and rewards,
carefully planning each one,
gradually accumulating to achieve wealth and establish my estate.
Thus given equal land,
the worthy can maintain it;
given equal wealth,
the wise can manage it.
Bái Guī's warehousing,
Zǐ Gòng's amassing of thousands of gold—
did they necessarily rely on the people?
They moved it with their six-inch abacus,
transformed it through profit and loss,
taking it from price fluctuations!"
The Literati said:
"In ancient times,
people did not pursue multiple occupations,
nor combine profits and salaries,
thus various livelihoods didn't differ greatly,
and poverty and wealth weren't widely separated.
Those using rank and salary for humility
are too numerous to mention;
those using power and position to seek profit
are too many to count.
Controlling lakes and ponds,
managing mountains and seas—
gatherers of firewood cannot contend with them for marshes,
merchants cannot contend with them for profit.
Zǐ Gòng achieved this as a commoner,
yet Confucius criticized him—
how much more those who use power and position to seek it?
Thus ancient ministers contemplated benevolence and righteousness to fulfill their positions,
not using power and profit to satisfy their selfish desires."
The Grand Master said:
"When mountains have abundance,
then the common people are provided for.
When rivers and seas have moisture,
then the people obtain sufficiency.
Ordinary puddles
cannot irrigate marshes;
trees from small hills
cannot build palaces.
The small cannot encompass the large,
the few cannot provide for the many.
None who cannot satisfy themselves can satisfy others.
None who cannot govern themselves can govern others.
Thus those good at serving others
can act for themselves;
those good at governing others
can govern themselves.
If the Literati cannot manage their own households,
how can they manage external affairs?"
The Literati said:
"Those traveling far borrow chariots,
those crossing rivers and seas rely on boats.
Thus worthy scholars achieving merit and fame
rely on resources and borrow tools.
Gōngshūzǐ could use his ruler's timber
to construct palaces and towers,
but couldn't build himself a small hut—
not because of lacking material,
but because of its purpose.
Ōu Yě could use his lord's copper and iron
to make great bells and metal cauldrons,
but couldn't make himself pots and basins—
not for lack of material,
but for lack of use.
The noble person can use his ruler's proper court
to harmonize the common people,
enrich the masses,
but cannot enrich his own family—
the circumstances are unsuitable.
Thus Shùn farmed at Lìshān,
his kindness not reaching beyond his village;
Tàigōng butchered oxen at Zhāogē,
his benefits not reaching his wife and children.
When they were employed,
their kindness flowed to the eight wildernesses,
their virtue overflowed the four seas.
Thus Shùn borrowed from Yáo,
Tàigōng relied on Zhōu—the noble person can cultivate themselves and borrow the Way, but cannot distort the Way to borrow wealth."
The Grandee said:
"The Way hangs in heaven,
things are spread upon the earth;
the wise expand upon them,
while the foolish are constrained by them.
Zǐgòng became illustrious among the feudal lords through accumulation of goods,
while Táo Zhūgōng was honored in his time through trade.
The wealthy associated with them,
and the poor were supported by them.
Thus, from the sovereign above
down to the common scholars below,
none failed to record their virtue
and praise their benevolence.
Yuán Xiàn and Kǒng Jí
suffered from hunger and cold in their time;
Yán Huí was often destitute in impoverished alleys.
At such times,
confined to caves,
bound by coarse robes,
even if they wished to borrow wealth and trust flatterers,
they could not do so."
The Literati said:
"Confucius said:
'If wealth were attainable,
even as a carriage driver
I would do it;
if it is not attainable,
I follow what I love.'
The nobleman seeks righteousness,
not merely wealth.
Hence, he criticized Zǐgòng for not accepting fate and engaging in trade.
When a nobleman encounters opportunity, he becomes wealthy and noble;
if not,
he withdraws and delights in the Way.
He does not burden himself with profit.
Thus, he does not transgress righteousness to grasp recklessly.
Living in seclusion, he cultivates integrity,
unwilling to hinder his conduct,
so he does not ruin his reputation to chase trends.
Even if entrusted with the households of Hán and Wèi,
if it contradicts his will,
he will not dwell there.
Wealth and honor cannot glorify him,
nor can slander harm him.
Thus, Yuán Xiàn's coarse robe
is worthier than Jì Sūn's fox furs;
Zhào Xuān Mèng's fish meal
is sweeter than Zhì Bó's fine meats;
Zǐsī's silver pendant
is more beautiful than Yú Gōng's Chuíjí jade.
Lord Wèi Wén halted his carriage at Duàngānmù's alley,
not because of his power;
Duke Wén of Jìn saw Hán Qìng,
descended his chariot and hurried to him,
not because of his wealth,
but because he was rich in benevolence
and full of virtue.
So why must honor come from wealth?
It is simply about benevolence and righteousness!"
4.3 Chapter 18: "Criticizing Learning"
The Grandee said:
"To harbor crookedness yet speak of uprightness,
claiming to have no desires but not truly following through—
is this not the true nature of scholars?
Once Lǐ Sī and Bāo Qiūzǐ both studied under Xún Qīng;
later, Lǐ Sī entered Qín,
attained the rank of one of the three highest ministers,
wielded imperial power to control the realm,
achieved merits matching Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng,
and his fame loomed as large as Tài Shān;
yet Bāo Qiūzǐ could not escape living behind a broken jar window in a humble hut,
like frogs in a flooded year—
not that their mouths aren't numerous,
but they end up dying in ditches.
Now, with nothing to sustain internally,
and nothing to commend externally,
being poor and lowly yet fond of righteousness—
even if they speak of benevolence and righteousness,
they are not worthy of honor!"
The Literati said:
"When Lǐ Sī was chancellor of Qín,
the First Emperor trusted him,
and no other minister rivaled him,
yet Xún Qīng refrained from eating for him,
foreseeing he would meet an unforeseeable disaster.
Bāo Qiūzǐ ate coarse greens in poverty,
cultivated the Way under a thatched roof,
delighted in his aspirations,
and was as content as if in a mansion with fine food.
Without grand power,
he also had no deep worries.
The Chuíjí jade of Duke Xiàn of Jìn
was not un-beautiful,
but Gōng Zhīqí sighed upon seeing it,
knowing Xún Xì's plot behind it.
Zhì Bó's wealth across the three Jìn states
was not un-impressive,
yet he did not know of Xiāngzǐ's scheme against him.
Jì Sūn's fox furs
were not un-splendid,
but he was unaware of the Lǔ lord's anxiety over him.
Thus, Duke Xiàn of Jìn used precious horses to bait Yú and Guó,
and Xiāngzǐ used a city to lure Zhì Bó.
So Zhì Bó was captured by Zhào,
and Yú and Guó were eventually annexed by Jìn,
because they strove for gain without considering the consequences,
coveting land and coveting precious horses.
Confucius said:
'If a person lacks long-term plans,
they will surely have immediate worries.'
Those in power today
see profit without anticipating harm,
crave gain without regard for shame,
trading their well-being for profit,
their lives for wealth.
Without the virtue of benevolence and righteousness,
yet holding the emoluments of wealth and honor—
it is like stepping into a pitfall,
eating beneath a suspended gate;
this is why Lǐ Sī suffered the five punishments.
In the south, there is a bird called Yuānchú,
which eats only bamboo seeds,
drinks only from sweet springs;
flying over Tài Shān,
the owls of Tài Shān,
pecking at rotten mice below,
look up, see the Yuānchú, and screech at it.
Now, the high officials ridicule the Confucians with their wealth and honor, as if it's normal behavior—
are they not like the Tài Shān owls screeching at the Yuānchú?"
The Grandee said:
"Learning is meant to guard against stubborn speech,
and ritual to refine crude behavior.
Thus, learning aids virtue,
and ritual adorns substance.
In speech, think of what can be said;
in action, think of what can bring joy.
Let no harsh words leave your mouth,
let no wicked deeds touch you.
Movements should accord with ritual,
composure should hit the mean.
Hence, act with ritual,
speak with humility.
So one may speak all day
without oral fault;
act a lifetime
without blame or error.
Now, rulers establish offices and courts to govern the people,
bestow ranks and divide salaries to honor the worthy,
yet you speak of 'suspended gates and rotten mice'—
how crude and contrary to what we've heard is this language!"
The Literati said:
"The sage ruler sets up offices for appointments,
which the capable occupy;
he divides salaries to employ the worthy,
which the capable receive.
Righteous honor needs no high position,
righteous gain needs no abundance.
Thus, Shùn received Yáo's empire,
and Tàigōng did not decline Zhōu's three highest offices;
but if the person is unfit,
even a basket of rice and a bowl of soup would make them a dependent.
So with meager virtue and high position,
little strength and heavy tasks,
few avoid disaster.
The Tài Shān owls peck at rotten mice in desolate marshes and deep valleys—
they harm no one.
But today's officials
steal the ruler's wealth and feed beside the law,
unaware the trap is about to spring,
yet they also scare others—
how can their harm be compared only to the Tài Shān owls?"
The Grandee said:
"Sīmǎ Qiān said:
'All under heaven bustling,
all go for profit.'
Zhào women do not pick ugly or beautiful,
Zhèng women do not choose far or near,
merchants feel no shame for disgrace,
soldiers do not spare their strength in death,
scholars do not prioritize kinship,
serving their lord without avoiding difficulty—
all for the sake of profit and salary.
Confucians and Mohists are greedy inside but pretentious outside,
traveling around to persuade,
restless and still not attaining their goal.
So honor and glory are the scholar's desire,
wealth and rank are the scholar's hope.
When Lǐ Sī was at Xún Qīng's school,
he was level with the lowly;
but when he soared high,
like a dragon rising or a steed galloping,
surpassing the nine and outpacing the two,
hovering at ten thousand ren,
even swans and fine steeds became his peers—
how much more so the crippled sheep and sparrows!"
Holding the power of the world,
ruling over the masses within the realm,
with a hundred carriages following behind,
and enjoying a salary of ten thousand zhōng.
Yet the constrained scholar lacks even a complete set of coarse clothing,
and is not sated with dregs and husks.
It is not that they prefer beans and greens and despise grand mansions,
but rather that they have no other choice.
Even if they wished to intimidate others,
how could they do so?!"
The Literati said:
"The nobleman cherishes virtue,
the petty man cherishes land.
The worthy scholar sacrifices for fame,
the greedy man dies for profit.
Lǐ Sī coveted what he desired,
and brought upon himself what he detested.
Sūn Shū Áo foresaw things before they sprouted,
thrice left the position of chancellor without regret,
not because he delighted in lowliness and despised high salaries,
but because he considered dangers from afar and avoided harm with caution.
The ox for the suburban sacrifice,
fed for a full year,
clothed in embroidered silks,
to enter the temple hall,
the grand butcher grasps his bell-adorned knife
to part its hair;
at that moment,
it would wish to pull a heavy load up a steep slope,
but it cannot be done.
Shāng Yāng trapped in Péngchí,
Wú Qǐ lying by the king's corpse,
would have wished to wear coarse clothes and dwell in a thatched hut in a remote village,
but it could not be done.
Lǐ Sī served as Qín's chancellor,
wielding the world's authority,
his ambition belittling the sovereign;
by the time he was imprisoned,
torn apart by chariots in the market of Yúnyáng,
he too wished to carry firewood through the east gate,
walk the winding streets of Shàngcài,
but it could not be done.
Sū Qín and Wú Qǐ brought about their own deaths through power and influence,
Shāng Yāng and Lǐ Sī destroyed themselves through high status,
all drowned themselves by coveting salaries and chasing glory,
a hundred carriages in their train,
yet insufficient to carry their calamities!"
4.4 "Chapter 19: Praising the Worthy"
The Grand Master said:
"Bó Yí starved for his integrity,
Wěi Shēng died for his trustworthiness.
Losing the greater whole for a minor vessel,
such is the fidelity of common men and women.
They perish in ditches unknown.
What achievement or fame is there?
Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí,
their wisdom sufficient to strengthen the state,
their courage enough to awe enemies,
with one angered the feudal lords feared,
with them at rest the world was peaceful.
The lords of ten thousand chariots,
all without exception bowed their bodies and humbled their words,
offering rich gifts to seek friendship,
these are what we call famous scholars of the world.
Those whose wisdom is insufficient for planning,
and whose influence cannot impact the age,
are the lowest among the people.
Now you promote turning nothing into something,
emptiness into fullness,
commoners in worn shoes,
deep in thought and slow in step,
as if having lost something,
not the kind who establish merit and achieve fame,
yet still not free from worldly vulgarity."
The Literati said:
"Sū Qín became prominent in Zhào through the Vertical Alliance,
Zhāng Yí was employed in Qín through the Horizontal Alliance,
at that time,
they were not without honor and status,
yet men of wisdom followed with concern,
knowing that those who advance not by the Way will surely not retreat by the Way;
those who gain not by righteousness will surely not perish by righteousness.
The power of Jì and Mèng,
the wealth of the Three Huán,
could not be matched,
yet Confucius said of them, 'They are insignificant.'
As ministers,
those whose power equals the ruler's,
whose wealth rivals the state's,
perish.
Thus, the higher their position, the heavier their crimes;
the greater their salary, the more their offenses.
In action, one first preserves oneself and then seeks fame;
in office, one first avoids harm and then seeks salary.
Thus, the fragrant bait is not unappealing,
but the turtle and dragon hear of it and hide deep,
the phoenix sees it and soars high away,
knowing it harms the body.
As for crows, magpies, fish, and turtles,
they eat the fragrant bait and then fly and run wildly,
dodging heads and bending to escape,
but it avails nothing against death.
Now officials steal and wield state law,
advancing without regard for crime,
suddenly when crisis strikes,
then carriages race and people rush,
but it avails nothing against death.
What they stole is not enough to compensate for the plunder,
wives and children flee with nowhere to go,
they themselves in deep prisons,
with none to pity or visit them.
At such a time,
how could they find leisure to laugh?"
The Grand Master said:
"The Literati's conduct is lofty,
upright as if unrollable;
their words pure in high principle,
bright as if untaintable.
Yet the conscript Chén Shèng laid down his cart shafts,
first to rebel,
establishing himself as King of Zhàngchǔ,
originally without the conduct of recluses like Huí or Yóu,
nor the position of chancellor or ranked minister.
Rising in the great marsh,
in barely a month,
the Confucian, Mohist, and gentry followers of Qí and Lǔ,
let loose their long robes,
long robes, ceremonial attire. Carrying the ritual vessels of Confucius, the 'Odes' and 'Documents',
presented themselves as ministers.
Kǒng Jiǎ became Chén Shèng's erudite,
and eventually died with him in Chén,
becoming the great laugh of the world.
Are those who hide deep and flee high truly like this?"
The Literati said:
"The Zhōu house declined,
rites and righteousness crumbled,
unable to govern orderly,
the feudal lords of the world fought each other,
destroying one another,
merging into six states,
warfare unceasing,
the people unable to rest peacefully.
Qín, with the heart of a tiger or wolf,
nibbled away at the feudal lords,
swallowed the warring states to make commanderies and counties,
boasted of its ability and flaunted its achievements,
considering itself surpassing Yáo and Shùn and ashamed to be their equal.
Abandoning benevolence and righteousness to exalt punishments,
believing the present age not to learn from civility but decide by force.
Zhào Gāo administered justice within,
Méng Tián employed troops without,
the people were sorrowful and bitter,
united in suffering under Qín.
King Chén majestically rose, claws bared, initiating action for the world,
though his path was perilous, Confucians and Mohists involved themselves,
believing there had been no true king for long,
the Way blocked and unable to proceed,
from Confucius until then,
and Qín further heavily prohibited it,
hence they vented their fervor through King Chén.
Confucius said:
'If there were one to use me,
could I not create an Eastern Zhōu?'
Hoping perhaps for the achievements of Chéng Tāng, King Wén, and King Wǔ,
to rid the people of cruelty and brigandage,
how could they be coveting salaries and delighting in position?"
The Grand Master said:
"The Literati's words and actions may have the integrity of Bó Yí,
but not the steadfastness of Liǔxià Huì,
merely looking down from high and gazing up from low,
pure words and foul deeds,
over a cup of wine and dish of meat,
hesitating and yielding to each other,
refusing the small and taking the large,
chicken-like in small integrity but wolf-like in devouring.
Zhào Wǎn, Wáng Zāng, and their like,
promoted to high ministers through Confucian arts,
yet had hearts of treacherous profit and cruelty.
Zhǔfù Yǎn gained high office through eloquence,
stole weighty authority,
deceived the imperial clan,
accepted bribes from feudal lords,
and all were eventually executed.
Dōngfāng Shuò claimed himself peerless in debate and strategy,
melting hardness and dissolving stone,
unmatched in his time;
yet examining his private conduct,
even a madman would be unwilling to do,
and without Dōngfāng Shuò's eloquence,
what is there worth seeing in the rest?"
The Literati said:
"Those who aim at goodness forget evil,
the cautious in small matters achieve great ones.
In the space of sacrificial vessels, one can observe ritual,
within the women's quarters, one can judge conduct.
Those who wear ancient attire,
recite the ancient Way,
and yet turn to wrongdoing—
such are few."
Thus, a nobleman speaks only at the appropriate time,
takes only what is rightfully his,
and does not retain anything acquired through improper means.
Full yet not overflowing,
prosperous yet not arrogant.
Therefore, although Yuǎn Àng was close to Emperor Jǐng,
his stables held no more than four horses;
Gōngsūn Hóng, even when occupying the position of one of the Three Excellencies,
had no more than ten carriages at home;
although Dōngfāng Shuò's advice, words, and actions were heeded by Emperor Wǔ,
he was not arrogant or excessive;
Zhǔfù Yǎn had long experienced hardship and distress,
and was pained that those in power did not cherish the Way yet enjoyed wealth and honor,
with no one caring for the scholars.
Thus, he took his surplus resources to relieve the urgent needs of impoverished scholars,
not for the sake of his private household's estate.
The current age is noisy with complaints,
not because they worry about the scholars' chicken-like frugality,
but because they fear those in power are like tigers and owls, gorging themselves,
leaving nothing behind in their search for gain. "
5.1 "Mutual Criticism, Twentieth"
The Grand Master said:
"In ancient times,
they organized the well-field system,
regulated the residential areas,
men managed their fields,
women worked their hemp and flax,
there was no uncultivated land,
no idle people.
Thus, unless one was a merchant or artisan, one could not live by secondary pursuits;
unless one was a good farmer, one could not live by harvests;
unless one held government office, one could not live by official salaries.
Now, Confucian scholars abandon their plows and hoes to study impractical talk,
wasting long days,
with no benefit to governance,
drifting about aimlessly,
eating without farming,
clothing themselves without sericulture,
cunningly deceiving good people,
thereby robbing farmers and hindering administration—
this is what the present age should worry about. "
The Literati said:
"Yǔ was troubled by the floodwaters,
personally toiled himself,
traveling through marshes and lodging on the road,
passing his own door without entering.
At that time,
if his hairpin fell, he wouldn't pick it up,
if his hat was caught, he wouldn't look back—
how could he have had time to plow?
Confucius said:
'The poet was so aggrieved he could not remain silent;
I, Qiū, am so aggrieved I cannot remain hidden.'
Therefore, he traveled east, west, south, and north, presenting his ideas seventy times without being employed,
then withdrew to cultivate the Kingly Way,
composed the 'Spring and Autumn Annals',
leaving it for ten thousand generations to come,
for the world to take as their standard—
how could this be the same as the plowing and weaving of common men and women!
The 'Tradition' says:
'If the nobleman does not act in his time,
the people have nothing to look up to.'
Thus, without the nobleman, none can govern the common people;
without the common people, none can support the nobleman.
It is not appropriate for the nobleman to plow and weave as common men and women do.
If the nobleman plows without studying,
it leads to the path of chaos. "
The Grand Master said:
"The Literati speak of governance as surpassing that of Táng and Yú,
speak of righteousness as higher than the autumn sky—
they have flowery words,
but we have not seen their substance.
In the past, during the time of Duke Mù of Lǔ,
with Gōngyí Zǐ as chancellor,
and Zǐsī,
Zǐliǔ as his ministers,
yet they lost territory north to Qí,
making the Sì River their border,
feared Chǔ to the south,
treated Qín with guest rites to the west.
When Mèng Kē resided in Liáng,
their troops were defeated by Qí,
the supreme general died and the crown prince was captured,
they were defeated west by Qín,
land was seized and territory reduced,
losing Hénèi
and Héwài.
Among the disciples of Zhòngní,
the seventy followers
left their parents,
abandoned their families,
shouldered their burdens and followed Confucius,
studying without plowing—
yet chaos only grew worse.
Thus, a chest full of jade fragments
does not count as having treasure;
reciting the 'Book of Songs' and 'Book of Documents' while carrying satchels
does not count as possessing the Way.
The essential lies in bringing peace to the state,
benefiting the people,
not in mere elaborate phrases and numerous words. "
The Literati said:
"Yú did not employ Bǎilǐ Xī's strategies and perished,
while Duke Mù of Qín used them to achieve hegemony.
Not employing the worthy leads to ruin—
how could one avoid territorial losses?
When Mèngzǐ went to Liáng,
King Huì asked about profit,
but he responded with benevolence and righteousness.
Their aims and rejections did not align,
so he was not employed and left,
holding his treasure with no one to speak to.
Thus, having grain but not eating it
does no good for hunger;
seeing the worthy but not employing them
does no good for preventing territorial loss.
During Zhòu's time,
he had inside the two lords Wēizǐ
and Jīzǐ,
outside had Jiāogé
and Jízǐ,
yet he could not preserve his state.
When advice is given but not used,
remonstrance is offered but not heeded,
even with worthies present,
how could they benefit governance? "
The Grand Master said:
"Oranges and pomelos grow south of the Yangtze,
yet all people find them sweet to taste—
flavors are the same;
beautiful music comes from Zhèng
and Wèi, yet all enjoy it in their ears—
sounds are the same.
Zǐzāng of Yuè,
Yóuyú of the Róng,
needed interpreters to communicate,
yet both became eminent in Qí
and Qín— human hearts are the same regarding good and evil.
Thus, when Zēngzǐ leaned against the mountain and sang,
the mountain birds descended and circled;
when Shī Kuàng played the qin,
all the beasts came dancing.
There has never been goodness that did not find response,
sincerity that did not meet with answer.
Is it that the intent is not sincere?
Why then are your words not followed,
your actions not in harmony? "
The Literati said:
"Biǎn Què cannot cure illnesses that refuse acupuncture and medicine;
sages and worthies cannot correct rulers who reject admonition.
Thus, Jié had Guān Lóngpáng yet Xià perished;
Zhòu had three humane men yet Shāng fell.
So the problem is not lacking arguments like those of Yóuyú
and Zǐzāng,
but lacking the listening ears of a Huán
or a Mù.
Therefore, Confucius traveled east and west with nowhere to meet acceptance,
and Qū Yuán was exiled in Chǔ.
Hence it is said:
'Serving others with the upright Way—
where can one go without being dismissed thrice?
Serving others with the crooked Way—
why leave the land of one's parents?'
Ultimately, it's not that their words were unpersuasive or unheeded,
nor that their actions found no harmony. "
The Grand Master said:
"Singers do not aim for shrill voices,
but value being in tune;
debaters do not aim for ornate phrases,
but focus on factual substance.
One who sings well but does not understand modulation
cannot be considered skilled in singing;
one who speaks well but does not understand adaptation
cannot be considered skilled in persuasion.
Holding a compass to deny the square,
grasping a level to reject the plumb line,
understanding one hole,
knowing one principle,
yet unaware of balancing—
disbelieving others about what one hasn't seen oneself,
like a cicada knowing nothing of snow;
stubbornly clinging to ancient texts to meet contemporary needs—
it's like the misalignment of Orion and Sirius,
gluing the tuning pegs to adjust the sè,
inevitably hard to harmonize.
This is why Confucius found no employment in his time,
and Mèng Kē was despised by the feudal lords. "
The Literati said:
"The light of the sun and moon
cannot be seen by the blind;
the sound of thunder and lightning
cannot be heard by the deaf.
To speak to those who do not understand
is like talking to the mute and deaf.
How is this different from a cicada not knowing heavy snow?
Even with the wisdom of Yī Yǐn
and the virtue of Tàigōng,
they could not persuade Jié
and Zhòu—not because the speakers were at fault,
but because the listeners were at fault.
Thus, Jīng Hé embraced his uncut jade and wept tears of blood,
saying:
'Where can I find a skilled craftsman to cut it open!'
Qū Yuán wandered chanting by the marsh,
saying:
'Where can I find a Gāo Yáo to examine my case!'
All rulers wish to seek worthy men to assist them
and employ capable men to govern the state.
Yet, misled by popular opinions
and confused by flattery,
the worthy and sage are obscured,
while slanderers and sycophants hold power.
This leads to the destruction of states and families,
while worthy scholars starve in mountain caves.
In the past, Zhào Gāo had no extraordinary talent,
yet occupied a position over ten thousand people,
thus overthrowing the Qín state and bringing disaster to its lineage.
He completely lost his zither—
how could it be tuned with glued pegs?"
The Grandee said:
"Those called top-ranking Literati
should have the wisdom to understand the methods of former kings
and the capability to carry out their ways.
Thus, at home they serve as teachers,
in office they become models for the world.
Now when the Literati speak of governance, they praise Yáo
and Shùn; when discussing conduct, they cite Kǒngzǐ
and Mòzǐ. Yet when entrusted with administration, they fail;
they cherish the ancient Way but cannot practice it.
Their words are straightforward but their actions crooked,
their principles correct but their intentions false.
In dress they differ from villagers,
but in substance they are no different from ordinary people.
What you scholars call 'upright and fair'
are merely those who happened to encounter opportunity
and were selected by chance.
They hardly match what true recommendation means,
and thus cannot be discussed with concerning governance."
The Literati said:
"Heaven established the three lights to illuminate the world;
the Son of Heaven established ministers to clarify governance.
Thus it is said:
Ministers are
the models for all under heaven,
the vermilion and blue of divine transformation.
Above, they bear the responsibility of assisting the enlightened ruler;
below, they undertake the task of continuing sagely influence.
They harmonize yīn and yáng,
adjust the four seasons,
pacify the masses,
nurture all living beings,
enable the common people to live in harmony,
without resentful expressions,
and make the barbarians submit to virtue,
free from worries of rebellion.
These are the duties of ministers
and what the worthy strive for.
Even with talents like Yī Yǐn,
the Duke of Zhōu, and Shào serving as three lords,
or Tài Diān
and Hóng Yāo as nine ministers,
we Literati may not meet the sage ruler's wise selection,
but today's administrators
also fail to match such great virtue."
The Grandee, displeased,
changed countenance and did not respond.
The Literati said:
"A court without loyal ministers leads to dark governance;
officials without upright scholars endanger their positions.
Rèn Zuò directly addressed his lord's faults,
and Lord Wén changed his conduct,
becoming known as a worthy ruler.
Yuán Àng confronted Jiàng Hóu about his arrogance,
and eventually gained his favor.
Thus, those who risk death to point out the ruler's errors
are loyal ministers;
those who offend dignity to correct ministers' mistakes
are upright scholars.
We rustics cannot speak contrary in alleys and to faces.
Currently, the grain procurement edict
is proclaimed but not implemented,
many salary recipients are unqualified,
hindering agriculture, trade, and crafts.
The profits of the marketplace
do not return to the people,
yet the people's expectations remain unblocked.
Moreover, the Way of emperors and kings
is largely ruined and unrepaired.
The Book of Songs says:
'Many are the officers.'
The meaning is truly to employ their counsel,
not just to present empty words."
5.2 Divergent Paths, Chapter Twenty-One
The Grandee said:
"The seventy disciples personally received the sage's teachings,
their names listed among Kǒngzǐ's followers,
all possessing the talent of feudal lords and ministers,
with several capable of facing south as rulers.
In governance, there were Rǎn Yǒu
and Jì Lù;
in rhetoric, Zǎi Wǒ
and Zǐgòng.
Zǎi Wǒ held office,
was favored in Qí,
but when Tián Cháng raised rebellion,
his Way failed,
he died in the court,
and Duke Jiǎn was killed at Tántái.
Zǐlù served in Wèi;
when Kǒng Kuī rebelled,
he could not save his lord from exile,
and was minced in Wèi.
Zǐgòng
and Zǐgāo fled,
unable to die for the crisis.
Receiving heavy salaries from others, they could not repay;
holding high office, they could not preserve their lord.
How selfish they were, valuing themselves over their lords!
They studied under the same master,
considered themselves knowledgeable in ancient and modern righteousness,
and clear on the rites between ruler and minister.
Yet some died, some fled—
these few took different paths.
How contradictory their ways were!"
The Literati said:
"Duke Shāng of Sòng knew of Kǒng Fù's worth but did not employ him early,
so he died.
Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ knew of Jì Yǒu's worth,
but entrusted him with governance too late, and the state fell into chaos.
The ruler of Wèi favored sycophants and distanced the worthy;
Zǐlù resided in Pú,
while Kǒng Kuī administered.
Duke Jiǎn did not heed Zǎi Wǒ, leaking his plan.
Thus, both rulers were exiled or killed,
and disaster reached loyal ministers.
These two disciples had duties but were excluded from planning,
so they could choose death
or life,
departure or stay—
their righteousness was the same.
Yàn Yīng did not die in the Cuī
and Qìng crisis;
can it be said he was unrighteous?
Wēizǐ left the chaos of Yīn;
can it be said he was unvirtuous?"
The Grandee said:
"The finest plain jade
needs no adornment;
the worthiest preserve authenticity,
no false ornament can enhance them.
Thus, gold and jade need no carving,
beautiful pearls no painting.
Now, Zhòng Yóu
and Rǎn Qiú lack the timber of sandalwood
or the uncut jade of Suí and Hé,
yet you forcefully embellish them,
like carving rotten wood or sharpening a lead knife,
adorning an ugly woman or painting a clay figure.
Covered with five colors,
they may appear splendid,
but when encountering flowing water,
they wash away.
Those who heavily cherish the ancient Way,
pillowing the Book of Songs
and Book of Documents,
cannot bring safety in danger,
nor order in chaos.
Chasing a chicken through the village,
does the chicken have a faction?"
The Literati said:
"Without learning, there is no means to cultivate oneself;
without ritual, there is nothing to support virtue.
The uncut jade of Hé Shì
is a beautiful treasure of the world,
yet it requires the work of the jade-cutter to become brilliant.
Máo Qiáng,
the most beautiful woman in the world,
needs perfumes and cosmetics to enhance her appearance.
The Duke of Zhōu,
the most sagely man in the world,
required learned teachers and inquiry to become enlightened.
Nowadays, ordinary people of our age
do not love learning and inquiry,
but rely solely on their own foolishness to shoulder great responsibilities,
like crossing rivers and seas without oars or rudder
and encountering a great wind,
drifting to sink in abysses hundreds of fathoms deep,
flowing eastward into shoreless streams—
how could they be stopped and saved?"
The Grand Master said:
"Nature has its firmness and softness,
forms have their likes and dislikes;
the sage can follow them but cannot change them.
Confucius changed the attire of his disciples outwardly,
but could not transform their hearts.
Thus, Zǐlù laid aside his long sword,
removed his perilous cap,
and bowed in submission at the Master's gate,
yet when leading troops among friends,
he remained assertive,
and his coarse heart still remained.
Zǎi Yǔ slept during the day
and sought to reduce the three-year mourning period.
Confucius said:
'A wall of dung and earth
cannot be plastered,'
and 'Yóu (Zǐlù) seems to not die a natural death.'
Thus, if one lacks the inner substance but learns the external refinements,
even with worthy teachers and good friends,
it is like carving on grease or engraving ice—
a waste of time and effort.
Hence, a fine teacher cannot adorn the hunchback,
nor can perfumes transform Mó Mǔ (an ugly woman)."
The Literati said:
"If Xī Shī is covered with filth,
even a coarse man will cover his nose;
if an ugly person is richly adorned,
they can preside at the ancestral sacrifices to God.
Had these two not entered the gate of the sage,
they would not have escaped being poor men—
how could they have gained the names of ministers and grand masters?
Thus, the whetstone is what brings the blade to sharpness,
learning is what enables one to exhaust their talents.
Confucius said:
'A gū that is not a gū,
a gū indeed,
a gū indeed!'
Thus, with human effort added, it becomes a vessel for the ancestral temple;
otherwise, it is firewood for the cook's stove.
If the metal of Wú and Yuè is not tempered,
a commoner despises it;
if a craftsman applies his skill,
the ruler wears it at court.
The ugly person considers themselves beautiful,
and so does not adorn;
the foolish person considers themselves wise,
and so does not learn.
They are laughed at by others without realizing it themselves,
do not like to employ others,
and this is the fault of self-righteousness."
5.3 "Disputing Worthiness, Chapter 22"
The Grand Master said:
"The hard breaks,
the soft curls.
Thus, Jì Yóu (Zǐlù) died because of his strength,
Zǎi Wǒ (Zǎi Yǔ) was killed because of his weakness.
Had these two not studied,
they might not have met their deaths.
Why?
They boasted of themselves and flaunted their abilities,
with little wisdom but great responsibilities,
wishing others to follow them,
unable to follow others themselves,
seeing without being looked at,
valuing themselves without being priced,
this is why they were killed and ended as minced meat.
We do not see them as vessels for the ancestral temple,
but witness them being executed by the world.
At that time,
where did the eastward flow take them?"
The Literati said:
"When a fine horse pulls a salt cart,
hanging its head on the slope of Tàiháng Mountain,
the butcher holds his knife and eyes it.
When Lord Shàng was in poverty,
peddling goods in Zhāogē,
the disheveled crowds gathered and laughed at him.
At that time,
it was not that there were no talents with great potential,
but without King Wén
or Bó Lè, none knew their value.
Zǐlù
and Zǎi Wǒ did not live to meet Bó Lè's recommendation,
but encountered mad butchers,
hence the gentleman grieves for them.
If
'Yóu seems to not die a natural death,'
then 'Heaven is cursing me.'
The troubles of Kǒng Fù with Huá Dū
cannot be said to be unrighteous.
The disaster of Qiú Mù involving Sòng Wàn
cannot be said to be unworthy."
The Grand Master said:
"Today's scholars
lack the abilities of Lord Shàng,
the talents of fine horses,
but have the venom of wasps and scorpions that harms themselves.
Chéng Yǒng from Dōnghǎi
and Hú Jiàn from Hédōng are examples.
These two were recommended through crafty methods,
rose from the ranks of soldiers,
to become county magistrates.
Alone in their self-righteousness,
none could cooperate with them.
Pulled, they would not come;
pushed, they would not go;
arrogant and unruly,
spiteful and disrespectful,
they offended princesses,
and encroached upon high ministers.
Knowing it was impossible yet forcing it,
they sought to gain fame.
Their path was unrighteous,
and indeed it cost them their lives.
We do not see their achievements,
but witness the calamity of the eastern observation—
they incurred grave crimes,
and did not die a natural death.
Cunning, they considered themselves wise;
accusatory, they thought themselves upright;
unruly, they deemed themselves brave—
their encountering disaster
was thus fitting."
The Literati said:
"These two gentlemen cherished pure hearts,
practiced the way of loyalty and integrity,
were upright in serving their superiors,
exhausted their strength for the public good,
upheld the law and reasoned justly,
did not avoid the powerful,
did not favor their close ones,
did not value the support of wife and children,
did not care for their private family's affairs.
Yet ultimately they could not escape envious people,
and were pushed aside by the multitude of wrongs.
This is why they suffered unpredictable punishments and their merits were unfulfilled.
If the royal clan is not upright, laws and decrees will not be carried out;
if the key officials are not upright, treachery and evil will arise.
Zhào Shē enforced this on Píngyuán Jūn,
Fàn Jū enforced this on Ráng Hóu,
and two states were well-governed, two families preserved.
Thus, when the ruler errs, the minister corrects;
when the superior is wrong, the inferior criticizes.
If high ministers are upright,
what fault lies with the county magistrate?
Not reflecting on oneself but blaming others
is a great failure of governance.
When Qū Yuán drowned himself,
it was due to Zǐ Jiāo's slander;
when Guǎn Zhòng could practice his way,
it was thanks to Bào Shū's efforts.
Now, not seeing Bào Shū's efforts,
but witnessing the disaster of the Mìluó River,
even if one wishes to die a natural death,
how can it be achieved?"
5.4 "Following the Way, Chapter 23"
The Grand Master said:
"Censor!"
The Censor did not respond.
The Ministerial Secretary said to the Chancellor's Historian:
"The Literati began learning speech in their youth,
holding it close without letting go,
their words swirling in cycles,
turning like a potter's wheel.
Their prose blooms like spring flowers,
yet proves as futile as clutching the wind.
They adorn empty words to confuse reality,
praising antiquity to harm the present.
If we follow them,
the state's finances will be wasted,
and hollow statements cannot be implemented substantively;
if we do not,
the Literati deem us wrong,
with clamoring voices everywhere,
too numerous to heed.
You gentlemen have long served in the grand offices,
versed in ancient ways,
and clear about the contemporary world—
now, which path should we take to proceed?"
The Chancellor's Historian stepped forward and said:
"Duke Wén of Jìn was cunning but not upright,
while Duke Huán of Qí was upright but not cunning;
their paths differed,
yet both achieved hegemony.
To rigidly follow antiquity without change,
clinging to old ways without reform,
is to keep substance and form unchanged,
like still using crude carts.
Thus, some innovate,
others carry on traditions,
only then can laws harmonize with the people,
and tools become convenient for use.
Kǒngzǐ answered three rulers differently,
and Yànzǐ served three lords with distinct methods—
not arbitrarily opposing,
but responding to differing times.
Since the high officials have set the course for great endeavors,
establishing an inexhaustible foundation,
I hope they will not heed trivial arguments,
nor be swayed by Ruist
or Mohist doctrines."
The Literati said:
"When Master Kuáng tuned the five notes,
he never lost the gōng and shāng.
When sage kings governed the world,
they never strayed from benevolence and righteousness.
Thus, there may be names for reforming institutions,
but no change in the essence of the Way.
From Huángdì above
to the Three Kings below,
all illuminated virtuous teachings,
carefully maintained schools,
honored benevolence and righteousness,
and established education.
This is the unchangeable Way for a hundred generations.
Yīn and Zhōu followed it and flourished,
while the Qín king altered laws and perished.
The Shī says:
'Though there are no aged wise men,
the statutes and models remain.'
It speaks of laws and teachings;
thus, preserve them after their creators' passing,
uphold and thread them together,
thread and practice them—
why change anything?"
The Chancellor's Historian said:
"Praising Xīshī's beauty does not improve one's looks,
extolling Yáo
and Shùn's virtue does not aid governance.
Now the Literati do not speak of how to govern,
but claim our governance lacks merit,
like not discussing farming methods,
yet admiring a rich man's full granary.
Those who desire grain must heed the seasons,
those who seek order must adapt to the times.
Thus, Lord Shāng alone clearly saw that survival and perish cannot align with vulgar customs,
for they hinder achievement and favor shortsightedness.
Mediocre people cling to the old,
and fools stubbornly believe what they hear.
So, the regulation of boats and carts
took three years before the people accepted it.
Only after Lord Shāng's laws were established
did the people trust them.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Some may share learning,
but not discretion in weighing circumstances.'
The Literati may follow rules and carvings,
but are not fit to discuss beyond conventional ways."
The Literati said:
"The nobleman hears much and sets aside doubts,
transmits without inventing,
is sagely and plans greatly,
wise and undertakes little.
Thus, his achievements endure without collapse,
his fame stands without faltering.
The petty man, with shallow wisdom, aims high,
weak yet bears heavy burdens,
so he fails midway—
Sū Qín
and Shāng Yāng are such examples.
Without the former kings' laws,
rejecting the sages' Way,
and relying on themselves alone,
they thus perished.
The Yì says:
'When a petty man holds high position,
though elevated, he must fall.
Not filling his Way,
not constant in his virtue,
yet able to end well—
such a thing has never been.
Therefore, he first ascends to heaven,
then plunges into earth.'
When Yǔ managed the floods,
the people knew the benefits,
and all urged on his work.
When Shāng Yāng established laws,
the people knew the harms,
and all feared his punishments.
Thus, Xià Hòu achieved merit and became king,
while Shāng Yāng enforced laws and perished.
Shāng Yāng had unique insights,
but the world lacks proof of exclusive vision.
If the Literati cannot weigh contemporary affairs,
at least they bear no burdens or suffer calamities."
5.5 "On Criticism, Chapter Twenty-Four"
The Chancellor's Historian said:
"Yànzǐ once said:
'Ruists are flowery in speech but lacking in substance,
extravagant in music but negligent toward the people,
prolong mourning to harm life,
lavish burials to damage livelihoods,
rites so complex they are hard to practice,
the Way so迂遠難行難遵,
praising the past to slander the present,
disdaining the seen while valuing the heard.'
Such people are fundamentally crooked,
taking themselves as the standard.
This is why Yán Yì was executed and dismissed,
and Dí Shān died among the Xiōngnú.
Holding office yet opposing their court,
living in an era yet defaming their superiors,
ending up slain and losing their lives—
who alone bears the burden and suffers the calamity here?"
The Literati said:
"Rites prevent excess,
music transforms customs,
when rites thrive and music is correct, punishments fit.
Thus, with dikes built, people avoid floods,
with礼義 established, people avoid chaos and trouble.
If礼義 crumble,
and dikes break,
orderly governance
has never existed.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'In rites,
rather than extravagance,
prefer frugality;
in mourning,
rather than ease,
prefer grief.'
So rites are not made
to harm life or damage livelihoods,
nor are dignified ceremonies and rules
meant to disrupt transformation or hurt customs.
Orderly states carefully uphold rites,
while endangered states strictly enforce laws.
Formerly, Qín swallowed the world by force,
and Lǐ Sī
and Zhào Gāo aggravated its disaster with evils,
abolishing ancient methods,
destroying old rites,
solely relying on penal laws,
so that Ruist
and Mohist ways were lost.
Blocking scholars' paths,
stifling people's voices,
flattery daily advanced, and the ruler heard no faults—
this is why Qín lost the world and its altars fell.
Thus, when sages govern,
they first punish those
who use clever words to abet wrongs and overthrow states.
Now, why do you bring forth words from a perished state?
High officials in their positions,
not rectifying the Way,
but willfully flattering and following trends,
detest petty men's shallow compliance,
yet they complete others' errors.
Thus, those who know speech may die,
unwilling to follow the obsequious,
and so cannot avoid bonds.
Alas!"
The Minister's Historian said:
"Sandalwood and oak trees have their habitats,
reeds and rushes grow in clusters,
showing how things of a kind follow one another.
Confucius said:
'Virtue is never left to stand alone;
it always has neighbors.'
Thus when Tāng rose, Yī Yǐn came to him,
and the unprincipled stayed far away.
There has never been an enlightened ruler above with treacherous ministers below.
Now the late Emperor personally practiced the Way of benevolence and sageliness,
governing the entire realm,
summoning and promoting men of outstanding talent, worthies, and literati,
employing only the benevolent,
executing and banishing treacherous ministers,
without sparing even his own kin,
striving to seek the worthy while dismissing the unworthy,
just as Yáo promoted Shùn,
and Yǔ's clan,
executing Gǔn and exiling Huān Dōu.
Yet you claim
they were 'opportunistic followers',
implying the ruler was at fault and the ministers flattered him—
is this correct?"
The Literati said:
"Gāo Yáo replied to Shùn:
'The difficulty lies in understanding men,
even for the Emperor.'
During the great flood disaster,
Yáo alone worried and toiled yet could not control it,
until he obtained Shùn
and Yǔ, and the nine provinces were pacified.
without aides like Shùn
and Yǔ,
pure virtue could not spread.
The Spring and Autumn Annals criticizes having a ruler but no ministers.
In the late Emperor's time,
good ministers were not complete,
so evil ministers found opportunities.
When Yáo obtained Shùn
and Yǔ, Gǔn was executed and Huān Dōu punished,
and when Zhào Jiǎnzǐ obtained Shū Xiàng, Shèng Qīngjiān was dismissed.
It is said:
'Until you see the noble man,
you cannot recognize the hypocritical minister.'
The Book of Songs says:
'Before I saw my lord,
my heart was full of sorrow.
Having seen my lord,
my heart is at peace.'
This expresses it."
The Minister's Historian said:
"Yáo appointed Gǔn
and Huān Dōu,
but when he obtained Shùn
and Yǔ, he exiled and executed them for their crimes,
and all under heaven submitted,
because he punished the unprincipled.
A ruler employs men to govern the people,
yet Yán Yì,
formerly a village head of Jǐ'nán,
was raised by the late Emperor to high position,
attaining the rank of senior minister.
Dí Shān rose from common cloth,
became a Hàn advisory minister,
occupied positions like Shùn
and Yǔ's,
holding the central power of the realm,
yet failed to govern properly,
instead committing the offense of slandering his superior;
thus the punishment that befell Huān Dōu came upon him.
The worthy receive rewards while the unworthy suffer punishment—
this is only natural.
Why should the Literati find this strange?"
The Literati said:
"Debaters should support each other with righteousness,
enlighten each other with the Way,
follow goodness without striving to win,
submit to righteousness without shame in poverty.
If they mislead each other with falsehoods,
confuse each other with rhetoric,
boast about having the last word,
aiming only for temporary victory,
this is not honorable.
Now Sū Qín
and Zhāng Yí
deluded the feudal lords,
overthrew mighty states,
causing rulers to lose their grasp;
not that they weren't eloquent,
but theirs was the way of chaos.
The noble man detests the vile who cannot serve a ruler properly,
fearing their compliance that leads to any extreme.
Now you fail to heed true righteousness in assisting ministers,
but instead follow and flatter them,
fond of momentary arguments,
without considering the consequences.
If you, as an official,
deserve severe punishment,
you should simply remain silent!"
The Minister's Historian said:
"I have heard that a scholar in this world
should have clothing sufficient to cover his body,
food and drink enough to support his parents,
internally able to provide comfort,
externally not dependent on others.
Thus only with self-cultivation can one manage a family,
and only with family management can one govern in office.
Hence, one who eats coarse vegetables cannot speak of filial piety,
one whose wife and children suffer hunger and cold cannot speak of kindness,
one who fails to maintain his livelihood cannot speak of management.
Living in this world,
behaving thus,
and having these three failings—
this too is reason enough to remain silent."
5.6 "Filial Support, Chapter Twenty-Five"
The Literati said:
"Good support does not necessarily mean fine meats,
good clothing does not necessarily mean brocades.
Using all one has to serve one's parents
is the height of filial piety.
Thus even a commoner's diligence
can fulfill ritual requirements,
eating beans and drinking water
can express respect fully.
Confucius said:
'Nowadays filial piety
is called being able to support;
but without respect,
how is it different?'
Thus the highest filial piety nurtures the will,
the next nurtures the countenance,
the lowest nurtures the body.
Value lies in the ritual,
not in coveting the support;
when ritual is harmonious and hearts are at peace,
even if support is incomplete,
it is acceptable.
The Book of Changes says:
'The eastern neighbor slaying an ox
is not as good as the western neighbor's simple sacrifice.'
Thus wealth and honor without ritual
are inferior to poverty and humility with filial devotion.
Within the household, practice filial piety fully,
outside it, practice brotherly respect fully,
with friends, practice trust fully—
these three
constitute the height of filial piety.
Managing a household well
does not mean accumulating wealth;
serving parents filially
does not mean offering rare delicacies,
but rather having harmonious expressions,
following their wishes, and fulfilling ritual righteousness."
The Minister's Historian said:
"Eighty is called dié,
seventy is called mào.
The mào-aged cannot be satisfied without meat,
cannot be warm without silk clothes.
Thus filial sons offer sweet and crisp foods to please the palate,
light and warm garments to comfort the body.
When Zēng Zǐ supported Zēng Xī,
there was always wine and meat.
Without formal attire,
even Gōngxī Chì could not maintain decorum.
Without dishes and meals,
even Mǐn
and Zēng could not complete their support.
Ritual is not empty form;
thus there must be substance before ornamentation.
Better to have abundant support with insufficient ritual
than abundant ritual with insufficient support.
Washing a cup to fill it with water,
bowing while presenting coarse food—
though ritual is complete,
this is not honorable."
The Literati said:
"King Xiāng of Zhōu's mother certainly had wine and meat;
her clothing and food were no less than those of Zēng Xī,
yet she bore the reputation of being unfilial,
because she failed in serving her parents.
The nobleman values the rites,
while the petty man covets material support.
Even if you call out 'Here!' and beckon,
or toss something to them,
a beggar would still not accept it.
If a nobleman lacks the proper rites,
he will not eat even fine food.
Thus, if the host does not personally serve the meal,
the guest will not perform the sacrificial rite.
This shows that the offering is light, but the rites are weighty."
The Chancellor's Secretary said:
"No filial piety is greater than supporting parents with the resources of the empire or a state,
next is supporting them with an official salary,
and the lowest is supporting them by manual labor.
Thus, kings and dukes, the rulers of men,
represent the highest form;
ministers and high officials,
the next.
Speaking in terms of ordinary families,
if there is a worthy son holding office in the world,
the parents enjoy lofty halls and deep chambers,
comfortable carriages and large horses,
wearing light and warm clothing,
eating sweet and delicate food.
Without such a son,
they wear coarse garments and leather caps,
dwelling in impoverished alleys,
with mornings but no evenings secured,
eating coarse vegetables and rough greens,
only seeing meat during the Lóu and Là sacrifices.
An elderly parent's belly is not a garden plot,
yet it is filled only with vegetables.
Coarse vegetables and rough food
are what even beggars would not take,
yet a son uses them to support his parents.
Even if he wishes to observe the rites,
it is not honorable."
The Literati said:
"To hold a position without the ability for it,
to enjoy a salary without the merit for it,
even with wealth and honor,
is like the support provided by Zhí
and Jué.
Gazing from a high tower,
with a table of food spread far and wide,
one cannot be called filial.
An elderly parent's belly is not a thief's sack;
why should it constantly hold ill-gotten goods?
To take what is not rightfully yours or within your duty,
wealth comes but trouble follows.
If one meets death and disaster,
how can they enjoy meat at the Lóu and Là sacrifices?
Zēng Shēn
and Mǐn Zǐ lacked the support of ministers or chancellors,
yet had the name of filial sons;
King Xiāng of Zhōu possessed the wealth of the empire,
yet bore the burden of being unable to serve his parents.
Thus, meager rites with abundant support
is not filial piety.
To plunder granaries to provide support
is not filial piety."
The Chancellor's Secretary said:
"The highest filial piety pleases the parents' countenance,
the next best brings peace to the parents,
the next preserves one's own person.
In the past,
Chén Yú turned against the Hàn,
and was beheaded at the Zhī River;
Wǔ Bèi, through wicked rebellion,
had his three clans exterminated.
In recent times,
Zhǔfǔ Yǎn acted unlawfully and was executed with his family;
Lǚ Bùshū wagged his tongue and was put to death;
if one does not conduct themselves carefully,
punishment may extend to innocent relatives.
From this we see:
Empty rites bring no benefit to oneself.
Substance and form must match in action,
both rites and support must be applied,
then one can speak of filial piety.
Filial piety lies in genuine substance,
not in ornamental appearances;
preserving one's person lies in caution and care,
not in glib talk."
The Literati said:
"To speak without sincerity,
to make promises without keeping them,
to be cowardly in facing difficulties,
to be disloyal in serving one's lord—
these are the greatest forms of unfiliality.
Mèngzǐ said:
'The scholars of today,
the high officials of today,
are all criminals.
They all迎合 their lord's wishes to indulge his faults.'
Now you, lacking loyalty and trustworthiness,
use clever words to disrupt governance,
flattering to seek favor.
Such as you
are not tolerated by the world.
The Spring and Autumn Annals say:
'A scholar holds to one principle without shifting,
follows reason without seeking external aid,
and simply fulfills his duty.'
Thus, for one in a low position to speak of high matters
is a crime;
to speak when it is not one's place to speak
is presumption.
There is an edict for the dukes and ministers to discuss this matter;
why do we merely wage a war of words?"
5.7 "Criticizing Deliberations - Chapter 26"
The Chancellor's Secretary said:
"Mountains do not refuse small pebbles and steps,
thus achieving their height;
a nobleman does not refuse the words of firewood carriers,
thus broadening his reputation.
Therefore, he who sees much is broad,
he who hears much is wise,
he who rejects advice is obstructed,
he who is self-willed is isolated.
Thus, he who consults with those below has no failed strategies,
he who enlists the masses has no abandoned achievements.
The Book of Songs says:
'Consult even the grass and firewood gatherers.'
Thus, even commoners can offer opinions,
how much more so the secretaries of dukes and ministers?
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, scholars are not recorded,
but Xuān is written about,
because he was a steward-official.
Confucius said:
'Though I am not employed,
I am still consulted.'
Though I am not clever,
I have often listened attentively from a lower position,
holding up my gown and bending my fingers,
receiving instruction on the path of the nobleman.
If what the Literati say is right,
how can my words do harm?
If what the Literati say is wrong,
even without me, the Chancellor's Secretary,
who would not criticize them?"
The Literati said:
"To assist others with correctness is called loyalty;
to mislead others with wickedness is called flattery.
He who rejects faults and accepts good counsel
is a loyal minister to the ruler,
an upright scholar among officials.
Confucius said:
'If a high official has three remonstrating ministers,
even if he is unprincipled,
he will not lose his family.'
Now you stand in the ranks of steward-officials,
yet lack a loyal and upright heart.
You cannot straighten what is crooked,
cannot correct what is evil,
but go with the flow to preserve yourself,
follow the wind to please your superiors.
Whatever the superior says, you heed without question;
whatever the superior does, you bend to follow,
like a shadow following the form,
an echo responding to the sound,
never determining right or wrong.
You wear the robes of a Confucian,
don the cap of a Confucian,
but cannot practice its Way—
