you are no true Confucian.
You are like an earthen dragon:
it has the patterns, head, and eyes, but is not a dragon.
Dǐnglì resembles a vegetable but tastes different;
jade and stone look alike but are of different kinds.
You are not the kind of Confucian who upholds the classics and preserves the Way like the followers of Confucius,
but rather a Confucian who flatters the dukes and ministers to their faces;
you are not of our kind.
Rǎn Yǒu, as steward to the Jì family, added to their excesses,
and Confucius said:
'My disciples, you may beat the drum and attack him;
it is permissible.'
Thus, to assist a Jié is not wisdom;
to collect taxes for a Jié is not benevolence."
The Chancellor's Secretary fell silent and did not reply.
5.8 "Debating Profit - Chapter 27"
The high official said:
"The enlightened rulers of our age,
concerned and laboring for the myriad people,
mindful that the northern borders remain unsettled,
therefore dispatched envoys to select virtuous and worthy men,
and eminent scholars of literature,
extensively inviting those who possess the Way,
intending to observe extraordinary proposals and unique strategies,
opening their minds and inclining their ears to listen,
hoping perhaps to gain something.
Yet you scholars are incapable of producing marvelous plans or long-term schemes,
or strategies to attack the Xiōngnú and pacify the borders.
Clutching dried bamboo scrolls,
clinging to empty words,
you know not what is appropriate to embrace or discard,
nor the changes of the times.
Your discussions lack any foundation,
like scratching one's back when the knee itches.
Debating noisily beneath the court's gates,
your clamor is unbearable to hear.
It is as if by mere chatter you could accomplish anything.
Is this what an enlightened ruler wishes to hear?"
The scholars of literature replied:
"The responses in our memorials,
though varied in approach, converge in purpose,
aiming to exalt ritual and righteousness,
push back wealth and profit,
restore the ways of antiquity,
and correct the errors of the present age.
All speak of achieving great peace;
though not entirely practicable,
surely there are some feasible points among them.
Those in authority are blind to the clarity of ritual,
yet well-versed in the trivialities of profit.
Thwarting affairs and ruining proposals,
in their calculations and schemes,
they have thus left matters unresolved to this day.
It is not that the Ru fail to accomplish things;
it is that the high ministers seek only to secure profit."
The high official said:
"Fierce in appearance but weak within—
such are those who confuse the genuine.
Embroidered on the surface but coarse inside—
such are those who confuse the substantial.
You scholars, in wide sleeves and broad belts,
steal the attire of Zhōu Gōng;
bowing and scraping with nervous deference,
you steal the demeanor of Zhòngní;
in your discussions and recitations,
you steal the words of Zǐgòng and Zǐxià;
in criticizing and speaking of governance,
you steal the talents of Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Yīng.
Your hearts despise the high ministers and chancellors,
your ambitions belittle the sovereign.
Yet when entrusted with governance,
you bring chaos and fail to administer.
Thus, to select men by their words
is like judging a horse by its hair.
This is why so many prove unworthy of recommendation.
The imperial edict states:
'We admire the scholars within the realm,
hence extensively invite the brave, brilliant, and learned scholars from all quarters,
promoting them to official posts and emoluments.'
Those who speak well need not possess virtue.
Why so?
Because speaking is easy, but acting is hard.
Some abandon their carriage yet recognize their ox,
valuing its silence while it accomplishes much.
The Wú bell destroys itself with its own clapper;
Zhǔfù Yǎn brought about his own death with his tongue.
The nightjar calls at night,
but it does not help the dawn;
Zhǔfù Yǎn hooted like an owl,
but it did not save him from death.
It is not that the officials seek only profit;
rather, you scholars are shackled by outdated methods,
tethered by idle talk."
The scholars of literature said:
"Those who can speak
and act accordingly
are like Tāng and Wǔ.
Those who can speak
but cannot act
are the officials.
We scholars may steal Zhōu Gōng's attire,
but you officials steal Zhōu Gōng's positions.
We scholars are shackled by outdated methods,
but you officials are shackled by wealth and profit.
Zhǔfù Yǎn died by his own tongue,
and you officials are trapped by your own greed.
A steed capable of a thousand lǐ—
without Zàofǔ, none can drive it;
Yǔ's wisdom worth ten thousand men—
without Shùn as his minister, it could not be employed.
Thus, when Jǐ Huánzǐ assumed governance, [101 Liǔxià Huì suddenly disappeared;
when Kǒngzǐ became minister of crime,
only then did depravity cease to flourish.
For a steed, its recognition lies with Bó Lè,
but its achievement lies with Zàofǔ.
When Zàofǔ takes the reins,
be the horse inferior or fine,
all can tread the path.
In Zhōu Gōng's time,
whether scholars were worthy or not,
all could discuss perfect governance.
Thus, a skilled driver is good at handling horses,
and a worthy minister is good at employing scholars.
Now, to promote exceptional talent and have stable grooms drive them
is like yoking a steed to a salt cart and demanding it run swiftly.
This is why so many virtuous and worthy scholars
and men of literature prove unworthy of recommendation."
The high official said:
"Alas!
You scholars are base and without conduct,
full of words but of no use,
your inner feelings and outer appearance mismatched.
Like burglars who dig through walls,
you have been a plague since ancient times.
This is why Kǒng Qiū was driven out by the ruler of Lǔ,
and found no use in his time.
Why so?
Because he initiated too many doctrines,
out of step with the times and lacking essence.
Thus, the Qín king burned his teachings and did not practice them,
burying his followers in the Wèi River and not employing them.
How then can you wag your tongues,
raise your eyebrows,
and step forward to debate,
passing judgment on the affairs of the state?"
5.9 "The Nation's Afflictions, Chapter 28"
The scholars of literature said:
"When a state has worthy scholars but does not employ them,
it is not the fault of the scholars,
but the shame of the ruler.
Kǒngzǐ,
a great sage,
was not used by the feudal lords.
Holding a minor post in Lǔ,
within three months,
his influence spread without orders,
and prohibitions ceased without being enforced,
abundant like a seasonal rain irrigating the myriad things,
causing all to flourish.
How much more could he have achieved, positioned in the court of all under heaven,
disseminating the virtuous teachings and grace of a sage ruler?
Now, the high ministers occupy esteemed positions,
holding the reins of the world,
for over ten years,
yet they have bestowed no merit or virtue upon the realm,
only toiling the common people.
The people are impoverished and destitute,
while private households amass fortunes of ten thousand gold.
This is what the noble man considers shameful,
and what the 'Felling the Sandalwood' ode condemns.
In the past,
when Shāng Yāng served as minister of Qín,
he relegated ritual and deference,
prioritized greed and baseness,
exalted military achievements,
and strove for advancement,
showing no virtue or kindness to the people,
but imposing harsh punishments in the state.
Customs deteriorated daily, and the people's resentment grew,
so King Huì had him boiled and minced,
to apologize to the world.
At that point,
he too could no longer discuss affairs.
Now, those in power worry that the Ru are poor and lowly yet talk too much;
the Ru also worry that those in power are wealthy and noble yet full of troubles."
The high official looked at the scholars of literature,
sullen and silent.
The Minister's Historian said:
"When debating state policies
and discussing the merits and faults of governance,
why not proceed gradually with reasoned persuasion?
Why must you be so vehement!
The Grandee opposes abolishing salt
and iron monopolies
not out of personal interest,
but from concern for the state's expenditures
and border defense costs.
You scholars vehemently dispute salt
and iron policies also not for yourselves,
but wishing to restore ancient ways and promote benevolence and righteousness.
Both sides have their guiding principles,
but times differ and affairs change -
how can one rigidly adhere to ancient methods and condemn present reasoning?
Moreover, if one criticizes others,
one must have alternatives to offer.
If you scholars can bring order to the state,
attract distant peoples,
eliminate border invasions and disasters,
then all taxes would be abolished for you -
let alone salt,
iron, and equitable distribution!
The reason we value Confucian scholars
lies in their humility and deference,
using the Way to persuade others.
Now your arguments are so confrontational,
lacking the eloquence of Chì
or Cì,
but showing rude and contrary expressions -
this is not what we have heard of proper conduct.
The Grandee spoke excessively,
but you scholars did likewise,
only you scholars haven't properly apologized to the Grandee."
The Worthies and
Literati all rose from their mats and said:
"We rustics are ignorant and limited,
rarely entering great halls.
Our wild words often miss the mark,
offending those in authority.
Medicine wine is bitter to taste but benefits illness,
loyal advice grates on ears but improves conduct.
Thus blunt speech brings fortune,
while flattering words bring harm.
The forest knows strong winds,
wealth and status attract sycophants.
In this court spanning ten thousand leagues,
daily we hear only obsequious agreement,
then come our scholars' blunt words -
this is the fine medicine and acupuncture for ministers."
The Grandee's expression softened somewhat,
facing the Literati and addressing the Worthies:
"Remote alleys breed twisted arguments,
the narrow-viewed are hard to enlighten.
You Literati cling stubbornly to nebulous sayings,
ultimately unwilling to change.
Regarding ancient affairs
and past sayings -
these we have already witnessed.
Observing recent times,
relying on what our eyes have seen
and ears have heard,
eras differ and affairs vary.
During the reigns of Wén and Jǐng,
at the beginning of Jiànyuán era,
people were simple and returned to fundamentals,
officials were honest and self-possessed,
all was prosperous and abundant,
populations grew and households prospered.
Now governance hasn't changed nor teaching altered -
why has the age become so shallow and customs so decayed!
Officials lack integrity,
people lack shame,
punishments fail to eradicate evil,
yet wickedness still doesn't cease.
People say:
'Rustic scholars比不上metropolitan gentlemen.'
You Literati all come from Shāndōng,
rarely engaging in great debates.
You, sir, have long debated in the capital -
we hope you'll clearly explain governance's successes and failures,
and the reasons for them."
The Virtuous and Talented said:
"The region east of the mountains is
the heartland of the empire,
the battlefield for worthy scholars.
Emperor Gāozǔ soared like a dragon and ascended like a phoenix between Sòng and
Chǔ,
supported by the sons of the eastern mountains such as Xiāo Hé,
Cáo Cān, Fán Kuài,
Lì Shāng, Téng,
and Guàn Yīng.
Though in a different era,
they were comparable to Hóng Yāo
and Tài Diān.
Yǔ emerged from the western Qiāng,
King Wén was born among the northern barbarians,
yet their sage virtue surpassed the world,
possessing the talent of ten thousand men,
bearing responsibilities that alternated among the masses.
Entering and leaving the capital cities,
if one day they failed to return,
after several such instances, they would end up merely as servants.
Although I was not born and raised in the capital,
with inferior talent and foolish nature,
unworthy to participate in great deliberations,
I humbly rely on what I have heard from the elders of the villages,
that in the past,
common people's clothing was warm without extravagance,
utensils simple, sturdy, and practical,
clothes sufficient to cover the body,
tools adequate for convenience,
horses enough for easy travel,
carts sufficient for self-transport,
wine enough for joy without excess,
music adequate to soothe the heart without indulgence,
indoors, no sounds of feasting and revelry were heard,
outdoors, no sights of idle wandering were seen,
walking meant carrying burdens,
stopping meant hoeing and weeding,
expenses were frugal yet wealth abundant,
fundamentals cultivated and the people prosperous,
sending off the dead with grief but not ostentation,
nourishing the living with comfort but not luxury,
high ministers upright and without desire,
governance lenient and not harsh;
thus the common people were content with their nature,
all officials secure in their positions,
at the beginning of the Jiànyuán era,
culture was revered and virtue cultivated,
the empire was peaceful and orderly.
Thereafter,
treacherous ministers each with their skills,
damaged and disrupted the utmost governance,
externally blocking mountains and seas,
internally promoting various profits.
Yáng Kě's denunciations for concealed wealth,
Jiāng Chōng's prohibitions on clothing,
Minister Zhāng's changing of decrees,
Dù Zhōu's handling of lawsuits,
fines, redemptions, regulations, and exiles,
both major and minor implemented together,
too numerous to record.
Xià Lán and his like arbitrarily seized people,
Wáng Wēnshū and his followers recklessly killed,
cruel officials sprouted up,
harassing the good people.
At that time,
the common people could not protect their own heads,
the wealthy and powerful could not ensure the safety of their clans.
The sage ruler became aware of this,
then executed Chōng and others,
exterminated the cruel villains,
to appease the resentment of those sentenced to death,
and quell the accusations of the empire,
thus the residents felt secure and were peaceful again.
Yet the damage lasted for generations without recovery,
the wounds have not healed to this day.
Therefore, the百官 still practice cruel governance,
and powerful officials still have hearts set on plunder.
High ministers arrogate power and make arbitrary decisions,
local bullies with many cohorts encroach and oppress,
the rich and noble are extravagant,
the poor and lowly resort to usurpation and murder,
women's work is hard to complete but easily ruined,
carts and tools difficult to make but quick to break,
carts not lasting a full cycle,
tools not enduring a year,
one cart costing a thousand shí,
one garment worth ten zhōng.
Common people use carved cups and painted trays,
tables and mats adorned with trimmings,
maids and concubines dressed in silk and wearing silk shoes,
ordinary folks eating refined rice and meat,
villages have their customs,
communities their grounds,
racing on broad roads,
playing kickball in narrow alleys,
those holding plows and embracing spades,
personally farming and weaving are few,
while those gathering to tighten waists, applying makeup,
powdering faces and painting eyebrows dark are many.
Pretending to have what they lack,
the poor强行 boasting,
outward show without substance,
silk trousers over hemp garments,
not providing for the living,
but giving lavish funerals for the dead,
bankrupting families for burials,
sending off daughters with full carts,
the rich wanting to exceed,
the poor wanting to match,
the rich emptying their stores,
the poor borrowing on credit.
Hence the people's years are urgent and time short,
poverty leads to少 shame,
want leads to little integrity,
this is why punishments and executions of the wicked do not stop the evil.
Thus, when the state imposes severe and urgent levies,
it gives rise to the malady of insufficiency and dispersion."
6.1 "Chapter 29: On Insufficiency and Dispersion"
The Grand Master said:
"I thought the Virtuous and Talented were somewhat better,
but instead they reverse darkness and light,
like barbarian carts following each other and honking.
Have you scholars not seen the cicadas in late summer?
Their sounds enter the ear,
but when the autumn wind comes, their voices are gone.
You scholars should not easily speak,
without considering the consequences,
for when trouble comes and then you fall silent,
it is too late."
The Virtuous and Talented said:
"When Confucius read the Historical Records,
he sighed deeply,
grieving over the abandonment of proper virtue,
and the peril of sovereign and minister.
For worthy men and gentlemen
take the empire as their responsibility.
Those with great responsibilities think far ahead,
and those who think far forget the near.
Sincerely compassionate and mourning,
with added sympathy,
thus their loyal hearts are alone but unburdened.
This is why the poet grieved and wrote,
why Bì Gān
and Wǔ Zǐxū sacrificed themselves forgetting the disaster.
If the hardship imposed on the people is so urgent,
how can we remain silent?
The Book of Songs says:
'Anxious heart as if burning,
I dare not speak in jest.'
Confucius was restless,
distressed by stubbornness.
Mòzǐ was hurried,
concerned for the world."
The Grand Master fell silent.
The Chancellor said:
"I wish to hear about insufficiency and dispersion."
The Virtuous and Talented said:
"Palaces and carriages,
clothing and tools,
funerals, sacrifices, food and drink,
music, women, and pleasures,
are things human emotions cannot cease from.
Therefore, the sages established regulations to prevent excess.
Recently,
scholars and officials pursue power and profit,
neglecting ritual and righteousness;
thus the common people imitate them,
greatly overstepping the regulations.
Now therefore I set it forth,
saying:
"In ancient times,
grains, vegetables, and fruits
were not eaten out of season,
birds, beasts, fish, and turtles
were not eaten if not properly killed.
Hence, fine nets were not used in marshes,
and mixed feathers were not taken.
Now the rich chase and hunt with traps and nets,
capturing fawns and nestlings,
indulging in excessive drinking as if filling a hundred rivers.
They feast on fresh lamb,
nearly fetal shoulders,
and the skin of young birds.
Spring geese and autumn chicks,
winter mallows and warm-growing leeks,
dug-up water plants and smartweed, perilla,
mushrooms, agarics, and edible fungi,
furry fruits, insects, and raccoon dogs.
"In ancient times,
they used rough-hewn rafters and thatched roofs,
earthen ridgepoles and multiple layers of reed mats,
sufficient only to ward off cold and heat,
and shelter from wind and rain.
In later ages,
the rafters were not polished,
the thatch was not trimmed,
there was no work of carving and cutting,
no effort of grinding and polishing.
High officials had squared pillars,
scholars had pointed ridge-ends,
and common people simply used wood shaped by an axe.
Now the wealthy have layered well-frame beams,
carved and patterned balustrades,
and adorned walls with polished jade-like decorations.
"In ancient times,
if clothing did not meet regulations,
or tools were not fit for use,
they were not sold in the market.
Now among the people there are carved and polished objects that do not meet standards,
engraved and painted playthings and useless vessels.
Dark yellow mixed with blue,
five-colored embroidered garments,
playful puppets and miscellaneous female figures,
hundred-beast circus acts and tiger fights,
Tángchí performers chasing people,
exotic insects and Húdá entertainers.
"In ancient times,
the feudal lords did not stable-feed their horses,
when the Son of Heaven gave orders,
they took their chariots to pasture.
Common people who rode horses
did so only enough to relieve their labor.
Therefore when traveling they would use yokes,
and when stopped would employ them for plowing.
Now the wealthy have continuous carriages and rows of riders,
with side-horses and covered carriages.
Those of middling means have light carriages with short hubs,
with decorated manes and shoed hooves.
A single horse in the stable
consumes what would feed a middle-class family of six,
wasting the labor of one able-bodied man.
"In ancient times,
common people wore silk only when old and gray-haired,
the rest wore only hempen cloth,
hence they were called 'the cloth-clad'.
Later on,
they had silk linings with hemp exteriors,
straight collars without lapels,
untrimmed joined robes.
Fine silks and embroidered patterns
were the garments of rulers and their consorts.
Silk tabby and fine white silk
were the fine adornments for marriages.
Therefore patterned thin-woven silks
were not sold in markets.
Now the wealthy have elaborate embroideries and fine silks,
those of middling means have plain silk and ice-bright brocade.
Common people wear the garments of consorts,
humble persons sport the adornments of weddings.
The price of fine white silk is double that of tabby,
yet tabby's usefulness is double that of fine silk.
"In ancient times,
their carts had solid wheels without rims,
their bamboo carriages had no uprights.
Later on,
wooden carriage boxes were not covered,
long hubs had several spokes,
with rush mats and bamboo covers,
the covers lacking lacquer or silk decoration.
Officials and scholars had single or double wooden fittings,
and coiled leather with soft hides.
Common people had lacquered carriages with large side-panels and Shǔ-made wheels.
Now wealthy commoners have silver and gold ornaments with floral left-grips,
with tied tassels and covered crossbars.
Those of middling means have inlaid bits and painted colors,
with jade ear-pieces and flying side-panels.
"In ancient times,
they wore deerskin fur and leather caps,
with hooves and feet still attached.
Later on,
officials and scholars had fox and raccoon dog furs with sewn armpits,
lamb and fawn skins with leopard cuffs.
Common people then had woolen trousers and red-lined garments,
ramie coats and leather breeches.
Now the wealthy have squirrel and sable,
white fox and duck-down.
Those of middling means have woolen clothes with gold thread,
Yànhé fur and Dài yellow.
"In ancient times,
common riders used rope bridles,
with leather soles and hide saddles only.
Later on,
they had leather saddles with yak hair,
and iron bits without decoration.
Now the wealthy have silver-bit cheekpieces with linked straps,
golden tinkling bridles,
woolen embroidered sweat-cloths,
bright and fresh floral trappings.
Those of middling means have lacquered leather connecting straps,
with painted designs sun-dried.
"In ancient times,
they drank from hollows in the ground and with cupped hands,
having no cups, beakers, vessels or stands.
Later on,
common people's utensils were merely of bamboo, willow, pottery and gourds.
Only ritual vessels like húlián, cups and stands later had carved patterns and red lacquer.
Now the wealthy have silver-rimmed vessels with yellow handles,
golden wine vessels and jade cups.
Those of middling means have Yěwáng ramie utensils,
gold-inlaid Shǔ cups.
A single patterned cup costs ten copper cups,
the price is cheap but the use is no different.
Jīzǐ's criticism
originally applied to the Son of Heaven,
now it applies to common men.
"In ancient times,
they roasted millet and ate coarse grain,
and split pigs to feast each other.
Later,
when villagers drank together,
the elderly had double portions of food,
the young stood while eating,
with one sauce and one meat dish,
simply drinking in turns.
Later still,
when guests were invited for weddings,
they had bean soup with white rice,
minced meat and cooked flesh.
Now among the people, at wine and food events,
dishes are piled in layers,
roasts and grilled meats fill the tables,
stewed turtle and minced carp,
fawn, eggs, quail, sparrows, oranges and citrons,
globefish, sweet wine, meat paste and vinegar,
numerous items with mixed flavors.
"In ancient times,
common people plowed and weeded in spring and summer,
gathered and stored in autumn and winter,
working strenuously from dusk to dawn,
continuing through the night.
The Book of Songs says:
'By day you go for the reeds,
by night you twist the rope,
hurry to mend the roof,
then begin to sow the hundred grains.'
They did not rest except at the Lǘ and Là sacrifices,
and had no wine or meat except for sacrifices.
Now wedding banquets and wine feasts
follow one upon another continuously,
sobering up only halfway,
abandoning work to accompany each other,
with no concern for future shortages.
"In ancient times,
common people ate coarse grain with wild greens,
and had no wine or meat except for village drinking ceremonies, Lǘ and Là sacrifices.
Therefore feudal lords did not slaughter oxen or sheep without reason,
officials and scholars did not kill dogs or pigs without cause.
Now in village lanes and country paths,
in field paths they slaughter and sell,
cooking and killing without reason,
gathering together in the open country.
They go carrying grain,
and return bearing meat.
The meat of one pig
equals the harvest of a middling year,
fifteen dǒu of millet,
equivalent to half a month's food for an able-bodied man.
"In ancient times,
common people made sacrifices with fish and beans,
repairing their ancestral shrines in spring and autumn.
Scholars had one temple,
high officials three,
performing ceremonies to the five sacrifices at proper times,
with no sacrifices conducted outside the gates.
Now the wealthy pray at famous mountains,
gaze toward rivers and hills,
butcher oxen and beat drums,
with entertainers dancing as images.
Those of middling means have southern residences facing the road,
with cloud-terraces over water,
slaughtering sheep and killing dogs,
playing zithers and blowing sheng.
The poor use chickens and pigs with five spices,
guardians scattered at the Là sacrifice,
gathering under makeshift shelters at the community grounds.
"In ancient times,
people cultivated virtue to seek blessings,
hence their sacrifices were simple.
They practiced benevolence and righteousness to seek good fortune,
thus divination was rare.
Nowadays, the common people are lax in conduct yet seek help from spirits,
negligent in rituals yet earnest in sacrifices,
disrespectful to parents but reverent toward the powerful,
extremely superstitious and trusting in auspicious days,
heeding deceitful words in hope of gain,
offering real goods to enjoy empty blessings.
"In ancient times,
noblemen diligently reflected on their virtue day and night;
common people diligently devoted themselves to their labor from dawn to dusk.
Thus, noblemen did not eat without merit,
nor did common people consume without work.
Today, the customs are full of pretense and deceit;
some become shamans or priests for the people,
to receive sacrificial rewards,
with hardened foreheads and glib tongues,
some even build careers and amass wealth this way.
Hence, those who dread labor
abandon their fundamental duties to imitate them.
Thus, shamans are found in the streets and alleys,
priests in every neighborhood.
"In ancient times,
there were no beds with carved posts or ornate stands.
In later ages,
commoners used wooden posts from felled trees,
and assembled planks for bed frames.
Scholars had unadorned beds,
officials merely used reed mats.
Now, the wealthy have embroidered canopies and curtains,
painted screens and inlaid stands.
The moderately rich hang high silk drapes,
adorned with paintings and red lacquer.
"In ancient times,
people used animal skins and grass mats,
without added cushions
or the beauty of fine rugs.
Later,
officials and scholars used layered grass mats,
plain rush and single-layered sedge.
Commoners had coarse grass mats tied with ropes,
merely simple reed and rough straw.
Now, the wealthy have embroidered cushions and soft pheasant feathers,
beds with fine mats.
The moderately rich use badger skins instead of rugs,
and flat sedge mats for seating.
"In ancient times,
no cooked food was sold,
nor was market food available.
Later,
there emerged butchers and wine sellers,
vending wine, dried meat, fish, and salt only.
Now, cooked food is displayed everywhere,
markets are filled with delicacies,
work is neglected and laziness prevails,
eating must follow the latest trends:
roasted suckling pig with leek eggs,
dog delicacies and horse parts,
fried fish and sliced liver,
salted mutton and chilled chicken,
fermented mare's milk wine,
dried tripe and stomach jerky,
stewed lamb with bean delicacies,
minced goose soup,
fragrant preserved fish and sweet gourds,
cooked millet and grilled meats.
"In ancient times,
people used earthen drums and clay beaters,
striking wood and patting stones,
to express their joy fully.
Later,
high officials had pipes and stone chimes,
scholars had lutes and zithers.
In the past,
folk drinking gatherings
followed local customs,
merely plucking zithers and beating pottery jars.
There were no exquisite melodies,
nor modulations in musical modes.
Now, the wealthy have bells, drums, and full orchestras,
with troupes of singing children.
The moderately rich play reed organs and tune zithers,
performing Zhèng dances and Zhào songs.
"In ancient times,
the dead were placed in earthen coffins,
enclosed with wooden planks,
sufficient to hold the body,
and conceal the hair and teeth.
Later,
paulownia coffins were unlined,
outer coffins were uncarved.
Now, the wealthy have embroidered burial chambers and assembled timber,
the moderately rich use catalpa inner coffins and nanmu outer coffins,
while the poor have painted shrouds and robed corpses,
with silk bags and orange-colored sacks.
"In ancient times,
burial objects had form but no substance,
showing the people they were unusable.
Later,
there were stores of pickles and sauces,
paulownia horses and figurines for sacrifices,
though the items were not complete.
Now, vast resources are buried,
with objects as if for the living.
Local officials use mulberry-wood figurines and dummy carriages with wheel covers,
commoners lack even a collar on their shrouds,
yet paulownia figures are dressed in fine silk.
"In ancient times,
there were no burial mounds or trees planted,
the post-burial sacrifice was held in the hall,
without altar buildings
or temple positions.
Later,
mounds were raised,
commoners' graves were half a ren high,
just enough to lean on.
Now, the wealthy pile earth into mountains,
plant rows of trees to form woods,
with pavilions and connecting towers,
gathered viewing platforms and added storeys.
The moderately rich have ancestral halls with screens and gates,
walls, gate towers, and decorative nets.
"In ancient times,
when a neighbor had a funeral,
pounding rice omitted rhythmic chants,
and no songs were sung in the lanes.
Confucius, eating beside mourners,
never ate his fill;
on days he wept,
he did not sing.
Now, customs exploit others' funerals to seek wine and meat,
gladly sitting briefly and demanding entertainment,
with singing, dancing, and comedians,
continuous laughter and skillful performances.
"In ancient times,
the interactions between men and women were esteemed,
but wedding attire
was not recorded.
After the Yú and Xià dynasties,
it was likely cloth outside and silk inside,
bone hairpins and ivory earrings,
with feudal lords' wives adding brocade and over-garments.
Now, the wealthy wear fur coats with red trim,
adorned with pendants and jade rings.
The moderately rich have long robes with overlapping lapels,
jade pendants and hairpin earrings.
"In ancient times,
the living were served with full love,
the dead sent off with full grief.
Thus, the sages established frugal rites,
not empty additions.
Now, people cannot show love and respect while alive,
but compete in extravagance after death;
though without sorrowful hearts,
those who practice lavish burials and spend heavily
are praised as filial,
gaining fame in the world,
and glory in society.
Hence, the common people emulate them,
even to the point of selling houses and livelihoods.
"In ancient times,
the bond of husband and wife,
one man and one woman,
formed the way of family life.
Later,
scholars had one concubine,
officials two,
feudal lords had nine women including nieces and younger sisters.
Now, feudal lords have hundreds,
high officials tens,
the moderately rich have attendants,
the wealthy fill their chambers.
Thus, some women suffer loneliness and miss their time,
some men die abandoned without a partner.
"In ancient times,
during years of scarcity, provisions were not fully stocked;
in abundant years, losses were replenished,
maintaining the old ways without alteration.
Now, artisans pursue novel changes and officials harbor divergent intentions,
ruining completed achievements,
thereby concealing their true purposes.
Their aims are fixated on merit and accomplishments,
focusing solely on appearances.
They accumulate deeds to buy reputation,
showing no concern for the people's hardships.
Fields remain uncultivated,
yet they adorn villages and settlements;
towns lie in ruins,
but they heighten their outer walls.
"In ancient times,
human labor was not sacrificed for the sake of beasts,
nor were people's resources seized to feed dogs and horses,
thus wealth was ample and strength abundant.
Now, fierce beasts and strange creatures cannot plow or till,
yet those who should be farming are made to feed them.
Some commoners lack even coarse clothing to cover themselves,
while dogs and horses are clad in embroidered silk;
some black-haired people go without even chaff and husks,
yet beasts feast on fine grains and meat.
"In ancient times,
rulers attended diligently to affairs and cherished their subordinates,
employing the people according to the seasons,
with the Son of Heaven considering the world as his home.
Subjects and servants each performed their public duties in due time—
this is a universal principle across ages.
Now, officials hoard numerous slaves and maidservants,
who idly consume food and clothing from the granaries,
engage in private industries,
seek illicit profits,
and do not exert their full effort in labor,
causing the government to lose substance.
Some commoners lack even a peck or pint of reserves,
while government slaves accumulate hundreds of gold;
the people toil from dawn till dusk without rest,
yet slaves and maidservants idle about with folded arms.
"In ancient times,
the close were favored and the distant kept at a distance,
valuing those of shared kind and disdaining outsiders.
No rewards were given to the meritless,
no support to the useless.
Now, the Mán and
Mò tribes, though without merit,
are housed in government markets,
in spacious rooms and grand residences,
idly consuming food and clothing.
Some commoners struggle to sustain themselves day and night,
while the Mán and Yí tribes grow weary of wine and meat.
The people labor until drenched in sweat,
yet now the Mán and
Yí tribes sit cross-legged and sprawl at ease.
"In ancient times,
commoners wore coarse sandals of grass and rushes,
with simple cords and leather bindings.
Later on,
they had plain shoes without fastenings,
and leather boots.
Now, the wealthy employ famed craftsmen for fine leather,
light and elegant to enhance appearance,
with silk linings and intricate stitching,
adorned with Yue embroidery and fringed edges.
The middling class wears shoes from Dènglǐ, interwoven with rush fibers.
Even foolish servants and lowly maids
don leather boots and silk slippers.
Runners sport fluffy rush shoes with decorative ties.
"The ancient sages toiled personally to nurture their spirits,
restrained desires to suit their nature,
honored heaven and revered earth,
practicing virtue and benevolence.
Thus, heaven was pleased,
granting long reigns and abundant years.
Hence, Yáo, with his elegant brows and radiant demeanor,
ruled for a hundred years.
But when Qín Shǐhuáng indulged in the strange and absurd,
believing in omens and auspices,
he sent Lú Shēng to seek Xiànméngāo,
and Xú Fú and others to sea in search of the elixir of immortality.
At that time,
scholars from Yān and Qí
laid down their hoes and plows,
vying to speak of immortals and spirits.
Thousands of fangshi hurried to Xiányáng,
claiming that immortals ate gold and drank pearls,
thereafter enjoying longevity as enduring as heaven and earth.
Thus, he repeatedly toured the Five Sacred Mountains
and seaside lodges,
seeking the realms of immortals like Pénglái.
In the counties and prefectures he frequently visited,
the rich contributed wealth to assist,
while the poor built roadsides.
Later,
the lesser ones fled,
the greater ones went into hiding;
officials arrested and dragged them off,
without regard for reason.
Beside the famed palaces,
huts and villages lay in ruins,
with no seedlings sprouting or trees standing;
the people's hearts turned away,
and half of them harbored resentment and longing.
The 'Book of Documents' says:
'Offering requires many rites;
if rites do not match the offerings, it is as if not offered.'
Thus, the sages would not bear anything without benevolence and righteousness,
nor approach anything not aligned with the right path.
Therefore, the previous emperor executed Wénchéng,
Wǔlì, and others,
while Emperor Xuān established educational offices,
drew close to the loyal and virtuous,
aiming to eradicate the roots of strangeness and evil,
and illuminate the path of supreme virtue.
"Lavish palaces and halls
are the worms of timber.
Exquisitely carved tools and implements
are the worms of resources.
Extravagant and beautiful clothing
is the worm of cloth and silk.
Dogs and horses eating what humans eat
are the worms of the five grains.
Indulging the mouth and belly freely
is the worm of fish and meat.
Unrestrained spending
is the worm of the treasury.
Unchecked drainage and accumulation
are the worms of the fields.
Unregulated funerals and sacrifices
are the worms that harm life.
Destroying achievements and altering traditions injure merit,
while artisans and merchants rising high harm agriculture.
Thus, a single cup rack consumes the labor of a hundred people,
a single screen requires the work of ten thousand—
how numerous are the harms they cause!
Eyes indulged in the five colors,
ears absorbed in the five sounds,
the body seeking the lightest and thinnest,
the mouth craving the sweetest and most delicate,
effort accumulated on the useless,
wealth exhausted on the non-essential—
such indulgence of mouth and belly should not be excessive.
Hence, when a state suffers from accumulated insufficiency, governance slackens;
when a person suffers from accumulated insufficiency, life is endangered."
The Chancellor said:
"How to remedy accumulated insufficiency?"
6.2 "Saving from Depletion - Thirtieth"
The Virtuous and Capable said:
"To straighten what is crooked, one must overshoot;
to correct ornamentation, one must use simplicity.
In the past,
when Yànzǐ served as minister of Qí,
one fox-fur robe lasted thirty years.
Therefore, when the people are extravagant,
show them frugality;
when the people are frugal,
show them ritual propriety.
Now, if the sons and grandsons of dukes, ministers, and officials
truly can reduce their carriages and chariots,
moderate their clothing,
personally practice thrift and economy,
lead with sincerity and simplicity,
abandon gardens and ponds,
reduce fields and residences,
refrain from involvement in market stalls internally,
and avoid encroaching on mountains and marshes externally,
then farmers will have means to apply their labor,
and women weavers will have means to sell their products.
If so,
then the vital energy will be harmonious and balanced,
and the ailment of accumulated insufficiency will be no more."
The high official said:
"Orphans speak of filial piety,
the lame speak of canes,
the poor speak of benevolence,
the lowly speak of governance.
It is easy to praise discussions that do not involve oneself,
easy to approve of those commenting from the sidelines,
but those in charge become confused.
Thus Gōngsūn Hóng wore cloth covers,
Ní Kuān wore plain robes,
dressed like servants and concubines,
ate like common laborers.
With Huáinán rebelling internally,
the Mán and Yí tribes raging externally,
bandits not being restrained,
extravagance not being checked;
they were like shamans in a plague year,
only able to flap their mouths,
how could they possibly manage the insufficiency and dispersion?"
The worthy and virtuous said:
"During Emperor Gāo's time,
Xiāo and Cáo served as dukes,
while officials like Téng and Guàn served as ministers,
such illustrious assembly was indeed worthy.
During the reigns of Emperors Wén and Jǐng,
and at the beginning of the Jiànyuán era,
senior ministers still upheld the principle of contending for and maintaining correctness.
After that period,
many followed desires and迎合ed wills,
few dared to speak frankly in audience or criticize directly,
using public office for private ends.
Thus Chancellor Wǔ'ān disputed over garden fields,
arguing right and wrong before the sovereign.
Once a nine-story tower collapses,
even Gōngshūzǐ cannot right it;
once the court becomes corrupt,
even Yī and Wàng cannot restore it.
Therefore, Chancellor Gōngsūn
and Minister Ní humbled themselves to practice the Way,
shared their salaries to nurture the worthy,
lowered themselves to treat scholars with respect,
achieving illustrious accomplishments,
yet time was insufficient,
with no successor like Zǐchǎn of Zheng.
But others like Géyì
and Péng Hóu
ruined what they began,
tangled their governance,
destroyed guesthouses and council halls,
turning them into stables and women's quarters,
showing no courtesy in nurturing scholars,
only displaying arrogance,
as integrity and shame declined while they contended for profit.
Thus, with fine fields and vast estates,
the people had nowhere to go;
those unashamed of profit-seeking filled courts and markets,
those with lined fields and herds overflowed commanderies and states,
acting violently and coercively.
Beside great mansions and huge residences,
even roads became impassable.
This indeed is hard to cure and beyond remedy."
The high official flushed with anger,
silent and unresponsive.
6.3 Admonition and Stone Needles Chapter 31
The Chancellor said:
"I heard from Elder Zhèng:
'When the nobleman corrects his countenance,
he keeps away violence and disrespect;
when he moderates his speech and tone,
he avoids vulgarity and error.'
Thus his words can be related,
his actions emulated.
This is what we officials have long wished to witness.
As for arguments of swordsmen
or debaters of board games,
facing each other with fierce expressions,
establishing authority without yielding,
causing us officials unable to adopt the proposals of the worthy and virtuous,
and the worthy, virtuous,
and literary scholars bearing names of disrespect,
I secretly consider this inadvisable for you scholars.
Gōngsūn Lóng once said:
'The way of argument lies in debate,
thus one must not be inattentive;
inattention leads to leniency,
leniency leads to contention,
contention without yielding
descends into vulgarity.'
Now we officials, being unvirtuous,
and yet enjoying undeserved salaries,
have no means to atone or clear our shame.
The county officials' recommended worthy and virtuous
and literary scholars,
even those close to the people in great positions,
have not been seen to use stone needles to cure the people's ailments."
The worthy and virtuous said:
"Master Jiǎ once said:
'Frank words seem shallow and fail to penetrate;
profound words grate on ears and miss the mark.'
Hence it is said:
'How easy is it to speak?'
Speaking is not easy,
let alone acting upon it?
This is why Hú Jiàn did not meet a natural death,
and Wú Dé nearly could not avoid calamity.
A saying goes:
'Five thieves seize one good man,
warped wood hates the straightening cord.'
Now, wishing to apply stone needles,
to unblock the passages,
we fear the troubles of Shèng
and Hú;
carrying a pouch of needles and moxa,
we bear the name of unskillfulness.
'The wolf treads on its own dewlap,
and steps on its tail.'
The path of the nobleman,
the way of action and restraint, is indeed narrow.
This is why Zǐshí sighed in despair."
6.4 Removing Narrowness Chapter 32
The high official said:
"The worthy, even in great forests,
do not lose their way when encountering wind and thunder.
The foolish, even on open, broad roads,
still become confused.
Now, governors
and chancellors personally receive tallies and lead ceremonies,
governing the masses of a whole commandery,
a position equivalent to ancient regional chiefs.
They receive mandates to exercise control,
administer over a thousand li,
without interference from the court;
good and evil lie within themselves.
If they cannot manage, it's their own inability;
how can the Way be considered narrow?"
The worthy and virtuous scholars said:
"In ancient times, when advancing scholars to office,
they were selected from villages and neighborhoods,
their talents and abilities were evaluated,
and only then were they appointed to positions.
After they proved capable of handling their duties,
they were then granted ranks and emoluments.
Thus scholars cultivated themselves in rural communities,
were elevated to the court,
their conduct in obscurity
became sufficiently manifest and illustrious.
None worthy were overlooked no matter how remote,
no achievements were omitted regardless of size.
Therefore the worthy were promoted and employed,
while the unworthy were screened out and dismissed.
Now the path to officialdom is muddled without proper selection -
the wealthy buy offices with their money,
the brave seek merit through risking death.
Those who perform acrobatics on moving carriages or leap over cauldrons
all become supplementary officials.
Accumulating seniority over time,
some even reach the positions of ministers and chancellors.
Draped with blue cords,
girded with silver tortoise seals,
they wield the power over life and death,
controlling the fate of all people.
When weak persons hold such power,
it's like making a sheep lead wolves -
disorder is inevitable.
When strong persons hold it,
it's like giving a madman a sharp sword -
he will certainly kill recklessly.
Therefore in the past,
the common people in commanderies and states suffered mutual oppression that went unaddressed,
some even saw the innocent beheaded unjustly without correction.
Those upholding the law did not follow the proper way,
so disorder only grew worse.
In ancient times,
when enfeoffing the worthy and providing for the capable,
their territories did not exceed a hundred lǐ;
within this hundred lǐ area where the capital was located,
the borders extended no more than fifty lǐ.
They still considered that as one person alone,
their vision could not illuminate everything,
their hearing could not reach everywhere.
Therefore they established high ministers,
grand masters,
and scholars to assist them,
and only then was governance complete.
Now governors and chancellors
may lack the worthiness of ancient feudal lords,
yet administer territories of a thousand lǐ,
govern the masses of entire commanderies,
implement the virtue of a sage ruler,
monopolize the laws of life and death -
this responsibility is extremely heavy.
It cannot be entrusted to non-benevolent persons,
nor can it be implemented by unsuitable persons.
In one person's hands,
order or disorder rests,
transforming a thousand lǐ territory accordingly -
this selection must be made with utmost care.
Thus the ruler may grant wealth to individuals privately,
but not official positions privately.
He establishes rewards to await achievement,
arranges ranks to await the worthy.
He promotes the good as if there were never enough,
dismisses the wicked as if they were enemies,
precisely because without merit they would harm the people.
To assist the ruler's virtue,
open paths for ministers,
lies in selecting the worthy and employing them appropriately,
choosing and training governors and chancellors before appointing them."
6.5 "Criticizing Greed - Chapter 33"
The grand master said:
"Indeed.
Physicians who are unskilled
still demand excessive fees.
Officials who are already largely incompetent
further encroach upon and plunder the people.
Senior officials oppress minor officials,
minor officials oppress the common people.
Thus the problem is not inadequate selection,
but that what is sought differs from what is obtained;
not that their provisions are insufficient,
but that they are greedy and insatiable."
The worthy and virtuous scholars said:
"In the ancient system of ranks and emoluments,
high ministers and grand masters had enough to nurture worthies and support scholars generously,
scholars had enough to comfort themselves and their kin,
commoners who became officials
had enough to replace their farming and live on their salaries.
Now minor officials receive meager salaries,
while corvée duties in commanderies and states
extend as far as the Three Capital Regions,
grain prices are high,
and their income is insufficient.
In normal times they lack adequate clothing and food,
when emergencies occur they sell livestock and property.
Not only that,
when corvée officials dispatch them,
government offices press urgently,
petty clerks and low-ranking officials,
going about must borrow money,
senior officials encroach and plunder,
higher authorities demand from counties,
counties demand from townships,
where can the townships obtain it?
As the saying goes:
'Bribes flowing downward
are like water rushing downhill,
not stopping until exhausted.'
Now great rivers and large streams drink from the vast sea,
the vast sea receives them,
yet we expect mountain streams to refuse runoff;
the integrity of all officials
cannot be obtained.
Those who want straight shadows must straighten the marker,
those who want subordinates廉洁 must first be so themselves.
Thus greed and baseness lie with leadership not subordinates,
instruction and guidance lie with government not the people."
The grand master said:
"Worthiness and unworthiness are inherent in substance,
greed and baseness are innate to nature.
The gentleman can purify himself internally but cannot completely teach others.
Thus the Duke of Zhōu was not unjust in rectifying Guǎn Shū and Cài Shū's wickedness,
nor was Zǐchǎn unjust in rectifying Dèng Xī's deception.
When internally they don't follow parental and fraternal teachings,
externally they don't fear the punishment of criminal law,
even the Duke of Zhōu
and Zǐchǎn could not transform them -
this is inevitable.
Now to blame the authorities for each individual case -
how can the authorities bind their hands and feet to prevent them from wrongdoing?"
The worthy and virtuous scholars said:
"When carriage horses are unruly,
it's the driver's fault.
When the people are ungoverned,
it's the authorities' crime.
The Spring and Autumn Annals does not satirize commoners,
but blames their leaders.
Thus in ancient times when grand masters oversaw executions,
they avoided music and women,
though the punishment was appropriate,
they still sighed repeatedly over it.
They felt shame at failing to transform and sorrow at the incompleteness.
When governance and education are obscure and unmanifest,
and the people stumble and fall unsupported,
it's like an infant approaching a well,
letting it fall in.
If so,
how can they serve as parents to the people?
Therefore the gentleman prioritizes teaching,
and delays punishment.
Punishing one corrects a hundred,
executing one makes ten thousand cautious.
Thus the Duke of Zhōu executed Guǎn Shū and Cài Shū,
and Zǐchǎn executed Dèng Xī.
When punishments and executions are properly applied,
the people follow ritual principles.
When superiors transform subordinates,
it's like wind bending grass -
none fail to follow instruction.
Why bind them individually?"
6.6 "On Punishment Afterwards - Chapter 34"
The grand master said:
"The gentleman of ancient times
loved the good and hated the evil.
The ruler did not harbor evil people,
the farmer did not keep useless sprouts.
Useless sprouts
harm the crops;
useless people
plunder the people.
Remove one harmful plant and numerous sprouts thrive,
punish one evil person and ten thousand people rejoice.
Even the Duke of Zhōu
and Confucius could not abandon punishment and employ the wicked.
If a family has rebellious sons,
vessels and utensils find no rest,
let alone rebellious people!
People become arrogant when indulged but heed punishment.
Therefore punishment
serves to correct the people,
hoes serve to distinguish sprouts."
The Virtuous and Talented said:
"In ancient times,
they earnestly taught to guide the people,
and clarified laws to rectify punishments.
Punishment in governance
is like the whip in driving a chariot.
A skilled driver cannot drive without a whip,
nor have a whip and not use it.
The sage employs laws to accomplish education,
and when education is achieved, punishments need not be applied.
Thus, authority is stern but not lethal,
penalties are established but not violated.
Now, abandoning the guiding principles and unable to uphold them,
ruining the rites and righteousness without being able to guard against it,
the people fall into the net,
and then you hunt them with punishments—
this is like opening the pen gate
and shooting them with poisoned arrows.
It won't stop until all are exhausted.
Zēngzǐ said:
'When those above lose the Way,
the people have been dispersed for long.
If you understand their situation,
you should pity them and not take joy.'
Not grieving over the people's lack of order,
but boasting of one's ability to catch the wicked,
is like a hunter rejoicing at seeing birds and beasts caught in nets.
Now, those under heaven who are executed
do not necessarily have the treachery of Guǎn[Shū] and
Cài[Shū],
or the deceit of Dèng Xī,
fearing that the seedlings are all destroyed without distinction,
and the people are deceived without governance.
Confucius said:
'If a man is not benevolent,
and you hate him too much,
it leads to disorder.'
Thus, when the people are disordered, look back to the government;
when the government is disordered, look back to the ruler himself;
if the ruler is upright, all under heaven will be settled.
Therefore, the gentleman praises the good and pities the incapable,
extends kindness even to the punished,
and lets virtue moisten the poor.
Bestowing favors brings joy,
but carrying out punishments does not bring happiness."
6.7 "On Timely Governance, Chapter 35"
The Grand Officer said:
"Sharing the same land,
living in this age,
without disasters or epidemics,
yet alone in poverty—
if not due to laziness, then extravagance;
without unusual occupations or side incomes,
and still being wealthy and sufficient—
if not due to frugality, then hard work.
Now you say bestowing favors brings joy,
and carrying out punishments does not bring happiness;
this is to pity those without virtue,
and nurture the lazy and extravagant.
Thus, reckless giving is not kindness,
and showing favor to the wicked is not benevolence."
The Virtuous and Talented said:
"The flourishing of the Three Dynasties had no sprouts of disorder—
due to education;
the end times of Xià and Shāng had no obedient people—
due to customs.
Therefore, the king established schools,
clarified education and transformation,
to guide and lead his people,
and when governance and education harmonized,
their nature became benevolent and they understood goodness.
Thus, when rites and righteousness are established,
plowmen yield in the fields;
when rites and righteousness are ruined,
gentlemen contend at court.
When people contend, disorder arises;
when disorder arises, all under heaven becomes unequal,
so some are poor, some rich.
Wealth gives birth to benevolence,
sufficiency stops contention.
Knocking on someone's door at dusk,
asking for water or fire,
even a greedy man does not refuse—
why?
Because they are abundant.
If governance makes beans and grains like water and fire,
how could the people not be benevolent!"
The Grand Officer said:
"Those who indulge in gambling and racing—
all are children of rich families,
not those lacking sufficiency.
Thus, when people have plenty, they become extravagant;
when wealthy, they become arrogant and wasteful;
sitting idly,
rising to do wrong—
their benevolence is unseen.
If one manages affairs without effort,
uses wealth without restraint,
even if wealth is like water and fire,
poverty and want can arrive immediately.
If the people do not store up,
even if officials assist them in plowing and weaving,
can it make them sufficient?"
The Virtuous and Talented said:
"When the Duke of Zhōu assisted King Chéng,
the people were prosperous and happy,
the state had no poor—
not because he plowed and wove for them.
Cultivate their fields,
lighten their taxes,
and the people will be rich.
Above, to serve the ruler and parents;
below, without worries of hunger and cold—
then education can be achieved.
The Analects say:
'Since they are rich,
what more can be added?'
It says: Educate them.
Educate them with virtue,
regulate them with rites,
then the people will move toward righteousness and follow goodness,
none failing in filial piety at home and brotherly respect outside—
how could there be extravagance and violence?
Guǎnzǐ said:
'When granaries are full, people know rites and honor;
when the common people are sufficient, they know glory and shame.'
Thus, it is easy to lead the rich to rites,
but hard to lead them to the Way."
The Grand Officer said:
"The government's relation to the people
is like a kind father's to his son:
Can one be loyal without instructing?
Love them without making them labor?
Thus, in spring, plow personally to encourage farming,
provide relief loans to aid the insufficient,
dredge stagnant waters,
release those lightly imprisoned,
to make the people attend to the seasons.
Showered with grace and favor,
yet until now they remain in poverty—
so hard it is to lead them to the Way!"
The Virtuous and Talented said:
"In ancient times,
in spring, they inspected plowing to supplement insufficiency,
in autumn, inspected harvests to aid shortage.
When people were diligent in wealth, tributes were reduced;
when diligent in labor, construction works were rare.
Cherishing the people's strength,
not seizing even a moment,
thus Lord Shào held court under a wild pear tree,
to avoid hindering farming duties.
Now, timely rains moisten the land,
but seeds hang unused and cannot be sown;
autumn crops wither in the fields and cannot be harvested.
Fields lie barren and red,
while halted villages form markets;
after the spring begins,
hanging green banners and whipping the earthen ox—
this is hardly the enlightened ruler's intent to encourage farming,
nor what the spring ordinances meant."
6.8 "On Floods and Droughts, Chapter 36"
The Grand Officer said:
"Yǔ
and Tāng were sage rulers,
Hòu Jì
and Yī Yǐn were worthy ministers,
yet they had floods and droughts as disasters.
Floods and droughts
are acts of Heaven,
famine and abundance
are movements of Yīn and Yáng,
not by human power.
Thus, in the cycle of the Jupiter year,
in Yáng, it brings drought;
in Yīn, it brings flood.
Every six years, a minor famine;
every twelve years, a great famine.
Such is the Way of Heaven,
hardly the fault of the officials alone."
The Virtuous and Talented said:
"In ancient times,
when governance was virtuous,
then yin and yang were harmonized,
the stars and planets were orderly,
and wind and rain came timely.
Thus, when conduct was cultivated within,
reputation was heard abroad,
when good deeds were done below,
blessings responded from Heaven.
When the Duke of Zhōu carried the records, all under heaven was peaceful,
the state had no premature deaths or injuries,
the years had no famines.
At that time,
rain did not break clods,
wind did not make branches whistle,
it rained once every ten days,
and rain always came at night.
There were no high or low hills that did not ripen.
The Book of Songs says:
'Massed are the dense clouds,
gentle and slow comes the rain.'
Now if we do not examine the reasons for this,
but instead say
'it is the movement of yin and yang',
this is not what we have heard.
Mèngzǐ said:
'When there are corpses of the starved in the fields,
you do not know to gather them;
when dogs and swine eat human food,
you do not know to restrain them;
being parents to the people,
when people starve and die,
you then say,
it is not I,
it is the year -
how is this different from killing them with a blade,
and then saying,
it is not I,
it is the weapon?'
The urgent tasks of today
lie in removing the perils of hunger and cold,
abolishing salt
and iron monopolies, withdrawing profit rights,
distributing land,
encouraging fundamental occupations,
nurturing mulberry and hemp,
and exhausting the land's potential.
With few projects and frugal expenditures,
the people will naturally become wealthy.
If this is done,
then floods and droughts cannot cause worry,
and bad years cannot burden them."
The Grand Master said:
"Debaters value concise language that points clearly,
suitable for the hearing of the multitude,
not reaching elaborate phrases and dense rhetoric,
nor excessive words that harm the officials' plans for transforming customs,
speaking like common folk.
Táo Zhū made his livelihood
with fundamental and peripheral pursuits taking different paths;
one household engaged in several occupations,
and thus the way of managing livelihood was complete.
Now when the state manufactures farming tools,
it makes the people focus on fundamentals,
not engaging in peripheral pursuits,
then there will be no burden of hunger and cold.
What harm do salt and iron cause that they should be abolished?"
The Virtuous and Talented said:
"Agriculture
is the great enterprise of the world,
iron tools
are of great use to the people.
When tools are convenient,
then less strength is used yet more work is accomplished,
farmers happily work and encourage achievement.
When tools are inadequate,
then fields become barren,
grains do not grow,
strength is used sparingly,
and achievement is halved.
Between convenient and inconvenient tools,
their effectiveness differs tenfold.
When the state smelts and casts iron tools,
mostly they make large implements,
striving to meet quotas,
not supplying the people's needs.
When people's tools are blunt and worn,
cutting grass doesn't hurt it,
thus farmers work intensely,
yet gain little harvest,
and the common people suffer from this."
The Grand Master said:
"Soldiers, laborers, and craftsmen,
working daily on public affairs for the state,
have ample resources,
and complete equipment.
When common households work together,
they are limited by time and constrained in resources,
iron strength is not properly smelted,
hardness and softness are not harmonized.
Therefore, the officials request to control salt
and iron, to unify their use,
stabilize their prices,
for the convenience of the people, both public and private.
Even Yú
and Xià's governance
would not change this.
When officials clarify the teachings,
and craftsmen devote themselves to their work,
then hardness and softness are harmonized,
and tools become convenient.
Why then should the common people suffer?
And why should farmers complain?"
The Virtuous and Talented said:
"Soldiers, laborers, and craftsmen!
Previously, when people could pay taxes for smelting
and boiling salt,
salt was the same price as the five grains,
and tools were efficient and serviceable.
Now when the state makes iron tools,
they are mostly crude and poor,
production costs are not economized,
soldiers and laborers are numerous yet their work is incomplete.
When households work together,
fathers and sons join forces,
each striving to make good tools,
tools that are not good are not collected.
When farming is urgent,
they transport them along the field paths.
People trade together,
able to exchange goods with wealth, grain, or new currency;
sometimes they extend credit to people,
without abandoning their work.
Obtaining farm tools,
each gets what they desire.
Corvée labor was simplified and economized,
the state used laborers for reconstruction work,
repairing roads and bridges,
various measures that benefited the people.
Now controlling the sources,
unifying the prices,
tools are mostly hard and brittle,
with no choice between good and bad.
Officials are frequently absent,
tools are hard to obtain.
Households cannot store much,
if stored much they rust.
Wasting fertile days,
traveling far to buy farm tools,
they miss the good season.
Salt and iron prices are high,
the common people are not benefited.
Poor people sometimes farm with wooden tools and weed by hand,
breaking clods with earthen mallets and eating bland food.
Iron officials cannot sell their tools, or sometimes impose them on the people.
When soldiers and laborers fail to meet production targets,
they sometimes order assistance.
Levies and requisitions are unlimited,
corvée labor becomes uniformly burdensome,
therefore the common people bitterly complain.
In ancient times,
in settlements of a thousand households,
and families with a hundred chariots,
potters, smiths, artisans, and merchants -
the four peoples' needs
were sufficient to exchange with each other.
Thus farmers did not leave their fields,
yet had sufficient farm tools,
artisans did not cut timber yet had sufficient wood,
potters and smiths did not farm yet had sufficient grain,
the common people each obtained what was convenient for them,
and those above had no troubles.
Therefore, the king focused on fundamentals and did not engage in peripheral matters,
removed ostentation,
eliminated ornamentation,
immersed the people in ritual,
showed the people simplicity,
thus the common people focused on fundamentals and did not engage in peripheral pursuits."
37.1 "Honoring Ritual - Chapter 37"
The Grandee said:
"Decorating tables and canes,
preparing wine vessels and stands,
is for the guests,
not for the host.
Displaying rare curiosities,
is to exhibit them to the four barbarian tribes,
not for the common people.
Even in a common household with visitors,
there are still performances of extraordinary entertainment,
how much more so for the imperial court?
Therefore, displaying feathered banners,
arraying armored horses,
serves to demonstrate martial prowess;
rare insects and precious oddities
serve to show broad-reaching benevolence
and illuminate magnificent virtue,
so that distant states all come."
The Worthy and Literati said:
"The true king honors rituals and bestows virtue,
elevating benevolence and righteousness while disdaining strange forces,
thus the sages rejected them and did not speak of them.
Confucius said:
'Speak with loyalty and trustworthiness,
act with sincerity and respect,
even in lands of the Mán
and Mò barbarians,
this cannot be abandoned.'
Now when rulers from myriad distant states bring tribute,
they cherish the Son of Heaven's magnificent virtue,
and wish to observe the rituals and ceremonies of the Central States,
therefore we should establish Mingtáng
and Bìyōng to show them,
wield shield and axe,
display the Yǎ
and Sòng to inspire them.
But now we display playthings and useless objects,
rare insects and untamed beasts,
wrestling and various shows,
dazzling objects for exhibition—
this differs greatly from how the Duke of Zhōu treated distant peoples.
Formerly, the Duke of Zhōu interacted with humble scholars through modesty and deference,
held to ritual virtue to humble himself before all under heaven,
thus he declined the tribute of Yuècháng,
showing the ritual of respect and deference;
afterward, he accompanied them into King Wén's temple,
where they witnessed the ritual of great filial piety.
Seeing the spectacle of majestic ceremonies with shields and axes,
hearing the pure songs of the Yǎ
and Sòng,
their hearts filled with ultimate virtue,
they returned joyfully—
this is why the four barbarian tribes admire righteousness and submit,
not because of translators coming to see fierce beasts like bears and brown bears.
Rhinoceroses, elephants, wild buffaloes, and tigers
are plentiful in the southern barbarian lands;
mules, donkeys, and camels
are common livestock of the northern Dí.
What is scarce in the Central States,
foreign lands consider cheap;
in Nányuè, peacock feathers adorn doorways,
by the Kūnlún Mountains,
uncarved jade is used to ward off magpies.
Now to value what others consider cheap,
treasure what others have in abundance—
this does not enrich the Central States nor illuminate magnificent virtue.
Suí and Hé jades,
famous treasures of the age,
cannot secure safety or survival.
Therefore, to illustrate virtue and display majesty,
it depends on worthy ministers and good chancellors,
not on dogs, horses, or rare curiosities.
Thus the sage king takes worthies as treasures,
not pearls and jades as treasures.
In the past, Yànzǐ cultivated in the space between wine vessels,
and repelled the enemy a thousand lǐ away;
those without ability,
even with Suí
and Hé jades filling chests,
are of no benefit to survival."
The Grandee said:
"Yànzǐ served three rulers of Qí as chancellor,
yet Cuī and Qǐng acted without principle,
seized their lord,
threw the state into chaos—
Lord Líng's state was besieged;
Lord Zhuāng was assassinated;
in Lord Jǐng's time,
the Jìn people came attacking,
took Chuídū,
captured Línzī,
border territories were lost,
city walls burned,
palaces destroyed,
treasures exhausted—
what enemy could he have repelled then?
From this we see:
what the Worthy and Literati say,
that worthies are treasures,
then gain and loss have no weight."
The Worthy and Literati said:
"When Guǎn Zhòng left Lǔ for Qí,
Qí became hegemon while Lǔ declined—
not because he took his followers to Qí.
When Wǔ Zǐxū came with his bow to Hé Lü,
they crushed Chǔ and entered Yǐng—
not because he brought his troops to Wú.
Thus where a worthy is, the state is weighty;
where he leaves, the state becomes light.
When Chǔ had Zǐyù
Dé Chén,
Duke Wén slept uneasily;
when Yú had Gōng Zhīqí,
Duke Xiàn of Jìn could not sleep.
Where worthy ministers reside,
they open blockages and clear obstacles far and wide.
Therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals say:
'Where mountains have tigers and leopards,
mallows are not picked there;
where a state has worthy scholars,
its borders suffer no harm'
indeed."
7.2 Preparing Against the Hú, No. 38
The Grandee said:
"A common saying goes:
'The worthy can face humiliation.'
In common terms,
if a village has a tyrant,
people still avoid him.
Now with the enlightened Son of Heaven above,
the Xiōngnú openly raid,
harassing the border regions—
this is when benevolence is violated and wild herbs are gathered.
Formerly, the Dí people invaded Tàiwáng,
the Kuāng people threatened Confucius—
thus the unvirtuous
are thieves of virtue.
Therefore the court sharpens weapons to punish the unrighteous,
sets up mechanisms to guard against the unvirtuous."
The Worthy and Literati said:
"The Xiōngnú dwell in the desert,
living on barren land,
disdained and abandoned by Heaven,
with no houses for shelter,
no distinction between men and women,
taking the wilds as their village,
felt tents as their homes,
clothed in hides and fur,
eating meat and drinking blood,
trading in markets,
dwelling as herdsmen—
like the elk of the Central States.
Meddlesome ministers,
seeking righteousness from them,
demanding ritual of them,
have kept the Central States at war to this day,
with defenses spanning ten thousand lǐ—
this is what the 'Rabbit Net' ode criticizes,
thus petty men are not the heart or shield of lords."
The Grandee said:
"The Son of Heaven
is father and mother to all under heaven.
The multitudes from all directions,
in righteousness, all wish to be his servants;
yet we still build walls,
set up passes and bridges,
train warriors,
guard the palaces—
to ward off disasters and prepare for all contingencies.
Now the Xiōngnú have not submitted—
though there may be no incident,
to abandon preparedness—
how can we?"
The Worthy and Literati said:
"The reason the King of Wú was captured by Yuè
was his neglect of the near while bullying the distant.
The reason Qín perished
was preparing against the Hú
and Yuè abroad while ruining its governance at home.
Using troops abroad,
while government fails within—
preparations become the worry,
adding to the ruler's anxieties.
Thus if the ruler follows the Way,
far and near will march together to him—
King Wén was such;
if he loses the Way,
even servants become bandits—
the King of Qín was such.
When civility declines, military might prevails;
when virtue flourishes, preparations diminish."
The Grand Master said:
"In the past,
all the barbarian tribes were strong,
and together they committed robbery and violence;
Cháoxiǎn crossed the border,
plundering the eastern lands of Yān;
the Eastern Yuè crossed the Eastern Sea,
raiding south of the Zhèjiāng River;
the Southern Yuè invaded internally,
corrupting the orders of obedience;
the Dī, Bó,
Rǎn, Máng,
Suītáng,
and Kūnmíng tribes
harassed Lǒngxī,
Bā, and Shǔ.
Now the three frontiers have been pacified,
only the northern border remains unsettled.
With one move, the Xiōngnú would tremble with fear,
and both internal and external defenses could be relaxed,
so why speak of insufficiency?"
The Worthy and Literati said:
"In ancient times,
the nobleman established benevolence and cultivated righteousness,
to comfort his people,
thus those nearby practiced goodness,
and those far away submitted to him.
Therefore, when Confucius served in Lǔ,
within the first three months of his service, peace was made with Qí,
and within the later three months, peace was made with Zhèng,
striving to pacify the near and comfort the distant with virtue.
At that time,
Lǔ had no difficulties with enemy states
or troubles from neighboring borders.
Powerful ministers changed their conduct and became loyal and submissive,
hence Jì Huán dismantled his city walls.
Great states feared righteousness and sought harmony,
and the people of Qí came to return the fields of Yùn,
Huān, and Guīyīn.
Thus, governing with virtue
not only avoids harm and repels enemies,
but what is desired is obtained without seeking.
Now the reason why the common people are clamorous,
and there is unrest both internally and externally,
lies with the Xiōngnú.
They have no fixed dwellings to guard internally,
no accumulated fields externally,
but follow lush grass and sweet water to drive their herds.
If the Xiōngnú do not change their ways,
then the Central Plains will be disturbed.
They gather like wind and disperse like clouds,
approach them and they vanish,
attack them and they scatter,
they cannot be subdued in one generation."
The Grand Master said:
"In ancient times,
enlightened kings punished the violent and protected the weak,
settled the falling and supported the endangered.
Protecting the weak and supporting the endangered,
then the rulers of small states were pleased;
punishing the violent and settling the falling,
then the innocent people would submit.
Now if we do not campaign,
then violent harm will not cease;
if we do not prepare,
then we are abandoning the common people to the enemy.
The Spring and Autumn Annals criticized those feudal lords who lagged behind,
censuring them for not completing their garrison duties.
Military expeditions and garrison preparations,
have existed since ancient times,
not only today."
The Worthy and Literati said:
"The territory of the Xiōngnú is vast,
and their warhorses' feet are swift and nimble,
their situation makes them easily agitated.
When advantageous, they advance like tigers,
when disadvantaged, they retreat like birds,
avoiding the sharp and attacking the weary;
sending few troops is insufficient to rotate adequately,
sending many troops makes the people unable to bear the service.
Frequent service exhausts their strength,
excessive expenditure depletes resources.
If these two do not cease,
then the people will harbor resentment.
This is why Qín lost the people's hearts
and forfeited the altars of soil and grain.
In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven's domain extended a thousand lǐ,
corvée labor was required within five hundred lǐ,
so that voices could be heard,
and sicknesses could be mutually cared for.
There were no military campaigns that overstayed their time,
no labor services that exceeded their season.
Internally, they were moderate with the people's hearts,
and affairs were suited to their strength.
Thus, those who went were encouraged in their duties,
and those who stayed were content in their livelihoods.
Now the armored soldiers from east of the mountains garrisoning the border counties,
are cut off and extremely distant,
their bodies are among the Hú
and Yuè, but their hearts long for their old mothers.
Old mothers shed tears,
wives at home grieve and resent,
imagining their hunger and thirst,
thinking of their cold and hardship.
The Book of Songs says:
'When I left here,
willows shed tear.
I come back now,
snow bends the bough.
Long, long the way;
hard, hard the day.
My grief o'erflows.
Who knows? Who knows?'
Thus the sage pities them for this,
sympathizes with their long separation from parents, wives, and children,
exposed in the wilds,
dwelling in cold and bitter lands,
so in spring he sends envoys to console and reward them,
and raises those who have lost their positions,
to grieve for the distant people and comfort the old mothers.
His virtuous favor is very generous,
yet officials have not properly performed their duties to carry out the decree with care,
some bully and insult the soldiers,
making deals with them,
combining efforts and tasks,
employing them unreasonably.
Thus soldiers lose their proper positions,
and old mothers, wives, and children feel resentment.
Sòng Bójī's sorrowful thoughts caused fire in Sòng,
and the Lǔ concubine's dissatisfaction caused disaster in the Lǔ palace.
Now in the world, those who are dissatisfied
are not only the women of the western palace
or the old mothers of Sòng.
The Spring and Autumn Annals record mobilizing the masses,
showing the importance of the people.
The Sòng people besieging Chánggé
criticizes prolonged service.
The nobleman's intentions must be like this."
The Grand Master was silent and did not respond.
7.3 "Attending to Duties - Chapter 39"
The Chancellor said:
"The way of the former kings
is too distant and difficult to restore,
the words of the Worthy and Literati
are too profound and difficult to implement.
Praising the lofty conduct of supreme sages,
speaking of the beautiful words of ultimate virtue,
is beyond what the present age can achieve.
I wish to hear about the urgent tasks of today,
that can be implemented in governance;
enabling all the common people to have sufficient clothing and food,
without worries of want and hardship;
timely wind and rain,
ripening of the five grains,
no birth of insect pests;
the world safe and joyful,
no rising of bandits and thieves;
exiles returning,
each going back to their fields and villages;
officials all honest and upright,
reverently performing their duties,
and the common people each receiving their proper governance."
The worthy and virtuous said:
"Mencius stated:
'The Way of Yáo
and Shùn
is not distant from people;
it is that people do not reflect upon it.'
The Book of Songs says:
'Seeking but not obtaining,
waking and sleeping I think of it.'
If one seeks virtue as in 'Guān Jū',
and loves virtue as in 'Hé Guǎng',
how could there be any failure to succeed?
Therefore, we look up to the high mountain,
we tread the bright path;
though we cannot reach it,
we are not far from the Way.
Yán Yuān said:
'What kind of man was Shùn?
What kind of man am I, Huí?'
If one reflects on the worthy and admires the capable,
and follows goodness without cease,
then the customs of Chéng
and Kāng could be attained,
and the Way of Táng
and Yú could be reached.
The dukes and ministers have not reflected on it;
how far is the Way of the former kings?
Duke Huán of Qí, as a feudal lord, reflected on kingly governance,
was concerned for the Zhōu house,
rectified the difficulties of the various Xià,
pacified the barbarians
and Dí tribes' rebellions,
preserved the perishing and continued the severed,
