so faith and righteousness greatly prevailed,
and were renowned throughout the world.
At the meeting of Shàolíng,
he was acknowledged as leader.
The Tradition says:
'It is accumulated giving.'
Thus, earth accumulated becomes a mountain,
water accumulated becomes rivers and seas,
conduct accumulated makes a gentleman.
Confucius said:
'From the "Hé Guǎng",
I know the utmost in virtue.'
To desire to obtain it,
each should return to their root,
and restore antiquity.
In ancient times,
corvée service did not exceed the season;
if one left in spring, they returned in autumn,
if one left in autumn, they came back in spring.
Before the cold and heat had changed,
and clothes had not been altered,
they had already returned.
Husband and wife did not miss their time,
people were peaceful and harmonious as if at ease.
When lawsuits were just,
and punishments appropriate,
then yīn and yáng were harmonized,
and wind and rain were timely.
If those above were not harsh or oppressive,
and those below were not burdened or toiled,
each attending to their duties,
content in their nature,
then pests would not arise,
and floods or droughts would not occur.
If taxes were reduced and farmers did not miss the seasons,
then the common people would be prosperous,
and exiles would return to their fields.
If those above were pure and tranquil without desires,
then those below would be honest and not greedy.
But now, corvée duties extend to the remotest,
to the coldest and bitterest lands,
to dangerous and difficult places,
crossing the regions of the Hú
and Yuè peoples.
One goes this year and returns the next,
parents crane their necks gazing west,
men and women resent separation and long for each other.
Though the body is in Eastern Chǔ,
the heart is in the Western River.
Thus, when one person leaves, the village regrets,
when one person dies, ten thousand grieve.
The Book of Songs says:
'The king's affairs are never done,
we cannot sow millet and grain;
what can our parents rely on?'
'Thinking of those respectful people,
tears fall like rain.
Do I not wish to return?
But I fear this net of crime.'
Officials do not uphold the law to comfort and care,
but betray the public for private gain,
each using their power to satisfy their desires.
People are sorrowful and resentful,
and those above show no compassion or governance;
then evil governance prevails and wicked influences arise.
When wicked influences arise,
then insects and pests are born, and floods and droughts occur.
In such cases,
even if one prays and sacrifices,
serving the hundred spirits incessantly,
how can it harmonize yīn and yáng and quell bandits?"
7.4 Neng Yan Di Sishí
The Grandee said:
"A blind man can speak of black and white,
but has no eyes to distinguish them.
Confucians can speak of order and chaos,
but lack the ability to implement it.
To sit and speak without action,
then a shepherd boy could possess the strength of Wū Huò,
and a disheveled head could embody the virtue of Yáo
and Shùn.
Therefore, if words were close to action,
why would Confucians worry about order and chaos,
or blind men about black and white?
Not speaking out,
is shameful if one's actions do not follow.
Thus, for the lowly to speak of lofty matters,
to be able to speak but not to act—
this is what the gentleman finds shameful."
The worthy and virtuous said:
"Those who can speak but cannot act
are treasures of the state.
Those who can act but cannot speak
are tools of the state.
One who combines both
is a gentleman.
One who has neither
is a shepherd boy
or a disheveled head.
To have words filling the world,
and virtue covering the four seas—
this was Zhōu Gōng.
To speak with the mouth
and act with the body—
how could it compare to silently carrying out one's actions?
Then why should the officials have any worry or shame?
Now, the Way is not upheld, and petty profits are pursued,
admiring the unimportant to confuse the public's will.
Even if the gentleman is poor,
it is acceptable not to do so.
Medicinal wine
benefits illness;
upright speech
is the medicine for governance.
If the dukes and ministers can truly strengthen and restrain themselves,
feed on the ultimate words of literature,
discard power and deceit,
abolish profit-seeking offices,
and return everything to the people,
embracing the Way of Zhōu Gōng,
then the world will be well-governed, and songs of praise will arise.
Why would Confucians need to worry about order and chaos?"
7.5 Qǔ Xià Dì Sìshíyī
The Grandee said:
"Unruly people,
obstructing public benefits,
wish to monopolize mountains and marshes.
Following the opinions of the literati
and worthy and virtuous,
then profits go to those below,
and the government has nothing to do.
They criticize what the superiors implement,
they ridicule what the superiors say,
solely intending to reduce the superiors to follow the inferiors,
harming the ruler to suit the ministers.
How then can the righteousness between superior and inferior,
the rites between ruler and minister,
be maintained? And how can songs of praise arise?"
The Virtuous and Erudite said:
"In ancient times,
the rulers took in limited amounts,
and maintained themselves with moderation.
In plentiful years, they did not hoard,
and in years of famine, they were lenient.
They employed the people's labor
for no more than three days a year,
and the taxes collected
did not exceed one-tenth.
The ruler was deeply benevolent,
the ministers exerted their full efforts,
superiors and subordinates yielded to one another,
and the world was at peace.
'Open up your private fields'
shows the superiors yielding to the subordinates.
'Then extend to our private fields'
demonstrates putting public duties first.
Mèngzǐ said:
'There has never been one who was benevolent yet abandoned their parents,
or righteous yet neglected their ruler.'
With rulers being rulers and ministers being ministers,
how could there be no propriety and righteousness?
By the end of the Zhōu dynasty,
virtue and kindness were obstructed while desires multiplied,
rulers became extravagant and their demands increased,
the people suffered below,
and grew negligent in public duties above.
Hence, the land tax was implemented,
and the poem 'Great Rat' was composed.
When Duke Líng of Wèi mobilized crowds to dig a pond in deep winter,
Hǎi Chūn admonished him:
'The weather is cold,
the common people are freezing and starving,
I hope you will cease the labor.'
The Duke said:
'Is it cold?
Why am I not cold then?'
Hǎi Chūn replied:
'There is a saying:
"Those at ease cannot sympathize with the distressed,
the well-fed cannot understand the hunger of the starved."'
Thus, those with surplus grain and meat find it hard to speak of hardship and want,
those living in comfort find it hard to speak of toil and suffering.
Those in high halls and deep chambers,
spacious houses and inner rooms,
do not know the misery of those in single, narrow huts,
leaking above and damp below.
Those with a hundred teams of tethered horses,
treasures filling their stores,
and constant replenishment,
do not know the urgency of those who have nothing by morning and nothing by evening,
and must borrow.
Those with vast estates and grand gardens,
fertile fields stretching far,
do not know the toil of those without land enough to stand on,
hiding in makeshift dwellings.
Those with horses covering the hills,
sheep and cattle filling the valleys,
do not know the poverty of those without even a lean pig or a weak calf.
Those lying on high pillows, chatting idly,
with no cries of distress,
do not know the sorrow of those worried about private debts and oppressive officials.
Those clad in fine silks and treading in soft leather,
eating fine grain and chewing fat meat,
do not know the cold of coarse garments,
or the bitterness of chaff and husks.
Those moving leisurely between rooms,
dining with hands folded,
do not know the diligence of those tilling the fields with their own hands.
Those riding in solid carriages drawn by fine horses,
in rows of mounted attendants,
do not know the fatigue of those carrying burdens on foot.
Those on comfortable beds with woolen mats,
attended by servants all around,
do not know the difficulty of those pulling carts and boats,
climbing heights and crossing torrents.
Those wearing light and warm clothes,
draped in beautiful furs,
residing in warm chambers,
riding in comfortable carriages,
do not know the peril and cold of those guarding border towns,
exposed to the winds of Hú
and Dài, facing the clear, biting wind.
Those in harmony with wife and children,
with descendants to rely on,
do not know the haggardness of an aged mother,
or the grief and resentment of a lonely woman.
Those listening to the five notes of music,
watching entertainers perform,
do not know the death of those struck by flying arrows,
resisting enemies in distant lands.
Those leaning on desks facing east,
wielding brushes to compose elegant texts,
do not know the urgency of wooden cangues and ropes,
or the pain of whips and rods.
Those sitting on woolen cushions,
speaking of maps and records as if it were easy,
also do not know the hardship of those trekking on foot.
In the past, when Shāng Yāng served Qín,
he punished people like cutting reeds,
and used troops as if tossing pellets;
those in the army left their bones exposed at the Great Wall,
transport soldiers saw cart after cart,
going forth alive,
returning dead.
Were they not also someone's children?
Therefore, the noble man is benevolent with forbearance,
righteous with measure,
sharing his likes and dislikes with all under heaven,
and never imposing what is not benevolent.
Gōng Liú loved goods,
so those at home had stores,
and travelers had supplies.
King Tài loved women,
so there were no pining women inside,
and no lonely men outside.
King Wén established punishments,
yet there were no unjust cases in the state.
King Wǔ led armies,
yet officers were glad to die for him,
and people were happy to serve him.
If it were like this,
why would the people suffer and complain,
what would they seek and criticize?"
The high ministers looked dismayed,
silent as if no one was there.
Thereupon, they ended the debate and ceased discussion.
A memorial was presented:
"The Virtuous and Erudite
and Literary Scholars do not understand the affairs of the government,
and wrongly consider the salt
and iron policies inconvenient.
We request the abolition of the state monopolies on liquor in the commanderies and kingdoms,
and the iron officials in the Guānnèi region."
The memorial was approved.
7.6 "On Attacking, Number Forty-Two"
The Virtuous and Erudite
and Literary Scholars, having received their appointments,
all took the rank of Lieutenant Grand Master,
and took leave of the Chancellor
and the Imperial Censor.
The Grand Master said:
"In the previous discussion of public affairs,
the Virtuous and Erudite
and Literary Scholars cited antiquity,
greatly contradicting contemporary needs.
Debaters need not oppose each other entirely,
but should aim for feasibility.
In the past,
when the government was not dealing with the Hú
and Yuè,
border cities were attacked from all sides,
with the northern frontier suffering the most.
The late emperor ended the threats from three directions,
pacified the surrounding states,
using them as protective barriers,
and mobilized the entire resources of the commanderies and kingdoms
to campaign against the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú's territory is like a animal pen,
isolated and weak with no allies,
this is a time when they are trapped and near destruction.
If we fail to act due to the distance,
allowing them to recover their breath,
rest their troops and horses,
they will deceive the Western Regions.
The Western Regions, being close to the Hú bandits,
if they become disheartened and submit,
will surely become our vassals' worry.
Therefore, the sovereign wishes to eradicate them,
though it burdens the granaries' expenses.
To hunt all day,
only to release the prey when tired,
is not a wise strategy.
Shùn carried on the legacy,
and Yǔ achieved success.
Now we wish to mobilize the army and attack them,
what do you think?"
The Literati said:
"In former times,
the government lightened taxes,
public funds were abundant,
and the people were prosperous.
Later,
to protect against the Hú and
Yuè peoples,and to communicate with the Four Barbarians,
funds became insufficient.
Thus,beneficial and harmful policies were initiated,
carts and boats were taxed,
property was used to aid the frontiers,
crimes were redeemed and informers rewarded,
bringing calamity upon the people.
Soldiers died in military campaigns,
officials were exhausted by transport duties,
compounded by conscription laws,
the officials' demands reached their extreme.
To rest after labor,
to return to fundamentals at the extreme—
this is the way of antiquity,
which even Shùn and
Yǔ,were they to rise again,
could not change."
The Grand Master said:
"When in ancient times the Xià confronted the flood disaster,
the people were extremely toilsome,
exhausted by carrying baskets and spades,
yet by the end,
all enjoyed the fruits of their labor.
During the time of the late Emperor,
the commanderies and kingdoms were rather burdened by military affairs,
yet he also eased corvée duties on three frontiers.
As the saying goes:
'He who sees an opportunity but does not act ruins his achievement.'
To neglect the enemy for a single day
brings calamity for generations.
Rest follows toil,supplies are provided,
taking advantage of exhaustion and seizing the moment.
This is the way of emperors and kings,
which even sages and worthies cannot disregard.
Achievements have their sequence;
to dislike toil and not persevere
is like a farmer resting when weary and stopping when distressed.
Those who interrupt their tasks achieve nothing,
those who slacken in plowing gain no harvest."
The Literati said:
"A state that expands its territory without gaining security endangers itself;
those who rely on military strength to bully enemies will perish.
When tiger and rhinoceros grapple with each other,
ants and crickets may have their way.
When two enemies confront each other,
commoners may seize the opportunity.
Therefore,the sage king perceives benefits while considering harms,
looks afar while preserving what is near.
Now,for the government's planning,
nothing is better than laying down arms and resting the troops,
using generous gifts to cement peace through marriage alliances,
and cultivating civil virtue.
If one does not sympathize with people's urgency,
does not consider their difficulties,
exhausts their resources in futile lands,
losing ten to gain one—
this is not what we Literati can comprehend."
8.1 "Concluding Peace, Chapter 43"
The Grand Master said:
"Since Hàn's rise,
we have cultivated goodwill and concluded peace through marriage alliances,
presenting the Chányú with lavish gifts;
yet he does not abide by the bonds of weighty pledges and generous bribes,
but instead increases his violent harm.
The late Emperor saw that he could be subdued by force,
but not won over by virtue,
therefore he expanded the generals and commanders,
recruited fierce strikers,
to punish his crime;
their achievements shone brilliantly,
renowned throughout the realm,
preserved in the archives.
How can it be said
'losing ten to gain one'
?Those who seek temporary peace face later danger,
those who consider only the immediate worry about the near;
the worthy stand apart from the vulgar,
the wise act with discretion,
what the gentleman considers,
the masses doubt.
Thus,the people may observe success,
but cannot be involved in planning the beginning.
This is what the officials alone perceive,
and what you Literati fail to see."
The Literati said:
"In the past,
when the Xiōngnú concluded peace through marriage alliances,
and the various barbarians paid tribute,
then ruler and minister,inner and outer,trusted each other,
there was no trouble from the Hú or
Yuè.
At that time,
the court's demands were few and easily met,
the people were peaceful,joyful,and without troubles,
they plowed the fields for food,
cultivated mulberry and hemp for clothing,
households had stores for several years,
the government had surplus goods and wealth,
the elders in the villages,
all enjoyed this beneficence.
Since then,
civil means have been abandoned and military force employed,
armies have been distressed and masses toiled,
to seize useless lands,
establishing commanderies amidst sand and stones,
where the people cannot defend themselves,
they are sent to garrison the walls,
transporting supplies to sustain them.
I foolishly see only the loss,
and perceive no achievement."
The Grand Master said:
"The Xiōngnú trade on empty repute with Hàn,
but in reality do not comply;
repeatedly deceived by the Mán and
Mò peoples,
why do we not feel pain about this?
What is the reason?
Emperor Gāo took up the sword to stabilize the Nine Provinces;
now with the Nine Provinces,we cannot impose our will on the Xiōngnú.
Among commoners in the villages,
there are still leaders and followers,
how much more between the lord of ten thousand lǐ and the small state of Xiōngnú?
With the strength of All-under-Heaven,what cannot be crushed?
With the officers and people of All-under-Heaven,who would not submit?
Now we have the title of Emperor,
yet our might is not trusted beyond the Great Wall,
instead we give bribes while they still arrogantly resist—
this is what the Five Emperors could not bear,
what the Three Kings would utterly rage against."
The Literati said:
"Tāng served Xià yet ultimately subdued it;
Zhōu served Yīn yet ultimately destroyed it.
Thus,he who rules the great to master the small becomes king;
he who uses strength to bully the weak perishes.
The sage does not exhaust his people to annex states,
the skilled driver does not exhaust his horses to cover more road.
Thus,Zàofǔ in driving did not lose harmony,
the sage in governing does not violate virtue.
Qín seized the bit of profit to drive the world,
grasping the long whip to lash the Eight Poles,
until the team collapsed from exhaustion,
yet the whip lashes increased all the more,
hence the disaster of the broken bit and lost whip occurred.
Their officers and people were not few,
their strength and toil were not meager,
yet all turned against them within and attached without,serving none.
This is why Emperor Gāo took up the sword to take All-under-Heaven.
When two rulers are well united,
inner and outer communicate,
All-under-Heaven is tranquil and peaceful,
generations without calamity,
what tasks would officers and people have?
Why would the Three Kings be enraged?"
The Grandee said:
"When Bó Yì was first enfeoffed in Qín,
his territory was seventy lǐ.
Duke Mù established hegemony,
and Duke Xiào expanded the enterprise.
From humble beginnings to the highest position,
from small to great.
Thus the ancestors laid the foundation,
and the descendants completed it.
Xuānyuán fought at Zhuōlù,
killed Liǎng Hào
and Chīyóu to become emperor;
Tāng and Wǔ attacked Xià
and Shāng, executing Jié
and Zhòu to become kings.
Huángdì achieved success through warfare,
Tāng and Wǔ fulfilled filial duty through conquest.
Thus the toil of hands and feet
nourishes the belly and intestines.
The labors of the present age
benefit later generations.
Now the Four Barbarians invade internally—
if not repelled,
ten thousand generations will suffer this lasting affliction.
The late emperor raised righteous troops to punish the violent and strong:
eastward destroying Cháoxiān,
westward pacifying Rǎn
and Máng, south capturing Bǎiyuè,
north thwarting the powerful Hú,
pursuing the Xiōngnú to expand the northern regions—
these were the campaigns of Tāng and Wǔ,
the armies of Chīyóu.
Thus when a sage ruler expands territory,
it is not for personal gain;
when employing troops,
it is not merely to vent anger—
but to rescue from calamity and avert harm,
providing long-term consideration for the black-haired people."
The Literati said:
"Qín captured powerful Yuè in the south,
repelled strong Hú in the north,
exhausted the Central States to subdue the Four Barbarians.
The people were worn out yet the ruler showed no compassion;
the country crumbled internally yet those above remained unaware.
Thus when one man raised the call, the world responded:
troops were defeated by Chén Shè,
lands seized by the various lords—
what benefit did this bring to their descendants?
The Book of Songs says:
'Harmoniously cry the wild geese,
as the morning sun begins to dawn.'
Gaining immediate advantage,
they gave no thought to future disaster.
Thus King Wú of Wú knew the advantage of attacking Qí
but not the peril at Gānsuì.
Qín knew the benefit of aggression
but not the difficulty at Hóngmén.
This is knowing one but not ten.
Zhōu, cautious in small matters, gained greatly;
Qín, coveting greatness, lost even the small.
As the saying goes:
'When the front carriage overturns,
let the rear carriage take warning.'
'The mirror of Yīn is not far—
it lies in the age of Xià's sovereign.'"
8.2 Punishing Qín - Chapter 44
The Grandee said:
"Qín,
Chǔ, Yān,
and Qí were fiefdoms of Zhōu;
the rulers of the Three Jìn,
the Tián clan of Qí,
were retainers of feudal lords.
Guarding their states internally,
attacking the unrighteous externally,
they expanded territories and advanced borders,
thus establishing the title of 'Ten Thousand Chariots'
and becoming feudal lords.
The Zhōu dynasty cultivated rites and emphasized culture,
yet the state was diminished and weakened,
unable to preserve itself,
intimidated by the Six States in the east,
fearing Qín in the west,
its person exiled and relocated,
its ancestral temples left without sacrifices.
Relying on the great kindness of the late emperor,
their line was revived,
enfeoffed admirably at Yǐngchuān,
titled Lord Zhōu Zinán.
After Qín unified the world,
it cut off the Pèi River in the east,
annihilated Cháoxiān,
captured Lùliáng in the south,
repelled the Hú
and Dí in the north, westwards conquered the Dī
and Qiāng, established the imperial title,
and received tribute from the Four Barbarians.
Wherever boats and carts could reach,
wherever footsteps could tread,
none failed to come.
Not because they submitted to its virtue,
but because they feared its might.
When strength is great, others come to court;
when strength is small, one courts others."
The Literati said:
"Yǔ
and Shùn were assistants to Yáo;
Tāng and Wén
were ministers of Xià and Shāng.
The reason they could make the eight extremities follow and the world pay homage
was not due to the land of Lùliáng
or the might of arms and armor.
Qín, Chǔ,
and the Three Jìn, though titled 'Ten Thousand Chariots,'
did not devote themselves to accumulating virtue but to invading each other,
deploying troops to contend for strength until all ultimately perished.
Though they expanded territories and broadened lands,
it was like eating cè-herbs to fill the belly—
how could one expect them to remain secure?
How could it be possible?
Those who govern through ritual and deference
are like rivers and seas: flowing long without exhaustion,
because their source is abundant.
If there is no source,
like a blaze of wormwood that flares violently but has no continuation,
their demise can be expected immediately—
as seen in the Warring States.
When Zhōu's virtue declined,
it was then ranked among the feudal lords,
yet its line continues unbroken to this day.
Qín exhausted its strength and extinguished its clan—
how could it make others pay homage?"
The Grandee said:
"The central states and border regions
are like limbs to the heart and abdomen.
When the skin is cold externally,
the heart and abdomen suffer internally;
the internal and external toil together—
not for mutual reward!
When the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold;
when limbs are injured, the heart grieves.
Thus without hands and feet, the body is crippled;
without borders, the interior is harmed.
In the past,
the Róng and Dí attacked the Great King at Bīn,
crossed Qí
and Liáng to border Qín at Jīng
and Wèi, east to Jìn's Lùhún,
invading and oppressing the central states,
which suffered greatly.
Now the Xiōngnú nibble away with internal invasions—
those far off do not share the hardship,
only the border regions suffer the damage.
The Book of Songs says:
'Anxious heart, deeply pained,
thinking how the country is oppressed.'
Without punitive preparations,
violent harm will not cease.
Thus the late emperor raised righteous troops to punish their crimes,
breaking through Qílián
and Tiānshān,
scattering their gathered gangs,
advancing north to Lóngchéng,
surrounding the Xiōngnú greatly,
making the Chányú lose his spirit,
barely escaping with his life,
chasing the fleeing northwards,
decapitating and capturing over a hundred thousand.
Those who draw bows,
leaders in felt and fur,
all had their courage crushed,
broken and defeated, fleeing far,
whereupon our troops withdrew in triumph.
Húnyé led his followers to surrender;
five dependent states were established to keep out the Hú.
Then within the Great Wall,
beyond the rivers and mountains,
rarely was there plunder or trouble.
Thereupon edicts were issued,
garrison supplies reduced,
corvée labor eased.
Though initially toilsome,
ultimately there was celebration."
The Literati said:
"The Zhōu dynasty accumulated virtue over generations,
and all under heaven wished to have them as rulers,
thus they became kings without exertion,
their kindness spreading from near to far,
so that the Mán
and Mò barbarians came of their own accord.
The Qín relied on military victories to unite the world,
narrowed their domain within the seas yet coveted the lands of the Hú
and Yuè peoples,
sent Méng Tián to attack the Hú,
took Hé'nán to create new Qín territory,
yet lost their original Qín lands,
built the Great Wall to guard against the Hú,
but lost what they were defending.
In the past,
when weapons and armor were frequently mobilized,
and armies were repeatedly raised,
north of the Great Wall,
overturned chariots and lost arrowheads were visible everywhere.
When Lǐ Guǎnglì and others made reckless plans,
calculating the return of horses' hooves,
none were not filled with apprehension;
though they obtained Húnxié,
they could not recover what was lost.
This was not the best strategy for the state."
8.3 "Merit in Campaigning - Chapter 45"
The Grand Master said:
"Duke Huán of Qí crossed Yān to attack the Shānróng,
defeated Gūzhú,
and destroyed Lìngzhī.
King Wǔlíng of Zhào crossed Jūzhù Pass,
passed through Dàigǔ,
subjugated and destroyed the Línhú
and Lóufán.
Yān attacked and drove away the Dōnghú,
expanding their territory by a thousand li,
crossed Liáodōng and attacked Cháoxiǎn.
Lord Méng for Qín attacked and drove away the Xiōngnú,
like a bird of prey chasing a flock of sparrows.
The Xiōngnú were intimidated by this power,
and dared not look southward for over ten years.
Later,
after Méng's death and the feudal lords' rebellion against Qín,
the Central States were thrown into turmoil,
the Xiōngnú became active again,
and dared to resume their border raids.
Now, even small states like Yān
and Zhào were able to repel invaders and expand their territories,
today with the great Hàn state,
and the strength of its scholars and people,
which is not merely comparable to Duke Huán's multitudes,
nor just the armies of Yān and Zhào;
yet the Xiōngnú have long remained unsubdued
because the officials have not united their strength,
and those above and below have not been in harmony."
The Literati said:
"In ancient times, deploying armies
was not for coveting the profit of territory,
but to rescue the people from calamity.
When the people longed for them,
it was like yearning for rain during drought;
with bamboo baskets of food and pots of soup,
they welcomed the royal troops.
Thus, those who worried about people's sufferings
were united in the people's hearts and won their allegiance,
as with Tāng and Wǔ.
Those who did not care about the people's lives,
until strength was exhausted and rebellion erupted,
were exemplified by the King of Qín.
Mencius said:
'If a ruler does not incline toward the Way,
nor follow benevolence and righteousness,
but forces people to fight strenuously,
even if victorious, he will surely perish.'
This is why the Central States were thrown into turmoil,
not because Méng Tián died and the feudal lords rebelled against Qín.
In the past, when the Zhōu house was prosperous,
the Yuèshāng clan came with tribute,
and all barbarians presented offerings.
Later, when Zhōu declined,
the feudal lords fought with strength,
the Mán and Mò became dispersed,
each forming their own factions,
unable to unite,
thus Yān
and Zhào could achieve their ambitions.
Afterward,
the Xiōngnú gradually grew stronger,
nibbling away at the feudal lords,
thus defeating and driving away the Yuèzhī,
using military power,
relocating small states,
the bow-drawing peoples,
uniting them as one family,
single-minded and united in strength,
thus becoming difficult to control.
Previously, you devised strategies for the Late Emperor regarding the Xiōngnú:
'Deploy troops to occupy the Western Regions,
seize strategically advantageous positions from them,
and await their changes.
With Hàn's strength,
attacking the Xiōngnú multitudes,
would be like using a strong crossbow to burst an abscess;
Yuè's capture of Wú,
would hardly be worth mentioning!'
The Emperor considered this correct.
Employing your righteousness,
and following your strategies,
even Yuè's king's trust in Zhòng
and Lǐ was not greater.
You were promoted from Commandant of Grain Collection to Grandee Remonstrant,
holding power for over ten years,
yet we haven't seen the achievements of Zhòng
and Lǐ,
but witness the effects of exhaustion and deterioration;
the Xiōngnú have not become more submissive,
while the common people and black-haired masses are worn out.
Thus your strategies have failed to weaken the Xiōngnú,
but instead have depleted the Central States.
Is this how those skilled at planning
are supposed to act?"
8.4 "The Western Regions - Chapter 46"
The Grand Master said:
"In the past,
the Xiōngnú occupied the natural barriers of the Hé
and Shān,
monopolized the benefits of farming and herding,
their people were wealthy and soldiers strong,
when they came raiding,
the area within Jūzhù Pass was alarmed,
and territories south of Shàngjùn all fortified their cities.
During Emperor Wén's time,
the enemy entered Xiāoguān,
beacon fires reached Gānquán,
the officials were terrified and unsure what to do,
so they requested garrisoning troops in the capital to guard against the Hú.
The Hú controlled Dàyuān in the west,
and states like Kāngjū,
and connected with various Qiāng tribes in the south.
The Late Emperor pushed back and seized vast fertile lands,
established Zhāngyè and westward,
separated the Qiāng
and Hú, dividing their support.
Therefore, the states of the Western Regions
all internally resisted the Xiōngnú,
cutting off their right arm,
causing them to drag their swords and flee,
so we recruited people to farm and herd to expand our resources,
south of the Great Wall,
in the frontier commanderies,
horses and cattle roamed freely,
stores and goods covered the countryside,
I have not seen any faults in this strategy.
Even weak Yuè managed to satisfy its ambition against strong Wú,
though their abilities, territories, and numbers were unequal,
with rulers' concern and ministers' planning,
their success was inevitable."
The Literati said:
"Wú and
Yuè are pressed against rivers
and seas, with three waterways circling around them,
situated among the five lakes.
Their lands are pressed against each other,
their territories adjacent,
making it easy for them to capture one another.
Before the sound of war drums is heard,
before the banners are fully unfurled,
before the battle formations are set,
their troops are already engaged.
The army incurs no expense for supplies,
the soldiers no labor of scarcity and exhaustion.
This is what is called feeding from the kitchen storehouse while fighting in the suburbs.
Now the Xiōngnú roam in boundless marshes,
east, west, south, and north,
impossible to exhaust or reach.
Even with light chariots and swift horses,
one cannot catch them,
let alone pursuing them with heavy loads and weary troops?
The situation makes it impossible to reach them.
Vast as if traversing the nine swamps with no known stop,
boundless as if fishing rivers
and seas without nets—even if one reaches them,
the three armies are exhausted and worn out,
merely becoming bait left for them.
Thus, the enlightened king knows there is no benefit,
believing that campaigns should not be frequently launched,
and power cannot be stretched long.
Therefore, he summoned the high ministers,
worthy and virtuous,
and literati
to revive the path of rectifying wrongs and restoring what is subtle.
The high ministers should consider the people's urgency
and the harm of the Xiōngnú,
align with the sage ruler's heart,
and establish the task of peace and stability.
Now you focus on trivial strategies,
undermining fundamental discussions,
not complying with the emperor's intent,
which is not fulfilling loyalty."
The High Official said:
"Initially,
when the Ershī General failed to conquer Dàyuān and returned,
some argued to prevent the sovereign from pursuing his wrath,
but then the Western Regions would have collapsed and attached to the Hú,
and the Hú, gaining many states, would have grown stronger.
The late emperor rejected extraordinary advice,
exercised military might,
returned to attack Dàyuān,
and Dàyuān surrendered the whole country,
offering its artifacts,
and presenting its precious horses.
Tribes like Wūsūn were terrified,
and requested to become subjects.
The Xiōngnú lost their spirit,
fleeing and escaping.
Though not fully subdued,
they are far away in cold, bitter, and barren lands,
with their strong men dead at Qílián
and Tiānshān,
their orphans not yet recovered.
Thus, the ministers argued that the Xiōngnú, trapped by Hàn forces,
with broken wings and injured pinions,
could be attacked and subdued.
But then the late emperor passed away,
so the Xiōngnú remained unchanged.
It is like building a mountain,
stopping one basket short of completion,
estimating the achievement without reason to continue,
which is abandoning it to the Hú and aiding a strong enemy.
Halting near success and thwarting completion,
planning for the sovereign like this,
cannot be called fulfilling loyalty either."
The Literati said:
"Officials speak of foreign matters,
and debaters all seek momentary advantage,
without considering the consequences.
Zhāng Qiān spoke of Dàyuān's heavenly horses sweating blood,
and Ānxī's genuine jade and large birds.
The court, hearing this, became eager,
and launched a massive campaign against Dàyuān,
taking several years to conquer it.
To attack another state from ten thousand lǐ away,
with troops dying without battle over half,
even if Dàyuān was defeated and precious horses obtained,
it was not a sound plan.
At that time,
generals and soldiers were red-faced in dealing with the barbarians,
armies were everywhere,
commanderies and states mobilized together,
the people suffered,
deceit and falsity sprouted,
bandits arose together,
governors could not suppress them,
cities could not stop them.
Then, senior ministers in embroidered robes were sent to quell them.
At that time,
the common people
had no certainty of their lives,
so the bold in Shāndōng
harbored rebellious thoughts.
Thanks to the late emperor's divine wisdom, it was resolved.
The fault lies in wanting to finish the Xiōngnú and distant strategies.
Planning for the sovereign like this,
can it be called loyal?"
8.5 "On Worldly Affairs, Chapter 47"
The High Official said:
"You scholars speak recklessly!
Debates should be carefully applied,
not just clinging to outdated words,
slippery and unactionable.
The Hàn having the Xiōngnú
is like a tree having borers,
or a person having illness;
if not treated, it gradually deepens.
Thus, strategists advise attacking to exhaust them utterly.
You scholars speak of winning them with virtue,
which is a notion that cannot be put into practice.
You scholars, in the past, have nothing like the Three Sovereigns,
in the present, nothing like recent Qín,
so how can officials adopt and implement your ideas in this age,
to comfort the masses and pacify the borders?"
The Literati said:
"In the past, Duke Huán of Qí internally attached the people,
externally pacified the lords,
preserved the perishing and continued the severed,
and the world followed like the wind.
Later,
his virtue waned and conduct declined,
at the meeting of Kuíqiū,
he boasted and showed arrogance,
and nine states rebelled.
The Spring and Autumn Annals criticize him for not upholding virtue but relying on force.
Thus, relying on virtue,
even mighty Chǔ submitted,
and distant states came unsummoned;
relying on force,
then the near are not close,
and small states do not submit.
This is the proof.
Truly, looking up to how the Three Sovereigns flourished,
discussing below why Qín perished,
and recounting how Duke Huán of Qí rose,
abandon arms and practice culture,
discard force and esteem virtue,
dismantle passes and bridges,
remove barriers and fortifications,
and guide with benevolence and righteousness,
then the northern frontiers will have no worry of invaders,
and the central states no affairs of war."
The High Official said:
"If matters are not prepared in advance,
one cannot respond to emergencies.
Without internal preparedness,
one cannot resist enemies.
The Book of Songs says:
'Admonish your people,
be cautious in your lords' measures,
to guard against the unexpected.'
Thus, where there are civil affairs,
there must be military readiness.
Formerly, Duke Xiāng of Sòng trusted Chǔ and made no preparations,
suffering great humiliation,
himself captured and his state nearly lost.
So even with sincere and faithful intent,
not knowing flexibility,
is the path to peril and ruin.
The Spring and Autumn Annals do not approve of the Yí
and Dí capturing the central states,
for their lack of good faith.
The Xiōngnú are greedy wolves,
acting according to the time,
striking when opportunity arises,
sweeping like wind, arriving like lightning.
To wish with sincere and faithful hearts,
and treasures of gold and silk,
to trust in unrighteous deceit,
is like being close to Zhí
and Jué while supporting a fierce tiger."
The Literati said:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals states:
'The king has no enemy.'
This means his benevolence is profound,
his virtue is beautiful,
all under heaven submit as guests,
and none dare to engage in conflict.
His virtuous conduct extends beyond the borders,
wherever boats and carriages reach,
wherever footsteps tread,
none fail to receive his beneficence.
Even the savage tribes of different states,
come of their own accord through multiple translations.
At such a time,
all under heaven is harmonious and united,
sovereign and ministers share one virtue,
outer and inner trust each other,
superior and inferior are harmonious.
Weapons are established but not tested,
shields and spears are stored away and not used.
Lǎozi said:
'The rhinoceros has no use for its horn,
the stinging insect has no use for its poison.'
Therefore, if the sovereign is benevolent, none will fail to be benevolent;
if the sovereign is righteous, none will fail to be righteous.
How could there be any Zhí
or Jué to be intimate with in the world?"
The Grand Master said:
"To lay open one's heart and mind,
to pledge one's genuine feelings,
sincerity and trust felt inwardly,
righteousness manifested in one's countenance.
When Sòng Huà Yuán
and Chǔ Minister of War Zǐ Fǎn met each other,
their tallies matched inwardly,
there was truly something to make them trust each other.
Now the Xiōngnú harbor untrustworthy hearts,
conceal unfathomable deceit,
they press forward at the sight of profit,
seize opportunities to rise up,
sneak up by the market's side,
to attack the unprepared.
This is like placing heavy treasures on the road with no one to guard them.
To expect them not to be lost,
how can it be achieved?"
The Literati said:
"When sincerity and trust are evident throughout the world,
and pure virtue flows across the four seas,
then those nearby sing and rejoice in it,
while those far away come bearing gifts to pay homage.
Therefore, to correct those nearby, one does not use might,
to attract those far away, one does not use force,
but cultivates virtue and righteousness and employs the worthy and good.
Thus, when it comes to affairs,
the people decline ease and embrace toil,
when it comes to wealth,
they decline abundance and embrace scarcity.
Superiors and inferior yield to one another,
on the roads they move like wild geese in flight.
At such a time,
they despise goods and honor virtue,
value righteousness and slight profit,
even if rewarded, they would not steal,
what treasures would need guarding!"
8.6 Heqin Forty-Eight
The Grand Master said:
"In the past, King Yǎn of Xú practiced righteousness and perished,
Duke Āi of Lǔ loved Confucianism and was diminished.
They knew civility but not martiality,
knew one but not the other.
Therefore, the nobleman practices benevolence with dedication,
yet must build walls for self-defense,
set up weapons for self-preparation,
because of the harm that the unbenevolent may inflict.
Thus, in ancient times,
they conducted hunts and drills to count military supplies,
fearing the people might become complacent and forget hardship.
Therefore, weapons and armor
are the state's tools,
walls and fortresses
are the state's solidity;
to wish to abolish them
is to remove the surface and reveal the interior,
showing the Xiōngnú our heart and mind.
If the Xiōngnú lightly advance and sneak in,
to attack our emptiness,
it would be like standing unarmored in the path of arrows and stones,
the disaster would surely be irremediable.
This is what the border regions fear,
and what the officials worry about."
The Literati said:
"In the past,
when passes and bridges were open,
exchanging what was had and lacked,
from the Chányú down,
all were intimate with Hàn and submitted inwardly,
coming and going beneath the Great Wall.
Afterwards,
Wáng Huī's mistaken plan at Mǎyì,
caused the Xiōngnú to break the peace marriage,
attacking the frontier passes,
disasters tangled and unresolved,
warfare connected and unceasing,
border people never loosened armor or unstrung crossbows,
for several decades,
they plowed and weeded in helmet and armor,
held hoes while keeping watch,
beacon fires smoked and flamed,
able-bodied men went out to fight with bows strung,
the elderly leaped over walls to enter shelters.
To speak of it is enough to make one shed tears and chill the heart,
something the benevolent cannot bear.
The Book of Songs says:
'You throw to me a peach,
I require it with a plum.'
Never have we heard of good going forth and evil coming back.
Therefore, the nobleman is reverent and without fault,
with others respectful and courteous,
within the four seas,
all are brothers.
Thus, if introspection finds no guilt,
what is there to worry or fear!"
The Grand Master said:
"Since the Spring and Autumn period, the lords of Xià,
gathered and formed alliances,
but after three meetings,
they turned against and suspected each other,
attacking and fighting endlessly;
the six states formed vertical alliances,
their civilized territories connected,
yet never had a firm covenant.
How much more so for a state of beasts!
The Spring and Autumn Annals records the lord's presence in Chǔ,
at the Gàoyòu meeting it writes of the duke,
to deceive the barbarians
and Dí.
The Xiōngnú have repeatedly made peace marriages,
yet often first violate the treaty,
greedily invading, plundering, and driving off,
they are a state long given to deceitful schemes.
They are fickle and untrustworthy,
making a hundred treaties and betraying a hundred times,
like Zhū
and Xiàng who could not be changed,
or Shāng Jūn who could not be transformed.
To trust in their readiness for war,
and be intimate with them through virtue,
is indeed difficult."
The Literati said:
"The king remains central and listens to all under heaven,
his virtue spreads beyond the borders,
distant states with different customs
come to the court gates,
phoenixes perch in the rows of trees,
unicorns roam the suburban marshes,
all living beings and myriad things
receive his beneficence.
Not that he walks to them and personally administers benevolence,
but extending his benevolent grace makes it so,
through sincerity.
Fàn Lǐ came from Yuè,
Yóu Yú grew up among the Hú,
both became wise assistants to hegemon kings.
Therefore, governance may have unheeded teachings,
but the world has no people who cannot be transformed.
The Book of Songs says:
'Draw from that flowing puddle,
scoop it and pour it here.'
Thus, Gōng Liú dwelt among the Róng
and Dí, and the Róng
and Dí were transformed by him.
The Great King left Bīn,
and the people of Bīn followed him.
The Duke of Zhōu cultivated virtue,
and the Yuècháng clan came.
Their following goodness is like shadow and echo.
In governance, strive to be intimate through virtue,
why worry that they will not change?"
9.1 Corvée Labor Forty-Nine
The Grandee said:
"A butcher can dismember along the natural lines
and separate the joints with bare hands;
but when it comes to cutting sinews and splitting bones,
he cannot succeed without a metal axe.
A sage ruler governs according to human nature,
but when some refuse to obey,
he will raise armies to subdue them.
Thus Tāng executed the Earl of Gé,
and King Wén attacked the Quǎn Yí.
Later, when the Róng and
Dí tribes harassed Xià,
the Central States knew no peace,
until King Xuān of Zhōu and
Zhòng Shānfǔ drove back the invaders.
The Book of Songs says:
'We smote the Xiǎnyǔn,
as far as Tàiyuán.'
'Our chariots roll thunderously,
building fortifications in the north.'
Since ancient times, enlightened kings could not subdue the unjust without campaigns,
nor could they resist violence without walls and ramparts."
The Literati said:
"Shùn danced with shield and axe, and the Yǒumiáo submitted;
King Wén cultivated virtue and won over the barbarians.
The Book of Songs says:
'From the capital with its royal college,
to the west and east,
south and north,
none but submit.'
Under the wide heaven,
all human beings
crane their necks to submit to his righteousness.
Thus he could draw a line as his border,
and none would dare transgress.
The Master said:
'One may brave naked blades,
but not the Mean.'
This speaks of perfect virtue.
Thus, skilled attackers need no strong armor to conquer,
and skilled defenders need no moats to hold firm.
When King Wǔ attacked Yīn,
grasping the yellow battle-axe,
and pledged at Mùyě,
all under heaven's scholars wished to serve him.
Afterward, he sheathed his weapons,
and officials attended court with tablets;
all under heaven's people wished to be his subjects.
He gained it through righteousness,
and maintained it through virtue.
Qín gained it through force,
and maintained it through laws,
but missed the root and branch,
thus it perished.
Civil means can long endure,
but military means are hard to sustain."
The Grandee said:
"The Book of Songs says:
'The Xiǎnyǔn are fierce,
so we must be vigilant.'
'The warriors surge,
marching to the four quarters.'
Thus defense and attack
have existed since ancient times.
The Spring and Autumn Annals praises preparing defenses before invaders arrive.
Thus when limbs are strong, the body is firm;
when flowers and leaves flourish, the root is deep.
So securing the borders safeguards the Central States,
and deploying garrisons regulates labor.
When the ruler worries, ministers labor;
when the superior is endangered, subordinates die.
Our late emperor grieved that the people lacked sufficiency,
released forbidden funds,
reduced his carriage teams,
cut music and rations,
to relieve poverty and fund border defense.
We see no gratitude for such grace,
only obstruction of its completion;
this is not what we have heard is right."
The Literati said:
"When the way of Zhōu declined,
the kingly traces vanished,
the feudal lords struggled for power,
great and small trampling each other.
Thus strong states sought invasion,
weak states prepared defenses.
Soldiers wearied in battle arrays,
enslaved by warfare,
so rulers labored and people suffered.
Now the Central States are unified,
yet within the realm there is unrest,
because corvée extends far and burdens all.
In ancient times,
there were no year-long conscriptions,
no seasonal-long labor duties.
Now the near travel thousands of miles,
the far over ten thousand,
serving two terms.
Eldest sons do not return,
parents grieve and worry,
wives and children sigh,
resentment brews in their hearts,
accumulated longing pains their marrow.
This is why 'The Lone Tree'
and 'Gathering Ferns' were composed."
9.2 On Strategic Strongholds, Chapter Fifty
The Grandee said:
"Tigers and rhinos can seize bears
and subdue beasts
because their claws and teeth are sharp for grasping.
Qín surpassed the feudal lords,
devoured the world,
and annexed rival states
because its strategic barriers were solid and position advantageous.
Thus the turtle, with its shell,
cannot be caught by foxes;
the viper, with its sting,
makes people wary and not approach.
So with preparation, one controls others;
without, one is controlled.
Thus Zhòng Shānfǔ mended the royal robe's flaws,
and Lord Méng built the Great Wall's firmness,
to prepare against invaders
and repel enemies ten thousand miles away.
Now if we do not secure the exterior,
but seek peace within,
it is like a householder not strengthening his walls,
startled by dogs barking at night,
and acting blindly and recklessly."
The Literati said:
"Qín had Xiáo and
Hán Pass to the left, Lǒng Dǐ to the right,
Shǔ and
Hàn ahead, mountains and
rivers behind, fortified by four barriers,
a thousand-mile impregnable wall,
with fine generals and brave warriors,
deploying sharp weapons to guard passes and tunnels,
even Mòzǐ's cloud-ladder devices could be defended.
They thought even if Tāng or
Wǔ were reborn,
or Chīyóu rose again,
none would attack lightly.
Yet conscript Chén Shèng, without a commander's rank
or army's multitude,
raised empty fists and smashed a million troops,
facing no wall or fence difficulty.
Thus it lies in virtue, not in fortifications.
If indeed you use benevolence and righteousness as barriers,
morality as bulwarks,
wise men as soldiers,
sages as defenders,
then none can enter.
Then the Central States would need no dog-bark alerts,
and the borders no fear of deer-bolt or wolf-glance.
What recklessness could there be?"
The Grandee said:
"In ancient times,
governing a state required examining the land,
mountains and strategic barriers,
heaven's timing and earth's advantages,
then one could become king or hegemon.
Thus they built walls and cities,
dredged moats and ramparts,
to resist invaders and secure the state.
The Spring and Autumn Annals says:
'Dredging the Zhū River in winter.'
This cultivated earth's advantages.
The three armies follow heaven's timing,
striking emptiness with solidity,
yet may be trapped by rugged terrain,
thwarted by impregnable walls.
Lord Zhuāng of Chǔ besieging Sòng,
the Qín army defeated at rugged Xiáo,
are examples.
Thus it is said:
'Heaven's timing, earth's advantages.'
The Qiāng and Hú are entrenched,
close to our borders,
if we do not take them now,
they will long plague our four frontiers.
This is why Jìsūn worried about Zhuānyú,
and why Gōujiàn's revolt
made powerful Wú regret."
The Literati said:
"Favorable terrain is not as good as human harmony,
military might is not as good as civil virtue.
The reason Zhōu reached distant lands
was not through favorable terrain,
but through human harmony.
For a hundred generations it was not usurped,
not because of perilous defenses,
but because of virtue.
Wú had the natural barriers of three rivers and
five lakes,
yet was annexed by Yuè.
Chǔ had the strongholds of Rǔ River and
Liǎngtáng,
yet was destroyed by Qín.
Qín possessed Lǒngdǐ and
Xiáo's passes,
yet fell to the feudal lords.
Jìn had the Hé and
Huà rivers and Jiǔhé,
yet was seized by the six ministers.
Qí had Tàishān and
the vast sea,
yet was coerced by Tián Cháng.
Jié and Zhòu possessed the entire realm,
yet were overcome at Hào and
Bó.
The Qín king, who unified the six directions, was besieged by Chén Shè.
It was not that the terrain was not secure,
but that they lacked the method to defend it.
To neglect nearby concerns and worry about distant ones
is like Wú failing to stabilize its own state internally
while crossing the Huái River westward to contend for supremacy with Qí and
Jìn;
Yuè took advantage of its exhaustion,
striking where it was weak.
Had the king of Wú employed Shēn Xū,
cultivated virtue,
and not relied solely on his massive forces,
then Gōu Jiǎn would have remained a tributary lord by the sea's edge,
how would he have dared to devise any schemes?"
The Grandee said:
"Chǔ built its defenses from Wūshān to Fāngchéng,
connecting Wū and
Qiánzhōng,
establishing Hànguān to resist Qín.
Qín encompassed Shāng,
Luò, Xiáo, and
Hán to defend against the feudal lords.
Hán blocked Yíyáng and
Yīquē,
held Chénggāo and
Tàiháng,
to secure Zhōu and
Zhèng.
Wèi, bordering Luò, built walls,
relying on mountains and girded by rivers,
to protect the Jìn state.
Zhào secured Fēihú,
Gōuzhù, and
Mèngmén,
to preserve Xíng and Dài.
Yān fortified Jiéshí,
cut off Xiégǔ,
and controlled Liáo.
Qí held Ā and
Zhēn, controlled Róng and
Lì, leaned on Tàishān,
and had the sea and Hé at its back.
Passes and bridges are
the strongholds of a state,
and mountains and rivers are
the treasures of the altars of soil and grain.
When Xú destroyed Shū,
the Spring and Autumn Annals called it
'taking',
condemning its lack of preparedness,
and the ease with which it was acquired.
Thus, pity invites attack,
and excessive benevolence harms punishment.
When a nobleman governs a state,
he must have impregnable defenses.
The Yì Jīng says:
'Double the gates and sound the clapper,
to await violent intruders.'
This speaks of constant preparedness."
The Literati said:
"Relying on barriers is not as good as relying on righteousness.
In the past, Tāng with only seventy lǐ
governed the entire realm,
while Shū with a hundred lǐ
was destroyed by an enemy state.
This is why it was condemned.
Had passes and bridges been sufficient to rely on,
the six states would not have been annexed by Qín;
had rivers and mountains been sufficient to protect,
Qín would not have fallen to Chǔ and
Hàn.
From this we see:
war chariots do not constitute strength,
high walls do not constitute security.
Practicing good leads to prosperity,
practicing evil leads to ruin.
A true king extends broad love far and wide,
harmonizing internal and external relations,
so all within the four seas come with their duties to sacrifice,
why then sound the clapper and wait?
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says:
'That the feudal lords have passes and bridges,
and commoners have ranks and emoluments,
marks not the rise of peace,
but rather began from the Warring States period.'"
9.3 "On Courage, Chapter Fifty-One"
The Grandee said:
"Jīng Kē, harboring plans for years, failed in his mission
because a foot-long dagger could not be relied upon.
The Qín king, caught off guard,
could sever the strength of Bēn and
Yù,
protected by the advantage of a seven-foot weapon.
Had Zhuān Zhū been empty-handed,
he would not have escaped capture;
had Yào Lí been without water,
he could not have achieved his feat.
People speak of mighty Chǔ and powerful Zhèng,
with armor of rhinoceros hide,
and blades from Tángxī.
Internally, they relied on impregnable cities,
externally, they wielded sharp weapons,
thus their authority prevailed over the central states,
and they forcefully subdued enemy countries.
Hence, even Mèng Bēn raising his arm
is taken lightly by the crowd;
but a coward with preparation
doubles his own courage.
How much more so with the men of Wú and
Chǔ,
brandishing sharp swords,
drawing strong crossbows,
contending with the barbarian captives on the central plains?
One man against a hundred
is hardly worth mentioning!
If this is so,
then the Hú would have no valleys to guard,
no battles to fight,
their strength unable to match Hàn,
and they would inevitably surrender.
This is like how Lord Shāng made Wèi flee
and Sūn Bìn crushed Liáng."
The Literati said:
"Chǔ and
Zhèng's Tángxī and
Mòyáng blades
were not without sharpness,
rhinoceros hide armor
was not without strength,
yet they could not survive,
because sharpness cannot be relied upon.
Qín annexed the armies of the six states,
holding Xiáo and
Hán to rule the world,
with defenses strong as metal and stone,
and blades sharp as Mòyé.
Yet Chén Shèng, without the support of soldiers or people,
nor the use of armor or weapons,
with hoes and wooden clubs,
broke through their war chariots.
Wǔzhāo did not strike,
Wūhào did not shoot.
What is called an impregnable city
does not mean piling earth to make high walls,
or digging the ground to make deep moats.
What are called sharp weapons
do not mean the blades of Wú and
Yuè,
or the swords of Gānjiàng.
It means making morality your wall,
and righteousness your rampart,
so none dare attack,
none dare enter.
King Wén was such.
Making morality your armor,
and righteousness your sword,
so none dare oppose,
none dare resist,
Tāng and Wǔ were such.
Now, if you do not build an unassailable city
or wield an irresistible army,
but wish to rely on the strength of one man
and wield a three-foot blade,
that is indeed trivial!"
The Grandee said:
"Jīng Kē carried a dagger into the perilous strong state of Qín;
the Qín king was terrified and lost his guard,
and all his guards were frightened.
Zhuān Zhū, wielding his sword against a mighty sovereign,
assassinated the King of Wú,
eliminating the usurper and establishing the rightful ruler,
his fame spreading a thousand lǐ.
Niè Zhèng, coming from Wèi,
entered the Hán court to assassinate its lord,
achieved his goal and fulfilled his mission,
then retreated and inflicted punishment upon himself in the court,
his corpse exposed in the market.
If we could truly obtain such brave men today,
leveraging the might of the powerful Hàn,
to overwhelm the unrighteous Xiōngnú,
seize control of their fate,
and hold them accountable for their wrongdoings,
just as Cáo Guì coerced Duke Huán of Qí,
they would yield to our demands.
With our vanguard breaking their sharpness,
their felt tents thrown into chaos,
superiors and inferiors fleeing from each other,
we could then follow up with light and sharp troops.
The Xiōngnú would surely fold their arms, not daring to resist."
The Literati said:
"When Tāng obtained Yī Yǐn,
he used the small territory of Bó to unite and subdue all within the seas;
when King Wén obtained Tài Gōng,
he expanded from Fēng
and Hào to rule the world;
Duke Huán of Qí obtained Guǎn Zhòng and thereby dominated the feudal lords;
Duke Mù of Qín obtained Yóu Yú,
and the eight states of the Western Róng submitted.
We have heard that obtaining sages and worthies brings even the Mán
and Mò to offer tribute,
but we have never heard that coercing and killing rulers can win over distant lands.
The 'Book of Songs' says:
'Benefit this central state,
to pacify the four quarters.'
Hence,
'From those Dí
and Qiāng, none dare not come to acknowledge our king.'
It is not fear of their might,
but fear of their virtue.
Thus, righteousness subduing the unrighteous
is swifter than fine horses and strong bows;
virtue summoning the distant
is faster than relay stations and post-horses."
9.4 Discussion on Merits, Chapter Fifty-Two
The Grandee said:
"The Xiōngnú have no defense of city walls,
no solidity of moats and ponds,
no use of long halberds and strong crossbows,
no stores in granaries and treasuries.
Above, they lack righteous laws;
below, they lack cultural order.
Sovereign and ministers are disrespectful and changeable;
superiors and inferiors have no propriety.
They weave willow branches into dwellings,
use felt mats for roofs.
Their bows are plain, their arrowheads of bone;
their horses eat no grain.
Internally, their defenses are insufficient to inspire fear;
externally, their rituals are not worthy of praise.
The central states are the heartland of the world,
where worthy scholars gather,
where ritual and righteousness converge,
and where wealth and resources multiply.
Using wisdom to outwit the foolish,
using righteousness to attack the unrighteous,
is like shaking leaves off with the autumn frost.
The 'Spring and Autumn Annals' say:
'Duke Huán, with the Róng
and Dí, drove them away.'
How much more can be done with the strength of the entire world?"
The Literati said:
"The Xiōngnú's carts and utensils lack adornments of silver, gold, silk, or lacquer,
made plain yet sturdy;
their clothing has no patterned silks, embroidered skirts, or curved lapels,
all made uniformly yet complete.
Men engage no intricate carvings or clever crafts,
no labor on palaces or city walls;
women contribute no extravagant embroideries or excessive skills,
no weaving of fine silks or gauzes.
Their affairs are simple yet practical,
easy to accomplish and hard to wear out.
Though they lack long halberds and strong crossbows,
warhorses and fine bows;
each family has its own preparations,
each person has their use.
In an emergency,
they simply string their bows and mount their horses.
Without visible stores of supplies,
they sustain themselves for tens of days,
using mountains and valleys as their walls,
water and grass as their granaries.
Their laws are simple and easily understood,
their demands few and easily met.
Thus, punishments are few and offenses rare,
commands are followed with a wave of the hand.
They are lax in ritual but firm in trust,
brief in culture but swift in action.
So, though they lack books on ritual and righteousness,
carving on bones and rolling wood,
officials have means to record,
and sovereign and ministers, superiors and inferiors, have ways to command one another.
Those among our officials who plan for the court
all speak of it as easy,
yet it is truly difficult;
thus, when Qín tried to drive them out, it instead hastened its own downfall.
Hence, weapons are instruments of ill omen,
not to be used lightly.
Turning strength into weakness,
existence into extinction,
can happen in a single day."
The Grandee said:
"Lǔ Lián once said:
'Qín used its scholars as tools,
treated its people as slaves.'
Thus, its governance was harsh and short-lived.
The exalted Emperor Gāozǔ received the mandate to quell violence and chaos,
his merit and virtue towering,
matching Heaven in greatness.
And Emperors Wén
and Jǐng inherited and embellished this legacy.
When our late emperor campaigned against the unrighteous,
expelled the virtueless,
he illuminated the path of benevolent sages,
purified the foundation of ultimate virtue,
accumulating years of benevolent and righteous rule by sage kings.
Now the Literati cite the governance of fallen states and failed administrations,
comparing them to the present,
claiming the Xiōngnú are hard to subdue—
how fitting!"
The Literati said:
"In the time of Yǒuyúshì,
the Sānmiáo did not submit.
Yǔ wished to attack them,
but Shùn said:
'This is because my virtue has not reached them.'
He withdrew to improve his governance,
and the Sānmiáo submitted.
Lands that cannot be governed,
people that cannot be tamed—
a sage king does not send troops against them,
nor exert force,
deeming it not worth troubling the common people or burdening the central states.
Now our enlightened king continues the sage legacy,
promotes virtuous transformation,
yet the court has schemes of expedient use,
and glorifies deeds of counting heads;
I am truly perplexed by this.
When ministers rely on the power of the world,
wield the resources of the state,
enjoy the benefits themselves without regard for their lord,
this is how Wèi Tuó
and Zhāng Hán became kings,
and Qín lost its governance.
Sūnzǐ said:
'In state affairs today,
changes occur a hundred times a day,
yet if the state does not fall,
it can still be reformed.
But once troops are deployed on the plains and vast pastures,
with drums sounding and arrows flying,
even with the wisdom of Yáo
and Shùn,
it cannot be changed.'
Fight and win,
then withdraw to cultivate ritual and righteousness,
following the footsteps of the Three Dynasties,
and benevolence and righteousness will adhere.
To fight and win but not cease,
leading to personal death and state extinction—
the King of Wú is an example."
The Grandee said:
"Those who shout with the wind find it easy to gather breath;
those who act according to the times find it easy to exert strength.
King Wén and King Wǔ possessed surplus power,
yet failed to plan for their descendants,
thus within three generations their virtue declined.
King Zhāo campaigned southward,
and died without returning.
Fán Bó was imprisoned,
causing communications to be cut off.
Jìn seized Jiāo
and Pèi, while the royal army was defeated at Máo Róng.
Now the various southwestern barbarians
are descendants of King Zhuāng of Chǔ;
the king of Cháoxiǎn
consists of fugitives from Yān.
The Nányuè commander Tuó rose from within China,
established himself as king,
his virtue being extremely shallow.
Yet all lost the greatness of the realm,
each considering themselves a separate province,
stubborn and arrogant,
calling themselves 'old men.'
The late emperor planned for ten thousand generations,
fearing the burdens of Jìzhōu
and the troubles of Nánjīng,
thus dispatched General Zuǒ and the tower ships to pacify them.
Without bloodshed,
all became subjects of the county administration.
During the era of the Seven States,
each possessed ten thousand chariots,
faced south and called themselves kings,
holding jade pendants as rival states for generations.
Yet ultimately they could not avoid bowing their heads and being captured by Qín.
Now the Xiōngnú do not match the subject commanderies of Hàn,
lacking the resources of the Six States
or the strategies of worthy scholars.
From this, observing the difficulty and ease,
it is clearly visible."
The Literati said:
"Qín annihilated the Six States,
captured their seven kings,
abundantly possessing surplus strength,
believing even Chīyóu could not harm them,
nor Huángdì repel them.
Yet by the second emperor's regicide at Wàngyí,
and Zǐyīng tying a rope around his neck to surrender to Chǔ,
they never achieved the bowed heads of the seven kings.
Had the Six States coexisted,
Qín would still be a Warring State,
and certainly not perished.
How to clarify this?
From Duke Xiào to the First Emperor,
generation after generation they excelled among feudal lords,
for over a hundred years.
But upon unifying the realm,
they perished in fourteen years.
Why so?
Externally, without the worries of rival states,
internally, they indulged themselves wantonly.
Unless one is a sage,
who, upon achieving ambition, does not become arrogant and idle?
Such a thing has never existed."
9.5 Discussion on Zōu Chapter Fifty-Three
The Grandee said:
"Master Zōu lamented that later-day Confucians and Mohists
failed to understand the vastness of heaven and earth,
the way of clarity and breadth,
wanting to navigate nine bends with knowledge of one tune,
to know all directions while clinging to one corner,
like trying to discern heights and depths without a level,
or shapes and circles without compass and square.
Thus he deduced the cycles of the great sages from beginning to end,
to enlighten kings and dukes,
first listing China's famous mountains and accessible valleys,
reaching beyond the seas.
What is called China
is one part in eighty-one of the world,
named Chìxiàn Shénzhōu,
and divided into nine provinces.
Where mountains and lands are impassable,
they form one province,
with the great encircling ocean around it.
This is what is called the eight extremes,
where heaven and earth meet.
The 'Yǔ Gòng' also records mountains, rivers, heights, depths, plains, and marshes,
but does not know the remoteness of the great way.
Thus Qín sought to reach the nine provinces and square the encircling ocean,
herding the Hú and receiving homage from ten thousand states.
You scholars cling to field-bound worries
and alley-bound steadfastness,
unaware of the principles of the world."
The Literati said:
"Yáo appointed Yǔ as Minister of Works,
to level the waters and lands,
follow the mountains and cut markers,
determine heights and depths, and order the nine provinces.
Zōu Yǎn was no sage;
he created strange errors,
deluding the rulers of the Six States
to adopt his theories.
This is what the 'Chūnqiū' calls
'a commoner deluding feudal lords.'
Confucius said:
'If you cannot serve men,
how can you serve ghosts and spirits?'
If one cannot comprehend what is near,
how can one know the encircling ocean?
Thus, what has no practical use,
the gentleman does not do;
what brings no benefit to governance,
the gentleman does not follow.
The Three Kings trusted the classical way,
and their virtue shone throughout the four seas;
the Warring States trusted fine words,
and were destroyed like mounds of earth.
Previously, the First Emperor of Qín, having swallowed the world,
wished to annex ten thousand states,
yet lost his thirty-six commanderies;
desiring to reach the encircling ocean,
he forfeited his provinces and counties.
Knowing grand principles thus,
it is better to adhere to minor plans."
9.6 Discussion on Calamities Chapter Fifty-Four
The Grandee said:
"One should not share sacrifices with shamans and invocators,
nor debate with scholars,
for they trust the past and doubt the present,
rejecting others to affirm themselves.
Those who speak of antiquity should verify it with the present;
those who talk of distant matters should relate them to the near.
The sun and moon are in heaven,
their signs appear in humans.
Changes in calamities and anomalies,
the span of premature death and longevity,
the transformations of yīn and yáng,
the sequence of the four seasons,
water, fire, metal, wood,
responses to omens and auspices,
the spirits of ghosts and deities,
the blessings of sacrifices,
the movements of the sun and moon,
the patterns of stars and constellations—
to explain these in detail,
what is their origin?
If you do not know, remain silent;
do not recklessly confuse the ears."
The literati said:
"Formerly, the Minister of Jiāngdū, Master Dǒng, expounded on yin and yang,
how the four seasons follow one another,
the father begets them,
the son nurtures them,
the mother completes them,
the son stores them.
Thus spring's begetting
is benevolence; summer's growth,
virtue; autumn's completion,
righteousness; winter's storage,
propriety. This sequence of the four seasons
is what the sage kings emulate.
Punishments cannot be relied upon to accomplish transformation,
hence they broadly applied virtuous teachings.
To speak of the distant, one must examine the near,
thus they acted with inner compassion,
so that punishments felt as if applied to themselves,
and toils as if borne by their own bodies.
How then could they bear to slaughter their own children,
to serve useless ends,
exhausting what they depend on,
and reach across the seas?
The Yuè people prize clams and snails but neglect the grand sacrifice,
the vulgar delight in clamor but find Sháo and Huò music strange.
Thus those who know no flavors
take fragrance for stench;
those who know not the Way
take fine words as chaos to the ears.
Whether one dies young or lives long,
each has their likes and dislikes determining their fate.
Yì and Ào, with their skill and strength, did not die naturally,
Zhì Bó, through greed and ferocity, lost his life.
The evidence of heavenly disasters,
the response of auspicious signs,
are like giving while expecting return,
each according to its kind.
Thus those who delight in doing good,
heaven assists with blessings,
as seen in auspicious omens.
The Yì jīng says:
'Heaven protects him,
all is auspicious, nothing不利.'
Those who delight in doing evil,
heaven repays with calamity,
as seen in portents and disasters.
The Chūnqiū says:
'In response to this, there are heavenly disasters.'
King Wén
and King Wǔ of Zhōu honored the worthy and accepted remonstrance,
reverently cautious without negligence,
their pure virtue supremely excellent,
spirits and deities reciprocated.
The Shī jīng says:
'Down come blessings abundant,
down come blessings great.'
The sun is yang,
the yang way is bright;
the moon is yin,
the yin way is dark;
this signifies the ruler's尊 and minister's卑.
Thus when yang light flourishes above,
all yin types dissipate below;
when the moon is full in heaven,
clams and mussels thrive in the deep.
Hence if ministers are not ministerial,
then yin and yang fall out of harmony,
the sun and moon undergo changes;
if governance and teaching are uneven,
then floods and droughts occur untimely,
and insect pests arise.
This is the response of disasters and anomalies.
The four seasons alternate in order,
and humans emulate their achievements,
stars arrayed in heaven,
and humans imitate their movements.
The constant stars are like the high ministers,
the multitude of stars like the common people.
If the arranged stars are correct, the multitude aligns;
if the constant stars are disordered, the multitude falls."
The grandee said:
"The literati speak of categories of hard and soft,
the five phases overcoming in succession.
The Yì jīng clarifies yin and yang,
the Shū jīng excels in the five elements.
Spring begets, summer grows,
thus fire arises from yín wood,
a yang category;
autumn begets, winter dies,
thus water arises from shēn metal,
a yin entity.
The four seasons and five elements,
alternately decline and rise,
yin and yang are different categories,
water and fire do not share the same vessel.
Metal attains completion with earth,
meets its end with fire,
metal is born at sì,
what explanation or words affirm this?"
The literati said:
"Weapons are
instruments of ill omen.
Sturdy armor and sharp weapons
bring calamity to the world.
Using the mother to control the son,
thus one can endure long.
The sage kings modeled this,
subduing without resorting to aggression.
The Shī jīng says:
'Then store away shields and spears,
then bag bows and arrows,
I seek virtuous conduct,
to spread throughout this Xià.'
Decadent ages are not so.
They defy the heavenly way to indulge violent hearts,
corpses stiffened, blood flowing,
to contend for land.
Imprisoning others' rulers,
extinguishing others' sacrifices,
slaughtering others' children,
as if cutting down grass and trees,
the punished shoulder to shoulder on the roads.
Applying to others what one oneself detests.
Thus states are destroyed,
and they personally suffer the calamity,
as with the Qín king."
The grandee said:
"Metal is born at sì,
punishments are lightly applied,
hence shepherd's purse and wheat die in summer.
The Yì jīng says:
'Treading on frost,
solid ice is near.'
Frost begins to descend in autumn,
plants and trees wither and fall,
aligning with winter to carry out executions,
all things are stored away.
Spring and summer foster growth,
favorable for practicing benevolence.
Autumn and winter bring death and storage,
favorable for applying punishments.
Thus planting out of season,
even if it grows, it does not mature.
Practicing virtue in autumn and winter
is called defying the heavenly way.
The Yuè lìng states:
'Cool winds arrive,
the aura of killing stirs,
crickets chirp,
fur robes are made.
The Son of Heaven carries out minor punishments,
begins the autumn hunt,
to comply with heaven's command.'
The literati equate the four seasons,
harmonize yin and yang,
esteem virtue and abolish punishment.
If so,
then hawks would not seize,
fierce beasts would not snatch,
autumn would lack the hunt,
winter would see no chasing."
The literati said:
"The heavenly way favors life and abhors killing,
favors reward and dislikes punishment.
Thus it places yang in fullness to proclaim virtue and bestow,
and hides yin in emptiness to assist yang.
Yang is firm, yin is soft,
the younger cannot surpass the elder.
This is why heaven disdains winter and values spring,
elevating yang and subduing yin.
Hence the king faces south to govern the world,
turning his back to yin and facing yang,
placing virtue before punishment.
If frost and snow come late,
the five grains can still mature.
If hail and fog fall in summer,
all things are injured.
From this we see:
using harsh punishments to govern the state
is like relying on autumn and winter to grow grain.
Thus laws and decrees
are tools to control evil,
not the atmosphere of perfect governance.
Therefore, in ancient times,
enlightened kings enriched their virtuous teachings
and relaxed their punishments.
Though the net let pass fish that could swallow a boat,
and punishments were carefully applied beyond the strict rule,
by the time it reached the end,
none among the people violated prohibitions."
10.1 Punishments and Virtue, Chapter Fifty-Five
The Grand Master said:
"Decrees are meant to instruct the people,
laws are meant to suppress villainy.
When decrees are strict, the people are cautious;
when laws are established, villainy is restrained.
If the net is wide-meshed, beasts escape;
if the law is lax, crimes slip through.
When crimes slip through, the people become reckless and lightly violate prohibitions.
Therefore, if prohibitions are not enforced,
even cowards will gamble on luck;
if punishments are sincere,
not even Zhí or Jué would offend.
Thus, in ancient times, the five punishments were created,
carving flesh yet the people did not overstep bounds."
The Literati said:
"When paths are numerous,
people do not know which to follow;
when laws and decrees are numerous,
the people do not know what to avoid.
Therefore, when a true king establishes laws,
they are as bright as the sun and moon,
so the people are not misled;
as open as a great road,
so the people are not confused.
Even in secluded and distant places,
all understand them;
maidens and young women alike
all know what to avoid.
Thus, laws and decrees are not violated,
and prisons are not used.
In the past, Qin's laws were as dense as autumn weeds,
and its net tighter than congealed fat.
Yet, high and low evaded each other,
deceit and falsity sprouted,
and officials enforcing them
were like saving rot or quenching fire,
unable to stop it;
it was not due to a wide net and漏crimes,
but the abandonment of ritual righteousness and reliance on punishments.
Now, statutes and decrees exceed a hundred chapters,
texts are complex,
charges severe,
and commanderies and kingdoms applying them
are confused, some shallowly, some deeply.
Even officials well-versed in them
do not know how to proceed,
let alone the ignorant people!
Statutes and decrees gather dust and moths in archives,
officials cannot read them all,
let alone the ignorant people!
This is why court cases multiply,
and people's violations increase.
'Facing jail or prison,
clutching millet to consult divination,
how can one find goodness?'
This satirizes the complexity of punishments.
Kinship relations are numerous,
with reductions upward and downward,
yet mourning grades do not exceed five.
The five punishments have three thousand subcategories,
with attachments upward and downward,
yet offenses do not exceed five.
Therefore, the way to govern the people
lies solely in diligently educating them."
The Grand Master said:
"The Literati say that a true king's laws
are as open as a great road.
Now, the imperial roads are not narrow,
yet people openly violate them,
because penalties for offenses are too light.
A height of a thousand rèn,
people do not lightly climb;
a weight of a thousand jūn,
people do not lightly lift.
Lord Shāng punished those who discarded ashes on the road,
and the Qín people were well-governed.
Thus, stealing a horse warranted death,
stealing an ox incurred heavier punishment,
to emphasize fundamentals and cut off resources for petty theft.
Military provisions and rations
