support the borders and stress military readiness.
Injuring while stealing and killing incur the same penalty,
to weigh on their conscience and hold their intent accountable.
Just as Lǔ using Chǔ's army to attack Qí
was condemned in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Therefore, making light things heavy,
shallow things deep,
has its reasons.
The subtleties of law
are naturally beyond most people's understanding."
The Literati said:
"The Book of Songs says:
'The way of Zhōu is like a whetstone,
straight as an arrow.'
This speaks of its ease.
'What the gentleman treads,
the commoner observes.'
This speaks of its clarity.
Thus, when virtue is clear, it is easy to follow;
when laws are simple, they are easy to implement.
Now, imperial roads traverse hills and plains,
winding throughout the land,
making ten thousand lǐ a pitfall for the people.
Nets spread over valleys,
traps set on paths,
arrows decorated and aimed from above—
can they avoid entanglement?
Gathering what they desire,
opening what profits them,
while benevolence and righteousness decline,
can they avoid transgression?
Hence, in the end,
they attack cities and enter towns,
plunder treasury gold,
steal temple vessels—
is this merely a thousand rèn high or
a thousand jūn heavy? [121 Guǎnzǐ said:
'If the four bonds are not upheld,
even Gāo Yáo cannot serve as judge.'
Thus, when moral instruction is abandoned, deceit flourishes;
when ritual righteousness decays, villainy rises—
this speaks of lacking benevolence and righteousness.
Benevolence is
the manifestation of love,
righteousness is
the appropriateness in affairs.
Therefore, the gentleman extends love to all things,
governing the near to reach the far.
The Tradition says:
'Among all living things,
none is more precious than humans;
what the ruler values most,
is nothing heavier than humans.'
Thus, Heaven births all things to serve humans,
and the ruler loves people to comply with Heaven.
We hear of raising livestock to nourish people,
not of using what nourishes to harm people.
When the Lǔ stables burned,
Confucius left court,
asked about people, not horses—
valuing animals lightly and humans heavily.
Now, stealing a horse merits death,
stealing an ox incurs heavier punishment;
riding a carriage on the imperial road,
officials levy harshness without cease,
considering it horse theft,
and the penalty is also death.
If someone injures another and flees with their sword,
can it be called stealing arsenal weapons to kill?
If the ruler establishes laws and people break them,
can it be deemed rebellion and slighting the ruler's covenant?
Severity leading to death,
leniency to exemption—
this is not the intent of legal prohibitions.
Laws are
made according to human feelings,
not set with crimes to trap people.
Thus, in Spring and Autumn Annals' judgment of cases,
they determined guilt by intent.
Those with good intent but violating the law were exempted;
those with evil intent but complying with the law were executed.
Now, if injury causes no harm,
intent not very evil yet fitting the law,
is it called theft with injury?
Or is it the enforcers' fault?
How can it not discontent people's hearts!
In ancient times,
injuring with a wound incurred punishment,
theft with loot incurred penalty,
killing incurred death.
Now, taking another's weapon to injure
bears the same penalty as killing—
is this not contrary to its highest intent?"
The Grand Master bowed and hesitated, offering no response.
The Imperial Censor said:
"Law enforcement is
the bridle and bit of the state;
penalties and punishments are
the ropes and oars of the state.
Thus, if the bridle and bit are not properly maintained,
even Wáng Liáng could not travel far;
if ropes and oars are not properly set,
even a skilled boatman could not cross water.
Hán Zǐ lamented that rulers failed to clarify their laws and authority,
control their ministers and subordinates,
enrich the state and strengthen the military,
to overcome enemies and ward off difficulties,
being deluded by the elegant phrases of foolish Confucians,
doubting the strategies of worthy men,
promoting frivolous and parasitic elements,
placing them above those with real achievements,
yet hoping for the state to be well-governed—
this is like discarding the steps and wanting to ascend high,
or trying to control a fierce horse without bit or bridle.
Now with penal laws established and equipment in place,
the people still violate them;
how much worse if there were no laws?
Chaos would surely ensue!"
The Literati said:
"Bridle and bit are
tools for control,
which require a skilled driver to adjust.
Laws and authority are
tools for governance,
which require virtuous men to transform.
If the reins are held by the wrong person,
the horse will gallop wildly.
If the rudder is held by the wrong person,
the boat will capsize and be damaged.
In the past, Wú employed Bó Pǐ to hold the rudder and wrecked its boat;
Qín employed Zhào Gāo to hold the reins and overturned its carriage.
Now if we abandon the methods of benevolence and righteousness,
and entrust ourselves to followers of punishment and names,
then we repeat the affairs of Wú and
Qín.
A ruler should model himself on the Three Sovereigns,
a minister should model himself on the Duke of Zhōu,
and those practicing methods should model themselves on Confucius—
this is the unchangeable Way for a hundred generations.
Hán Fēi rejected the former kings and did not follow them,
abandoned proper orders and did not comply,
finally fell into a trap,
was imprisoned,
and died abroad in Qín.
Not comprehending the great Way but skilled in petty arguments—
this is sufficient only to harm oneself."
10.2 "Shēn and Hán, Chapter 56"
The Imperial Censor said:
"If we must wait for the Duke of Zhōu to serve as minister,
then there would be no states in the world.
If we must wait for Confucius to learn,
then there would be no Confucianism or
Mohism in the world. If a garment has a small tear,
a patch can mend it;
must we wait for a whole bolt of cloth to replace it?
If governance has a small flaw,
laws and orders can prevent it;
must we wait for the 'Yǎ' and
'Sòng' to govern?
This is like bypassing the neighbor's doctor,
and seeking Yú Fū to treat illness;
discarding the water in the pond,
and waiting for the Jiāng and
Hǎi rivers to put out a fire.
Circuitous instead of direct,
deficient and without practical effort,
thus orders are not obeyed and governance becomes troubled and chaotic.
Those skilled in governance
mend what is worn,
block what is breached;
thus Wú Zǐ used laws to govern Chǔ and
Wèi, while Shēn and
Shāng used laws to strengthen Qín and
Hán."
The Literati said:
"Rulers should select from the multitude and appoint the worthy;
scholars should study broadly and adhere to the good—
why must it be the Duke of Zhōu and
Confucius!
Thus it is said: simply model after them.
Now Shāng Yāng
opposed the way of the sages,
disrupted and confused Qín's customs;
afterwards, governance deteriorated into chaos and could not be ordered,
lost and irrecoverable;
like a fool setting fire to a marsh,
unable to restore it;
like a wasp or scorpion stinging a person,
even released to die, its poison does not cease.
Trying to stop disorder with more regulations,
calming agitation with force,
upper and lower ranks toil and disturb,
and chaos grows even more.
Therefore, the sages' transformative teachings,
above shine with the sun and moon,
below flow with heaven and earth—
how can this be called a minor repair!"
The Imperial Censor said:
"If a garment's tear is not mended,
it worsens daily;
if a leak is not blocked,
it spreads daily.
When the Great River first broke at Hùzǐ,
it was a mere trickle;
by the time it ended,
it flooded, becoming a disaster for the Central States,
afflicting Liáng and
Chǔ, destroying Cáo and
Wèi,
city walls crumbling and collapsing,
stores and accumulations washed away,
the people dwelling in trees,
for a thousand li no houses,
leaving the orphaned and widowed with nothing to rely on,
the old and weak with nowhere to return.
Thus the late emperor pitied and mourned this disaster,
personally inspected the river embankments,
revived Yǔ's achievements,
restoring the river's flow,
bringing peace to Cáo and Wèi.
The people revered his achievements,
sang praises of his virtue,
chanting
'With Xuānfáng blocked,
ten thousand blessings come'—
this is also like that;
how can one say not to make small repairs!"
The Literati said:
"If a river breach is like a jar's mouth,
yet it destroys a thousand li,
how much more when rites are breached?
The harm would be even greater!
Now court cases number tens of thousands annually,
law violations increasingly abound;
the disaster is not only in Cáo and
Wèi!
Knowing to block Xuānfáng for blessings to come,
but not knowing to block the source of chaos for the world to be governed.
When the Zhōu state employed this,
punishments were set aside unused,
the common people were harmonious,
the four seasons each completed their sequence,
and the world was not isolated.
The 'Sòng' says:
'Grant us long life,
aid us with abundant happiness.'
This bringing of blessings
is indeed not small!
If sincerity, trust, rites, and righteousness are like Xuānfáng,
with achievements already established,
one can rule effortlessly with folded hands,
what need for officials to repair,
what laws and orders to block?"
The Imperial Censor said:
"Sharp plows and hoes
benefit the five grains and harm the weeds in between.
Clear principles and upright laws
are hated by the treacherous and evil but are a blessing to the good people.
Thus crooked wood hates the straightening line;
the treacherous and evil hate upright laws.
Therefore, the sages carefully discern right and wrong,
observe order and chaos,
thus establishing clear laws,
displaying strict punishments,
to prevent wrongdoing and correct deviance,
like straightening warped wood with pressing tools.
Thus water is
a preparation for fire;
laws are
prohibitions to stop villainy.
Without laws and authority,
even worthy men cannot bring order;
without armor and weapons,
even Sūn and
Wú could not overcome enemies.
Thus Confucius advocated benevolence and righteousness, and the people followed like the wind;
Bó Yí secluded himself on Shǒuyáng, yet the people could not be transformed."
The Literati said:
"Laws can punish people but cannot make them honest,
they can kill people but cannot make them benevolent.
What we value in a good physician
is his ability to examine the rise and fall [of vital forces] and expel pathogenic influences,
not his skill in applying needles and stones to pierce the skin.
What we value in a good official
is his ability to stop evil before it sprouts,
preventing people from doing wrong,
not his skill in imprisoning people and executing them.
Those called good officials today
use detailed investigations to bring disaster upon the people,
and employ forceful measures to oppress their subordinates.
They do not follow the origins from which laws arise,
but indulge their own cruel hearts,
using elaborate accusations and false application of laws
to entrap the innocent,
implicate the guiltless,
extending from sons to fathers,
from younger brothers to elder brothers.
When one person is guilty,
the entire village is alarmed,
and ten households flee in exile,
like the spreading of abscesses,
or the connecting of wanton colors,
when one joint moves, a hundred branches shake.
The Book of Songs says:
'Leaving those who are guilty,
who have already been punished for their crimes,
while these who are innocent,
are all involved and suffer.'
It grieves over the innocent being implicated.
The problem is not with hoes and weeders being ineffective,
but with leaving the weeds and weeding the seedlings.
The problem is not with lacking accurate levels,
but with ignoring the crooked and straightening the straight.
Therefore, if those close [to power] who commit offenses are not necessarily punished,
it is like not using the hoe;
if those distant [from power] with achievements are not necessarily rewarded,
it is like not nurturing the seedlings.
Thus, the age does not suffer from lacking laws,
but from lacking laws that are necessarily enforced."
10.3 Zhou and Qin, Chapter 57
The Imperial Secretary said:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals gave criminals no name or title,
calling them thieves,
thereby demeaning the punished and cutting them off from human relations.
Thus, the ruler did not treat them as ministers,
scholars did not befriend them,
and they found no acceptance in the villages.
Therefore, the people were ashamed to commit crimes.
Nowadays, unruly people
violate public laws to gain favor,
abandon their relatives,
fail to uphold principles unto death,
flee and connect with each other,
plunging themselves into crime.
Is it not fitting
that they suffer punishment and execution?
Within one household,
among fathers and brothers,
like parts of the same body connected,
when one joint moves, the heart knows.
Therefore, now from the Marquis of Guannei down,
we organize by locality into squads of five,
households observe each other at home,
monitor each other when going out and coming in.
If fathers do not teach their sons,
elder brothers do not correct younger brothers,
who else should be held responsible?"
The Literati said:
"In ancient times,
they made their rituals comprehensive and their teachings clear.
With comprehensive rituals and clear teachings,
only those who did not comply were then graded with punishments.
When punishments were appropriate,
the people did not resent them.
Thus, Shùn imposed punishments on the four criminals and all under Heaven submitted,
because he punished the unvirtuous.
Light and heavy [offenses] each received their due punishment,
penalties were necessarily applied without pardon,
pardons were only for doubtful cases.
If this were so,
how could the age produce unruly people to be condemned?
Now murderers are spared,
while robbers and thieves become rich.
Thus, good people internally slacken,
cease farming and lose heart.
In ancient times,
noblemen did not approach punished persons,
for punished persons were not considered human,
their bodies exiled or executed, shaming later generations.
Therefore, whether worthy or unworthy,
all regarded it as shameful.
Nowadays, people without virtue
covet profit and plunge themselves [into crime],
suffer punishment and disgrace, abandoning ritual and righteousness,
constantly clinging to mere survival.
Why?
One day they enter the silkworm chamber [for castration],
before their wounds have healed,
they guard the sovereign,
enter and leave the palaces,
thereby receiving salaries,
enjoying feasts and gifts from the grand provisioner,
their persons honored and glorified,
their wives and children obtaining abundance.
Thus, some are ranked among ministers and chancellors,
yet face knives and saws without pity,
let alone the common masses?
What shame is there!
To abandon moral instruction,
and then demand ritual and righteousness from them,
is to oppress the people.
The Spring and Autumn Commentary says:
'If a son is guilty,
seize his father.
If a minister is guilty,
seize his ruler,
this is a great error in judgment.'
Now because of a son, the father is punished;
because of a younger brother, the elder brother is punished;
relatives are implicated,
squads of five and ten are connected,
like pulling the root affecting flowers and leaves,
or injuring a small finger involving the four limbs.
Thus,
the guilty cause the punishment of the innocent;
punishing the innocent
leaves few innocent people under Heaven.
Zāng Wénzhòng governed Lǔ,
boasted of himself for overcoming its thieves.
Zǐgòng said:
'The people will be deceived,
let alone the thieves!'
Therefore, an official is not considered good for making many judgments,
nor a physician skilled for making many incisions.
Zǐchǎn punished two people,
executed one,
and items dropped on the road were not picked up,
with no deceitful hearts among the people.
Thus, being parents to the people,
they should nurture them like ailing children,
extending kindness and generosity.
Since the law of mutual implication for concealing [relatives] was established,
the affection between flesh and blood has been abandoned,
and punishments have increased.
We hear that parents towards their children,
even if guilty, still conceal them,
not wishing them to submit to punishment.
Sons conceal for fathers,
fathers conceal for sons,
but we have not heard of fathers and sons implicating each other.
We hear of brothers delaying pursuit to avoid harm [to each other],
but not of brothers implicating each other.
We hear of hating the evil and stopping with the person,
detesting the beginning and punishing the chief villain,
but not of squads of five and ten implicating each other.
Lǎozi said:
'When those above are without desire, the people are simple;
when those above are without affairs, the people prosper of themselves.'
Let rulers be rulers, ministers ministers,
fathers fathers, sons sons.
What need for organizing by locality into squads,
and what responsibility for those in government to demand?"
The Imperial Secretary said:
"To bear a weight of a thousand jūn,
climbing to limitless heights,
hanging over steep cliffs and deep valleys,
looking down into unfathomable abysses,
even with the agility of Qìng Jì,
the courage of Bēn and Yù,
none would not tremble with fear,
knowing that falling would smear one's body, head, liver, and brains over the mountain rocks.
Thus, those who have never been burned dare not grasp fire
because they see it can burn.
Those who have never been cut dare not grasp a blade
because they see it can cut.
When they know that doing wrong
will surely bring punishment upon them,
and that execution will reach fathers and brothers,
they will surely fear and do good.
Therefore, establishing laws and penalties
is like facing a chasm a hundred rèn deep,
grasping fire or treading on blades:
then the people will fear and avoid [transgression],
not daring to violate prohibitions.
A kind mother may have a wayward son
because she cannot bear [to discipline] in small matters.
A strict household has no fierce slaves
because reproof is earnest and urgent.
Now, if we do not establish what strict households use to control subordinates,
but cultivate what kind mothers use to spoil sons,
then we are deluded."
The literati said:
"King Zhòu had the punishment of the roasting pillar,
and the Qín state had the law of confiscating families.
Zhào Gāo determined crimes with harsh statutes internally,
while officials executed judgments with severe laws externally.
The dead lay piled upon one another,
the punished could be seen everywhere,
the common people watched fearfully and walked cautiously,
shivering without being cold.
The Book of Songs says:
'They say Heaven is high,
yet I dare not but stoop.
They say Earth is thick,
yet I dare not but tread lightly.
Alas for the men of today,
why have they become like venomous lizards!'
At such times,
was it only about braving fire and treading on blades?
Rather, fathers and sons turned against each other,
brothers treated each other with contempt,
reaching the point where flesh and blood harmed one another,
and superiors and subordinates killed each other.
This was not due to light punishments or inconsistent penalties,
but because commands were too severe and benevolent grace was not extended.
Thus when governance is lenient, the people cherish their ruler;
when governance is strict, the people plot against their sovereign.
Duke Lì of Jìn was imprisoned,
the Second Emperor was killed -
how can it be said that harsh laws prevent offenses,
or that strict households have no defiant servants?
The sages understood this,
therefore they sought harmony rather than intimidation.
Thus Emperor Gāozǔ simplified Qín's harsh laws,
to comfort the resentful people,
and nurture hearts of harmony,
fearing only that punishments might be too heavy and virtue too thin.
Hence his grace extended boundlessly,
his beneficence flowed to later generations.
Shāng Yāng
and Wú Qǐ considered the laws of Qín
and Chǔ too lenient and piled on more,
endangering their rulers above,
and destroying themselves below -
how could they be anything but cruel mothers!"
10.4 "Edict of the Sage - Chapter 58"
The imperial secretary said:
"The Xià dynasty did not break promises,
the Shāng made oaths,
the Zhōu made covenants -
virtue and trustworthiness progressively declined.
Without men like King Wén
and King Wǔ,
attempting to practice their laws
was why Yīn
and Zhōu lost power,
and were stripped of authority by the feudal lords.
Thus when clothes wear out, they are remade;
when laws become defective, they are reformed.
During Emperor Gāozǔ's time,
when the realm was first stabilized,
he issued virtuous decrees,
implementing provisional orders -
this was expediency,
not the constant way of setting right what was disordered.
Afterward,
laws were gradually violated,
and justice was not upheld.
Thus when villainy sprouted, the 'Punishments of Fǔ' was created;
when the Kingly Way declined, the Book of Songs' satires became evident;
when feudal lords became violent, the Spring and Autumn Annals criticized.
A net with few meshes cannot catch fish;
the three-article law cannot govern a state.
Therefore commands must be increased,
laws must be multiplied.
Táng and Yú's painted garments and hats were not partiality;
Tāng and Wǔ's branding and tattooing were not arbitrary -
times differ,
and the priorities of severity and leniency vary."
The literati said:
"The people's reliance on law
is like fish relying on water.
When water is clear, they are calm;
when turbid, they are disturbed.
Disturbed, they cannot settle peacefully;
calm, they delight in their occupations.
Delighting in their occupations brings wealth;
wealth gives rise to benevolence;
when well-provided, contention ceases.
Therefore in the eras of King Chéng
and King Kāng,
rewards had no place to apply,
laws had nothing to add to.
It wasn't that punishments could be applied but weren't -
the people simply didn't violate prohibitions;
nor that rewards could be given but weren't -
the people were all benevolent.
If so,
what affairs could officials manage?
Those who govern the people today
are like clumsy drivers handling horses:
when moving, they check them;
when stopping, they beat them.
Their bodies wounded by whips,
their mouths injured by bits -
yet expecting no mistakes from them,
how can this be achieved?
The Gànxī campaign collapsed like crumbling earth;
the Liáng clan disintegrated from within;
severe punishments could not prevent it,
harsh laws could not stop it.
Thus an exhausted horse fears no whip;
an exhausted people fears no punishment.
Even if increased and multiplied,
what benefit would it bring to their ruin?"
The imperial secretary said:
"A wall three ren high,
even Lóu Jì would find difficult;
a mountain reaching the clouds,
a shepherd boy can climb.
Thus steepness makes three ren difficult for Lóu Jì,
while gentleness makes mountain peaks easy for shepherd boys.
Molten gold in a furnace,
even Zhuāng Qiāo would not touch;
coins on the road,
any common woman would pick up -
not because the woman is greedy and Zhuāng Qiāo honest,
but because the constraints of weight differ,
and the distinction between benefit and harm is clear.
Therefore laws and decrees can be relied upon but not transgressed;
they can be approached but not penetrated.
The Book of Songs says:
'I dare not tackle a tiger with bare hands,
I dare not cross a river on foot.'
Because it brings no benefit.
Lǔ esteemed ritual yet suffered the troubles of Jì
and Mèng;
Yān Kuài prized yielding yet had the rebellion of Zǐzhī.
Ritual and yielding cannot prohibit evil,
but punishments and laws can stop violence.
An enlightened ruler relies on law,
thus he can long control his subordinates,
and long preserve his state."
The literati said:
"In ancient times,
they clarified their oaths of benevolence and righteousness,
making the people not transgress;
to impose punishments above them,
killing without teaching,
is tyranny.
Rather than making punishments inviolable,
better to make righteousness inviolable.
We hear that when ritual and righteousness are practiced, punishments are properly applied;
we have not heard that when punishments are applied, filial piety and fraternal duty flourish.
A high wall with a narrow foundation
cannot stand;
severe punishments and harsh laws
cannot endure.
The Second Emperor trusted Zhào Gāo's schemes,
deepened severity and relied on executions,
until half those on the road were condemned,
and the dead accumulated daily.
Those who killed many people were considered loyal;
those who tormented the people completely were deemed capable.
The people could not bear their demands;
the commoners could not endure their punishments;
throughout the land all grieved and none could make a living.
Thus with excessive tasks,
fathers get nothing from sons;
with unceasing demands,
rulers get nothing from ministers.
Knowing death means no return to life,
a cornered rat will bite a cat;
a commoner will charge a war chariot;
a retainer will break his bow.
Chén Shèng
and Wú Guǎng exemplify this.
At that time,
the whole realm rose together,
attacking Qín from all sides.
We hear within one year the altars of soil and grain became ruins -
where was its ability to long control subordinates,
and long preserve the state?"
The imperial secretary fell silent and did not reply.
The Grand Master said:
"A blind musician cannot distinguish black from white but excels in discerning tones;
Confucian scholars do not understand governance but are skilled at criticism.
Those who skillfully discuss heaven should correlate it with humanity,
those who skillfully discuss antiquity should examine it against the present.
What should decrees implement?
What should laws enforce?
Though Tāng and Wǔ preserved physical integrity,
Yīn and Zhōu were well-governed,
while the Qín state employed laws,
they became corrupt and were violated.
The statutes measuring two feet four inches
remain consistent across ancient and modern times,
yet sometimes they bring order,
sometimes chaos.
The Spring and Autumn Annals traced crimes to their origins,
while the Punishments of Fǔ established judicial procedures.
Now we wish to hear about the root of order and chaos,
why Zhōu succeeded and Qín failed?"
The Literati said:
"In spring and summer, growth occurs,
so the sage kings modeled their decrees accordingly.
In autumn and winter, things wither and store,
so the sage kings established laws following this pattern.
Thus decrees
are teachings,
guiding the people;
while laws
are punishments,
restraining violence.
These two tools
determine order or chaos,
determine survival or demise,
depending on how the ruler employs them.
Tāng and Wǔ practiced ritual righteousness,
clarified good and evil,
and thereby guided their people,
so punishments needed no application
as people voluntarily practiced righteousness—
this is why Yīn and Zhōu were well-governed.
When those above lack virtuous teaching,
and those below lack legal standards,
relying solely on punishments and executions,
until severed noses fill baskets
and severed feet fill carts,
even all lands west of the Yellow River
would be insufficient to hold all the convicts—
this ultimately led to the downfall
of the Qín emperor.
Not because the two-foot-four-inch statutes differed,
but because their implementation contradicted antiquity and violated popular sentiment."
10.5 Great Discussions Chapter Fifty-Nine
The Grand Master said:
"Reciting dried bamboo strips
and chanting dead men's words—
in this, officials cannot compare with the Literati.
The Literati know lawsuits occur in court but not their substance,
hear about affairs but don't understand their practicalities.
Governing the people
is like a master carpenter's cutting:
he applies his axe accordingly,
stopping when it meets the guideline.
Minister Dù,
Commandant Wáng and their peers
constrained people with laws,
decided matters with punishments,
whereupon banditry ceased and villainy was prevented.
Thus as archers rely on their target,
governors rely on laws.
Yú and Xià used civil means,
Yīn and Zhōu used martial means—
different times required different methods.
Now wishing to govern corrupt people
with simple honesty
is like hesitating to save the drowning
or bowing courteously while putting out a fire."
The Literati said:
"When King Wén rose, the people favored goodness;
when Yōu and Lì rose, the people favored violence—
not due to different natures,
but customs made them so.
Thus why Shāng
and Zhōu flourished,
why Jié and Zhòu perished:
Tāng and Wǔ didn't govern people like Bó Yí,
nor did Jié and Zhòu have people like Zhí
and Jué causing chaos.
Thus order and chaos don't lie with the people.
Confucius said:
'In hearing litigation, I'm like anyone else,
but we should aim to make litigation unnecessary!'
Eliminating lawsuits is difficult,
hearing them is easy.
Not addressing the root but attending to the branches
was called foolish in ancient times,
but is called wise today.
Using whips to suppress chaos,
using legal documents to correct culture—
this was called villainy in ancient times,
but is called worthiness today."
The Grand Master said:
"Customs aren't from Táng
and Yú's era,
the world isn't populated by Xǔ Yóu's people,
yet you want to abolish laws for governance—
this is like trying to straighten wood
without using steam and axe.
Thus governors cannot wait for self-perfected people,
as wheel-makers cannot wait for naturally curved wood.
Previously,
Yìng Shǎo,
Bó Zhèng and their followers overran Liáng
and Chǔ; Kūnlú,
Xú Gǔ and their cohorts troubled Qí
and Zhào;
bandits from east of the mountains and within the passes
occupied strategic strongholds.
At that time,
without employing the axe,
without breaking them by force,
but instead establishing rituals and cultivating culture—
this would resemble an incompetent doctor
trying to cure abscesses with short needles,
or like Kǒng Qiū persuading Zhí with rituals."
The Literati said:
"A carpenter who wastes timber to build houses
is no master craftsman.
An official who harms the people while governing
is no good administrator.
Thus Gōngshū Zǐ worked with wood's natural grain,
and sages do not violate people's nature.
Therefore axes are used sparingly,
punishments are not heavily relied upon,
yet governance is established and transformation achieved.
Biǎn Què treated illnesses at the muscular texture level,
eliminating pathogenic factors,
so abscesses couldn't form.
Sages work on problems before they emerge,
so sources of chaos have no chance to develop.
Thus stone needles remain stored unused,
laws and decrees are established but not applied.
Dealing with what has already occurred,
treating what has already erupted—
this is ordinary people's approach.
Governing what hasn't yet formed,
foreseeing what hasn't yet sprouted—
this is the gentleman's approach."
The Grand Master said:
"The sage the Literati praise as wise
is Kǒngzǐ,
who failed to govern Lǔ successfully,
was expelled from Qí,
not employed in Wèi,
surrounded in Kuāng,
and trapped between Chén
and Cài. Knowing his times wouldn't use him yet still persuading—
this is obstinacy;
knowing his困境 yet not stopping—
this is greed;
not knowing he'd be deceived yet going—
this is foolishness;
suffering humiliation yet not dying—
this is shamefulness.
These four qualities
even common people wouldn't exhibit,
let alone a gentleman!
Shāng Jūn met the ruler through Jìng Jiān,
Marquis Yìng advanced through Wáng Jī.
Thus men rely on intermediaries,
women rely on matchmakers.
But achieving intimacy and prominence
doesn't depend on matchmakers or intermediaries.
Since Kǒngzǐ didn't use intermediaries for audience yet went anyway,
he was neither a worthy scholar nor a talented woman."
The Literati said:
"Confucius was born in an age of chaos,
yet he cherished the ways of Yáo
and Shùn.
He traveled east, west, north, and south,
enduring scorched head and drenched feet,
hoping that the rulers of the time might awaken.
But the world was full of mediocrity,
with lords benighted
and ministers jealous—
who would serve as matchmakers for virtue?
Thus, even Mómǔ adorned herself and boasted,
while Xīzǐ wandered homeless.
It was not that he did not know his plight and lack of employment,
but he grieved for the calamities of the world
like a loving mother bending over her dead child:
he knew there was nothing to be done,
yet he could not cease.
So when he went to Qí,
Duke Jǐng deceived him;
when he went to Wèi,
Duke Líng besieged him;
Yánghǔ slandered him,
and Huántuí sought to harm him.
Those who deceive and harm a sage
are foolish and deluded;
those who injure and destroy a sage
are mad and cunning.
The cunning and deluded
are not truly human.
Why should they feel shame?
Mencius said:
'To observe a minister at court, look at those he hosts;
to observe a minister from afar, look at his host.'
If the sage had feigned compliance and flattered,
without discriminating in conduct or choosing friends,
how could he have been Confucius!"
The Grandee looked disconcerted and felt ashamed within,
leaning on his mat in silence.
At that moment,
those who usually followed the wind and迎合ed will were lined up in rows,
their mouths agape and unable to close,
their tongues raised and unable to lower,
gloomily bearing a heavy burden as if under reprimand.
The Grandee said:
"Very well.
A glue-hardened cart meeting sudden rain—
I ask to dissolve the debate with you scholars."
10.6 "Miscellaneous Discussions, Chapter 60"
A guest said:
"I have observed the debate on salt
and iron,
witnessed the arguments of the high ministers,
literati,
and worthy and virtuous scholars.
Their intentions followed different paths,
each with its own origin:
some upheld benevolence and righteousness,
others pursued power and profit."
"How different from what I have heard!
The Zhōu and Qín dynasties were both illustrious,
each holding all under heaven and facing south as rulers,
yet their safety, peril, and duration differed across ages.
Initially, Zhū Zǐbó of Rǔnán told me:
at that time,
heroes and talents advanced together,
converging from all directions like spokes to a hub.
The worthy and virtuous Táng Shēng of Màolíng,
the literati Wàn Shēng of the state of Lǔ, and over sixty others
gathered at the court,
expounding the teachings of the Six Arts,
discussing the roots of great peace.
The wise demonstrated their foresight,
the benevolent clarified their measures,
the courageous displayed their decisiveness,
the eloquent presented their arguments.
With dignified debate
and earnest discourse,
though not exhaustive,
it provided a general view.
Yet obscured by clouds and fog,
it was ultimately abandoned and not implemented—
how lamentable!
The high ministers knew that employing force could expand territory,
but did not know that broadening virtue could attract distant lands;
they knew that power and profit could increase resources,
but did not know that farming could enrich the state.
If those nearby are drawn close
and those afar delight in your virtue,
what could not be accomplished,
what desire could not be fulfilled?
Instead of following this path,
they focused on amassing profit and enhancing might—
is this not misguided!
Liú Zǐyōng of Zhōngshān spoke of the kingly way,
rectifying the contemporary era,
restoring all to correctness,
devoted to returning to the fundamentals.
Upright yet not ostentatious,
earnest yet not harsh,
elegantly he could be called a broad-minded gentleman.
Zhù Shēng of Jiǔjiāng, inspired by the ideals of Yóu
and Lù,
upheld the integrity of Shǐ Yú,
vented his indignation,
criticized the high ministers,
resolutely upright and unyielding—
he could be called fearless against the powerful.
Lord Sāng, drawing on contemporary affairs,
adapting to the times,
promoting methods and arts,
elevating power and profit,
and employing subtle arguments,
though not aligned with orthodox principles,
left even great Confucians and seasoned scholars ashamed,
unable to vindicate themselves—
he could be called a man of broad learning and penetration.
Yet holding the position of minister,
he did not apply the standard measures,
nor transform the people with the Way,
but indulged in profit and trivial pursuits,
not emulating antiquity.
The Yìjīng says:
'Burn him, abandon him.'
Occupying an improper position,
acting contrary to the Way,
he indeed lost his life
and brought ruin to his clan.
Chancellor Chē, ranked with the likes of Zhōu
and Lǚ,
holding central authority,
tied his purse and remained silent,
preserving himself and withdrawing—
Ah, that man!
That man!
As for the multitude of officers in the offices of the Chancellor
and Imperial Censor,
they failed to offer correct counsel to assist the ministers,
forming cliques,
promoting like-mindedness,
acquiescing and flattering
to please their superiors—
petty individuals,
sycophantic followers, how could they count for anything!"
